The conditions of colonial life on the rim of a vast unexplored continent made their wants comparatively simple. In the early days of New England most of the manufacturing was done in the home, as we have seen. Wool, flax, and hemp were raised on the farm, and the spinning and weaving were done by the women and children of the family. The women made, among other things, soap and candles, while the men tanned and dressed leather, made their farm implements, and worked at the forge, sometimes going for aid to the neighborhood blacksmith. Not. all New Englanders belonged to

The Colonies the class of small farmers. These constituted the rank and file of the people, but there developed in the cities and towns of the coast a group of well-to-do merchants who constituted the gentry and who dominated public affairs until the Revolution and indeed for a generation thereafter. This class made use of servants and slaves in their homes and in their business enterprises. Similar classes of society existed in the middle colonies.

On the plantations in the South life was less exacting, and the large landholders enjoyed more leisure. Most of the manual labor was done in the earlier period by bondservants, but these were gradually supplanted by Negro slaves. The manufacture of farm implements, shoes, and clothing was carried on to a considerable extent on the plantation. Many slaves were trained to become expert carpenters, bricklayers, blacksmiths, and shoemakers. Spinning, weaving, and sewing were carried on by female slaves under the supervision of their mistresses. Finer qualities of clothing, furniture, and household utensils were, however, imported from England. 

These articles were brought direct to the plantations on the great rivers by vessels that came over for the tobacco crop. 

The fact that the main export crop of the South was sold in England accounts for the fact that the southern colonies were in much closer touch with the mother country than were the New England colonies. The South was not entirely a plantation country. A very large proportion of families did not have large plantations, but earned a living by cultivating small farms with no slaves or a very few. industries In addition to household and plantation manufactures, there were certain larger industries not connected with the Larger home that became of great importance. The mining of iron ore and iron manufacturing began at an early date in both Virginia and Massachusetts and later in the middle colonies, which also produced some copper. In fact the manufacture of goods made of iron assumed such

Colonial Life 

87 proportions that it seriously interfered with the market for British articles of iron, and Parliament tried to prohibit the erection of rolling mills and steel furnaces. At the same time the production of pig iron was encouraged by removing the duty on its import into England. Parliament also tried to check the woolen industry of New England and placed restrictions on the manufacture of hats. This legislation was a part of the general English policy to make the colonies supply England with raw materials and purchase from her manufactured articles. 

Naval suping The production of naval supplies became one of the first important industries. The American forests yielded an abundant supply of wood for masts and spars, also tar, pitch, and turpentine for the royal navy and plies and the merchant marine, which were expanding ship-buildrapidly. This industry developed first in New 

England, but later became an important factor in the economic life of North Carolina and other colonies. The abundance of fine timber made it possible to build ships at a much lower cost than in England, and by the time the industry got well under way, American-built ships were as good as any in the world. Sawmills were set up in all of the colonies, and some of them exported large quantities of lumber to the West 

Indies and to Europe. trade

Long before English colonies had become firmly established, British subjects had resorted annually to the famous banks, or shoals, of Newfoundland to engage in fishing. Fisheries 

They dried their catch on the uninhabited coasts and the fur of that island and then carried it to the markets of Europe. New Englanders soon entered the Newfoundland fisheries, and built up a great industry that survived the separation from England. By the end of the colonial period a thousand ships and ten thousand men were engaged in this industry. Ready markets for the dried fish were found in the West Indies (to feed slaves on the sugar plantations) and

The Colonies in the countries of southern Europe. Whaling was also found to be very profitable, and several New England ports became famous as centers of this industry. 

The fur trade was one of the earliest and most lucrative occupations engaged in by the colonists. In this trade the 

French in Canada were formidable rivals, and this rivalry frequently led to serious trouble with the Indians. Furs were purchased from the Indians, who were expert hunters and

Colonial Life 

89 No new country ever has enough cheap labor, and this is especially true of new agricultural communities where land is cheap and plentiful. Freemen will till the soil White for themselves rather than work for low wages. servitude 

The demand for cheap labor in Virginia, as in most of the colonies, was first met by the development of the system of white servitude, which made its appearance early and grew rapidly. There were three sources of supply. First, there were numbers of unemployed in the cities and towns of England who desired to go to the colonies, but had no money to pay their way. They would sign a contract or indenture with a ship captain agreeing that if he would take them over he could sell their services to a planter for a term of three to five years. They became known as indentured servants, or "free willers" because they came of their own accord. Second, unscrupulous ship masters or agents would kidnap children on the streets or get men drunk in taverns near the water front and take them over against their will. On reaching 

America they would sell their captives for a term of years. 

Third, as a result of the harsh laws of the day, many debtors, vagrants, and petty criminals were sentenced to deportation by the courts. These deported men were generally bound to service for a term of seven years. In some of the colonies white servants were called "redemptioners," because at the end of their term they redeemed their freedom. Laws for the protection of white servants were fairly adequate, and their status was much better than that of slaves. When a servant's time was up his master had to give him an outfit of clothes, to which were added sometimes a supply of grain, a rifle, and even a piece of land. Many very excellent people, including women and children, came over as indentured servants and later became prominent in their communities. 

In the seventeenth century white servants were the chief source of labor. In 1683 there were twelve thousand servants and three thousand slaves in Virginia.

The Colonies

Economic conditions rather than anything else determined the distribution of slaves. Though the evils of slavery were recognized, the only outspoken opposition to the system came from the Quakers of Pennsylvania. Many of the most

91 prominent and respected merchants of Boston and Newport were engaged in the slave traffic. Great excitement arose in

Trade with Indies

Most of the trade of the New England and middle colonies was with the West Indies. In addition to fish, lumber, and horses, provisions and a few British manufactures were exported. In return the colonial ships the West brought back sugar and other West Indian products, especially molasses for the New England distilleries. 

New England rum was consumed all through the colonies and a large amount was shipped to the coast of Guinea, where it was exchanged for Negro slaves who were sold in the West Indies and in the American colonies. Massachusetts and 

Rhode Island were largely engaged in this trade. 

A large part of the sugar and molasses was being bought from the French and Dutch colonies, and so, in 1731, the British merchants and sugar planters of the West Indies petitioned Parliament for relief. This led to the celebrated Molasses 

Act of 1733, which placed prohibitory duties on foreign sugar, molasses, and rum imported into the English colonies. The northern colonies were greatly opposed to this act and persistently violated it.

In the early eighteenth century piracy was widespread, especially in the West Indies, and several notorious characters infested the shores of America. Among them the Piracy best known were Captain William Kidd, Teach or 

Thatch, commonly known as Black Beard, and Steve Bonnet. 

Kidd was sent out by Lord Bellomont, governor of New York, to capture pirates, but ended by turning pirate himself. He was finally seized, sent to England for trial, and executed. In 

1718 Governor Spotswood of Virginia sent an expedition in search of Black Beard which engaged in a furious battle with him on the coast of North Carolina. Black Beard and sev-

The Bishop of London was a member of the Board of Trade, though he did not attend its sessions unless notified that some ecclesiastical matter was to come up. Church

The Anglican Church in America was somewhat different in organization from the mother body. No bishop ever set foot in the colonies before the American Revolution, and an Episcopal Church without a bishop is something of an anomaly. To remedy this situation, the bishop appointed representatives known as commissaries, but a commissary was granted only a small share of episcopal authority. The first 

American commissary was James Blair, who was sent to 

Virginia shortly after the Revolution of 1688. Blair strengthened the Church by disciplining the clergy and by bringing over new ministers to fill the vacant parishes. His greatest work was the founding of the College of William and Mary in 1693.

The Congregational Church was the dominant one in the New England colonies, where, except in Rhode Island, it was supported by public taxation. In Massa- The Congrechusetts the Church of England had been tolerated gational since 1660, but only at the express command of Church the king, and the first church of that denomination was established in Boston in 1686. The rigid Puritanism of the early days, however, was being somewhat relaxed, and the Congregational Church suffered from division into a conservative and a progressive faction. Under these conditions 

Quakers, Baptists, and Episcopalians began to make headway, and demanded exemption from taxes levied for the support of the Congregational Church. By 1730 they had been partially relieved of this burden in both Massachusetts and Connecticut, but the complete separation of Church and

This region, called Acadia by the French, became the scene of early conflicts between the English and the French. Champlain

Samuel de Champlain was the real founder of New France. 

In 1608, the year after the founding of Virginia, he selected Quebec as a permanent base of operations and formed a settlement there. Champlain had been and the associated with Monts at Port Royal, and was founding of Quebec, now made governor of New France, a position 1608 which he continued to hold when the new company of the Hundred Associates was organized. Champlain was a great explorer. He led exploring expeditions up the 

Saguenay, the Ottawa, along the shores of Lake Huron, and in the region around Lake Champlain. In 1609 he committed a most unfortunate indiscretion in accompanying a body of Algonquins in an attack on the Iroquois. They met a band of two hundred and fifty warriors on the shores of Lake Champlain near the point where Fort Ticonderoga was afterwards built, and, with the aid of firearms, won an easy victory. Later on he invaded the Iroquois territory 97

The Colonies with a body of Hurons. These expeditions against the powerful Iroquois tribes profoundly affected the whole future history of New France, for the Iroquois occupied a strategic position in the Mohawk Valley, and the hostility of the French drove them into friendly relations first with the Dutch and later with the English in New York.

The St. Lawrence and Ottawa rivers and the Great Lakes afforded easy access to the interior of the continent, and, in Fur traders spite of the efforts of Champlain and the later governors to develop agricultural communities around Quebec and Montreal, they found it impossible to prevent the settlers from spreading over the entire lake region and engaging in the fur trade on their own account. There grew up a class of woodrangers, or coureurs de bois, who became the boon companions of the Indians, adopted their modes of life and methods of hunting, and intermarried with them. They interfered seriously with

the monopoly of the fur trade which the company reserved for itself, and edict after edict was issued against them, but to no effect.

Close on the heels of the coureurs de bois followed the Catholic Jesuit missionaries. They soon learned from the Indians of the great river to the west. The Jesuits displayed in 

America their usual zeal and activity, and the history of their strenuous labors among the Indians is a fascinating and unsurpassed record of self-sacrifice and devotion.

It was by way of Lake Michigan and Green Bay that the Mississippi was first reached. In 1673 Father Jacques Marquette, accompanied by Louis Joliet, went from Green Bay up the Fox River, thence by an easy portage to the Wisconsin, and thence down the Wisconsin to the Mississippi. At the start of their history-making expedition, Marquette and

They then retraced their course and Joliet hurried back to Quebec with news of the discovery.

Salle with his expedition entered the Mississippi River by way of the Illinois in February, 1682, and after sailing down its course for two months reached its mouth. Louisiana

The discoverer returned to Canada and from there back to France, where he received a commission as governor of the country between Lake Michigan and the Appointed Gulf of Mexico, which he had named Louisiana governor of in honor of the king. In 1684, La Salle sailed from Rochelle with four ships and four hundred men to take possession of his new province. The expedition, unable to find the mouth of the Mississippi, was forced to land on the coast of Texas. Finally in January, 1687, after the last of his four ships had been wrecked, La Salle set out for Canada with a few followers on horses secured from the Indians. 

Two months later, on the banks of the Trinity River in Texas, he was assassinated by one of his companions. La 

Salle was an explorer of great energy, ability, and resourcefulness, but as a leader he had too many traits of the French nobility. He was haughty and harsh towards his inferiors and made bitter enemies. Notwithstanding his failure to settle the country, La Salle is justly remembered as the founder of Louisiana.

The work of La Salle was taken up ten years after his death by the two sons of Charles Le Moyne of Quebec, Pierre, the elder, known from his seigniory as Iberville, and The settle- 

Jean Baptiste, the younger, known as Bienville. ment of

They sailed from Brest in 1698 with two hundred Louisiana, 1699 soldiers and colonists and landed in Biloxi Bay, where they built Fort Maurepas in February, 1699. In 

1710 the town of Mobile was founded by Bienville. He also founded New Orleans in 1718 and made it the capital of the province. Bienville served as governor most of the time until his death in 1743.

In Europe the accession of William and Mary to the English throne in 1689 had brought on a war between England

The Colonies 

Change in England's foreign policy and France. Since the revocation of the Edict of Nantes a few years before, Louis XIV had been regarded as the great enemy of Protestantism, and William of Orange, who for years had headed the European alliance against Louis, was regarded as its champion. The 

English people were strongly Protestant in their sympathies, but their Protestantism had had little influence on the foreign policy of the country during the reigns of Charles II and James II, both of whom were Catholics. In fact, English diplomacy had been wavering and inconsistent. 

In the secret treaty of Dover in 1670 King Charles had committed England to the support of Louis's schemes, and England had coöperated with France against the Dutch in 1672. 

William's accession to the throne brought about a radical change of foreign policy.

King William's War began in Europe in April, 1689, but it was several months before hostilities broke out in the colonies. King William's 1697 Frontenac, who was now sent out as governor of New France for the second time, was a soldier War, 1690of wide experience and great ability and by far the ablest of all the French governors of Canada. 

There was no leader on the English side who could be compared with him. In addition to this Canada was one colony and strongly centralized. There were practically no restrictions on the governor and he had all his resources well in hand. The diversity and lack of one government among the English colonies, on the other hand, were a great disadvantage to them from a military point of view. 

The main episodes of this war in the colonies were the capture of Schenectady by Frontenac in February, 1690, the futile attempt of Governor Phips of Massachusetts to take Quebec with a New England fleet later in the year, and Frontenac's raids into the Mohawk Valley in 1693 and 1696. The war in America was on the whole indecisive, though during the closing months the French had somewhat

the advantage, and their influence over the Indians had been strengthened. The war was brought to a close in 1697 by the Treaty of Ryswick, which was a truce rather than a treaty of peace as far as the general questions at stake were concerned. In America each party received back the possessions which it had held at the beginning of the struggle.

Within five years the great War of the Spanish Succession broke out, in which England was again opposed to France. 

The first years of the war in America were marked Queen by French and Indian raids on the frontier towns Anne's War, of New England. In 1704 occurred the most harrowing episode of the war, the night attack on Deerfield, in which men, women, and children were murdered and a hundred prisoners carried off to 

Canada, many of them never to return. Several expeditions against Canada were planned, but the only one successfully carried out was that against 

Acadia. In 1710 Nicholson, with the aid of New

England militia and some British war ships, captured Port Royal. The name was changed to 

Annapolis in honor of the queen, and Acadia became the royal province of Nova Scotia.

As we saw in the last chapter, England secured from Spain by this treaty the asiento, or contract, for supplying the Spanish colonies with African slaves. This lucrative monopoly made England the great slave-trading power of the world. Slavery began to increase very rapidly in the English colonies, and act after act was passed by colonial assemblies, especially that of Virginia, restricting or prohibiting the importation of slaves, but they were all disallowed by the home government. The vetoing of these bills was one of the indictments against England placed by Jefferson in the original draft of the Declaration of Independence, but stricken out by the committee in the revision. of 1713 gives 

England a monopoly of the slave trade This slave-trading monopoly or asiento proved the entering wedge for an extensive smuggling trade with the Spanish colonies on the part of English freebooters. As a result of these narrow restrictions her West Indian and South American colonists secretly encouraged English smuggling, and the illicit trade grew to enormous proportions. In order to break up this commerce, which was seriously interfering with her own trade, the Spanish government began to stop and search English ships on the high seas, and frequently resorted to inexcusable outrages. Thus the two countries gradually drifted into a state of war, which was formally declared October 19, 1739.

The second general European war of the eighteenth century, known in Europe as the War of the Austrian Succession, soon overshadowed the struggle between Eng- King land and Spain. News of the declaration of war George's between England and France in 1744 reached War, 17441748

Louisburg two months before it was received in Boston, and the British outposts in Nova Scotia were attacked without warning. When news of these attacks reached Boston, Governor Shirley of Massachusetts at once began making plans for the capture of Louisburg. In March, 1745, the expedition left Boston under command of William Pepperell, a wealthy merchant, and with the aid of a British fleet captured Louisburg after a siege of six weeks. The news was received at Boston with unbounded enthusiasm and created great rejoicing throughout the other colonies and also in England. Plans were at once outlined for an attack on Quebec and Montreal, and if the British government had shown the energy that it did later under Pitt, the conquest of Canada might have been effected at this time. But the government failed to send the promised support and the appearance of a French fleet in American waters put an end to further efforts in that direction. 

During this time along the New England and the New York frontier a savage border warfare was in progress, in the course of which the Indians led by French officers William committed the usual atrocities. In the arts of Johnson 

Indian diplomacy the French were usually and the Iroquois superior to the English and they had long been tampering with the Iroquois. But their endeavors in this direction were thwarted by the skill and shrewdness of a young Irishman named William Johnson, who had acquired a large estate in the Mohawk Valley, and whose remarkable influence over the Iroquois stood the English in good stead.

The Colonies 

The Treaty of Aix-la- Chapelle, 1748

In 1748 the Peace of Aix-la-Chapelle brought to a close King George's War in Europe and America. So far as general results were concerned, the contest, like King William's War a half century earlier, was a drawn battle. All conquests were restored. This was a severe disappointment to the New Englanders who had shed their blood in taking Louisburg, and many of them openly expressed their indignation against the home government. It was felt that local interests had been sacrificed to the general interests of the British empire. 

The govern It is always surprising in view of the vast territory covered by New France to recall that its population at the middle of the eighteenth century was only about ment of New 80,000. The English settlements, though con- 

France fined largely to the seaboard strip east of the Alleghenies, had a population of at least a million and a quarter. New France was divided into two provinces, Canada and Louisiana. The government of each was highly centralized and modeled after that of a French province. 

Quebec was the capital of Canada and all authority was vested there in three autocrats: the governor, the intendant, and the bishop. The governor had charge of both civil and military affairs; the intendant had a general supervision over financial matters and the administration of justice, presided over the council and acted as a check upon the governor by making confidential reports directly to the king; the bishop looked after the interests of the Church and the spiritual welfare of the inhabitants, and through the parish priest exercised a powerful influence over local affairs. 

The enormous province of Louisiana, extending from the Great Lakes to the Gulf of Mexico, had as a nerve center a long line of forts connecting the Lakes with the Mississippi. This company was regarded as a Virginia enterprise. It numbered among its incorporators many prominent Englishmen, as well as several Virginians, among the latter being George Washington's two brothers, Lawrence and Augustine.

Finally Washington set out with three hundred Virginians. 

At Wills Creek he met Trent, who had been driven from the Ohio by the French and their Indian allies. Without waiting for reënforcements, Washington continued his advance, but after defeating one body of the enemy, he was compelled by a larger force to take refuge behind a hastily constructed palisade at Great Meadows, and finally to capitulate. 

He retired to Wills Creek. The French completed the fort at the forks of the Ohio, and named it Fort Duquesne. 

The first general representative meeting or congress of the

1754 colonies met at Albany in June, 1754, at the suggestion of the British government, for the purpose of treating with the Iroquois, who were being tampered with by the The Albany French, and for the further purpose of formulat- Congress, ing a plan for colonial union. Representatives from Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Rhode Island, Connecticut, New York, Pennsylvania, and Maryland were present. Among them were several men destined to play important parts in the later history of the colonies, such as 

Benjamin Franklin of Pennsylvania, Thomas Hutchinson of Massachusetts, Stephen Hopkins of Rhode Island, and 

William Johnson of New York.

The Albany Congress adopted a plan of union providing for a president-general appointed by the king and a council of representatives from the several colonies, to have special authority over Indian relations, public lands, and military affairs. The scheme was rejected by the colonies and failed to receive the approval of the British government. No further attempt at colonial union was made until the calling of the Continental Congress which adopted the Declaration of Independence.

The British government finally sent General Edwin Braddock to America with two Irish regiments, in answer to 1755 

Governor Dinwiddie's appeals. When Braddock Preparations arrived at Alexandria, a conference with the for the camgovernors of Virginia, Massachusetts, New York, paign of

It was decided to make a strong campaign against the French at four different points: Braddock was to go against Fort Duquesne, Shirley and Pepperell were to attack the French fort at Niagara, the key to the lake route, William Johnson was to move against Crown Point on Lake Champlain, and Colonel Robert Monckton was to reduce Fort Beauséjour on the isthmus connecting Nova Scotia with the mainland.

The Colonies 

In common with most English officers of his day, General Braddock regarded with contempt the colonial militia, but Braddock's he invited Washington to accompany him as aid defeat, 1755 with the rank of major. He also took with him a force of 450 Virginia militia, most of them experienced frontiersmen, and 50 Indian scouts. When the expedition reached Fort Cumberland, Braddock waited a month for his cannon before the march was resumed. The French meanwhile had strengthened the garrison of Fort Duquesne and sent out a mixed force of about 870 men, mostly Indians, under Captain Beaujeu. On July 8, 1755, while passing through a wide and bushy ravine, about eight miles from Fort Duquesne, Braddock was attacked by Beaujeu. 

Braddock was not ambushed, as has often been stated, for he had known for some time that the Indians were hovering on his flanks. It was a typical frontier fight such as the 

Englishman trained in the methods of European warfare was unable to comprehend. The Virginians, used to Indian fighting, scattered and sought cover, while Braddock insisted on making his men fight in ranks. Their regular volleys fired at command did more harm to the Virginians than to the Indians. Washington wrote to Dinwiddie. that "two thirds of both killed and wounded received their shots from our own cowardly dogs of soldiers." After the fight had lasted for about two hours, Braddock was shot, and the command devolved upon Washington. After vainly endeavoring to rally the British, he retreated to Fort Cumberland.

Braddock died from his wounds on the march. Fortunately the Indians did not pursue. At news of the disaster British traders and settlers fled over the mountains, leaving the French in absolute control of the trans-Allegheny region. 

The expeditions against Crown Point and Niagara were also failures. The only successful campaign of the four was that of Monckton against Fort Beauséjour, which he captured with a force of a few regulars and two thou-

Under the influence of their French The fate of priests the majority of them had refused to take the Acadians the oath of allegiance to Great Britain, and the disaffected element had gathered around Fort Beauséjour. They were once more ordered to take the oath, but they again refused. 

About seven thousand of them, half the population of the peninsula, — were deprived of their property, placed aboard transports, and scattered among the English settlements from Massachusetts to Georgia. After great hardships and suffering some of them escaped to the French West Indies, others made their way to Louisiana, while a few, after years of wandering, managed to get back to Acadia.

The conspiracy of Pontiac, 17631765 Pontiac, the chief of the Ottawas, was the chief actor in the last scene of this far-reaching drama. The pro-French 

Indians on the upper lakes were not disposed to accept the terms of the Peace of Paris, and during the summer of 1763 most of the English frontier posts were attacked and the entire frontier terrorized by scalping parties. Virginia and Maryland were especially active in defending the frontier, but Pennsylvania refused to render any assistance. The Indian confederacy finally went to pieces, and in 1765 Pontiac came to terms.

PART II THE AMERICAN REVOLUTION CHAPTER VI CAUSES OF THE REVOLUTION 

War

In a nonmilitary or political sense, the American Revolution lasted for twenty years, from 1763 to 1783. Twelve years of skillful debate on constitutional questions Results of and political theories preceded the eight years of the French warfare. The French and Indian War showed and Indian grave defects in the British colonial system, which the British government decided to correct. The colonies, however, were not in a mood to be brought under stricter control, for the conquest of Canada had removed the most serious danger that threatened them from the outside and made independence a political possibility. Furthermore, the war had given the Americans military experience and had shown them that they were the equals of the best British soldiers. 

Another factor that brought on the Revolution was the arrogance of the British officers and soldiers and the open contempt in which they held the colonial troops. This brought the latter closer together and made them aware of the differences between themselves and the English. Some idea of the lack of cordial feeling may be formed from the opinions of the two noblest men engaged in the war. After 

Braddock's defeat Washington wrote to Governor Dinwiddie: "The dastardly behavior of the English soldiers exposed all those who were inclined to do their duty to almost certain death." Wolfe, on the other hand, when he heard 121

of the defeat of Abercrombie at Ticonderoga, wrote to Lord 

George Sackville: "The Americans are in general the dirtiest most contemptible cowardly dogs that you can conceive.

There is no dependence upon 'em in action. They fall down dead in their own dirt and desert by battalions, officers and all.

Such rascals as those are rather an encumbrance than any real strength to an army." 

Any one can see that with these sentiments existing it was a bad time to try to

III came to the throne. He had been poorly educated, was ignorant and narrow-minded, and was bent on following the advice which his mother had repeatedly given him in his youth: "George, be a king." His one fixed purpose was to exalt the power of the crown at the expense of Parliament. For half a century the government had been in the hands of a Whig oligarchy. In order to overthrow the Whig leaders, George III built up a party known as the King's Friends. This party brought on the 

American Revolution and controlled the British government during the war. The ablest statesmen of the age, Chatham, Burke, and Fox, belonged to the opposition, and their efforts to bring about reconciliation with America were treated with scorn.

England was now supreme in America, in India, and on the high seas. Through the genius of Pitt this magnificent empire had been created. Now the need for a Defects in more efficient system of imperial control had come the colonial to be felt. The war in America naturally suggested certain reforms. First, it showed that the old system of making requisitions on the several colonies for troops could not provide a sufficient force for their defense. Some of the colonies refused to provide the levies at all, others failed to send the full number, and none of them could be counted upon to send their full quotas into the field at the appointed time. system 

CHARLES JAMES FOX 

Second, the war showed that new measures were necessary to enforce the acts of trade. 

The Molasses Act of 1733 had never been rigidly enforced; in fact, the prosperity of the northern colonies was to a great extent based on its violation. The British West Indies could not furnish an adequate supply of molasses for the manufacture of New England rum, which was extensively used in the fisheries and was absolutely indispensable in the 

Indian trade and in the slave trade. The

New Englanders had therefore continued to buy molasses in the French West Indies. This illicit trade had been winked at by the British officials in time of peace, but its continuance in time of war neutralized to a large extent the work of the British navy. 

Illicit trade with the 

French West

Indies Colonial governors connived at this trade by issuing commissions to vessels, authorizing them to visit French colonies.

The ships were supposed to exchange prisoners and were popularly called "flags of truce." The greatest sinners in this matter were Rhode Island and Pennsylvania. The governor of the latter colony openly sold such passes for large sums of money. This trade not only directly helped the enemy, but seriously interfered with military operations by 

JAMES OTIS making foodstuffs expensive. 

Such large quantities of foodstuffs were taken to the 

French West Indies, where they brought high prices, that provisions had to be brought from Europe to supply the needs of the British army in 

America. Amherst and other

British commanders protested vigorously against this trade with the enemy and openly denounced it as disloyal. The attempt of the customhouse officials in Boston to break it up led to the celebrated controversy over "writs of assistance." 

Writs of 99 Writs of assistance were general search warrants issued to customs officials to aid them in finding smuggled goods. 

These writs were first issued by the superior assistance court of Massachusetts during the French and Indian War for the purpose of enabling the customs officers to break up the illicit trade with the French West Indies. 

James Otis resigned the office of advocate general because he believed the writs to be illegal and tyrannical, and the merchants of Boston. hired him as their lawyer to contest their legality. In his famous speech before the court he denounced the writs as the worst instrument of arbitrary power and as contrary to the principles of civil liberty and of

right. He boldly declared that the exercise of this kind of power had "cost one king of England his head, and another his throne." The case was decided against him and the writs continued to be issued, but his argument made a great impression on the people, and he was the popular idol of New England in the opening scenes of the Revolution. The

The undercurrent of discontent was growing in Virginia, too. This was revealed by Patrick Henry's argument in the famous "Parson's Cause." In 1758 the tobacco crop failed, and the Assembly enacted that for "Parson's 

Cause " one year all debts might be paid either in tobacco or in money at the rate of twopence a pound. As the salaries of the clergy were paid in tobacco which was then selling at sixpence a pound, this meant that the clergy were really receiving only one third of the money value of their pay. 

As a result they sent an agent to London to lay their case before the Board of Trade. The act was disallowed by the king in council, and several of the clergy brought suit to recover the full amount of their salaries in tobacco.

The suit which attracted most attention was one in which 

Patrick Henry, then twenty-seven years of age, appeared for the defendant. In his argument before the jury he declared that the disallowance by the king of the act was an instance of misrule and that "by this conduct the king, from being the father of his people, had degenerated into a tyrant and forfeited all right to his subjects' obedience." At this point there was a subdued murmur of "Treason, treason," to which Henry paid no attention. He concluded with a severe arraignment of the clergy, whose cause was by no means popular. The result was that the jury brought in a verdict of one penny damages for the plaintiff. Patrick

Henry and the "Parson's Cause" were both ever afterwards famous. His speech made a profound impression and his

attack on the royal prerogative tended to bring to a focus the growing dissatisfaction over English interference with the acts of the Assembly. 

A new colonial policy an. nounced

The new minister, Grenville, announced in 1763 that Great Britain would keep an army of 10,000 men in America and tax the colonies for its partial support. These troops were to be used to garrison the 'forts that had been taken from the French, to protect the frontier against the Indians, and to guard against foreign attack. There was also no doubt the more remote idea that they might be used in securing a more rigid enforcement of the acts of trade. 

In order to raise the money, Parliament passed the Sugar 

Act of 1764 and the Stamp Act of 1765. The Sugar Act 

The Sugar was a comprehensive measure designed to raise Act of 1764 revenue and reform the old colonial system. The 

Molasses Act of 1733 had placed a duty of sixpence a gallon on molasses. This duty was prohibitory and, as noted before, had never been enforced. By the new act the duty on molasses was reduced to threepence. The old prohibitive duty had not produced a revenue, but the new duty did. High import duties were also imposed on wines brought to the colonies from the Madeiras and from southern Europe.

The earlier acts of trade had not been primarily fiscal measures - that is, their main purpose had not been to raise a revenue, but to regulate commerce. The Sugar Act was the first act whose main purpose was to tax the colonies and as such it marked a new departure in colonial policy and aroused opposition, but this opposition was confined to New England and the middle colonies. The southern colonies were not affected very much by it. It was difficult to find a ground on which to assail the new measure, for, in outward form at least, it resembled other acts of Parliament the validity of which had never been seriously questioned.

Next year, however, the Stamp Act raised a very different question, by imposing internal as distinguished from external taxes. It required that every newspaper, pam- The Stamp phlet, bill, note, bond, lease, license, insurance Act of 1765 policy, ship's clearance paper, college diploma, and all other legal documents should be written or printed on stamped vellum or paper to be sold by public officials. 

The people of course did not like this measure, but at first there was no organized opposition to it. James Otis, the leading spirit in New England, said: "It is the duty of all humbly and silently to acquiesce in all the decisions of the supreme legislature. Nine hundred and ninety-nine in a thousand of the colonists will never once entertain a thought but of submission to our sovereign and to the authority of 

Parliament in all possible contingencies. They undoubtedly have the right to levy internal taxes on the colonies." 

A majority of the governors wrote to the British ministry that the act would be enforced.

In Virginia the House of Burgesses took up a consideration of the new stamp duties. Patrick Henry, who had recently been elected, offered a set of five resolutions, in Patrick which he asserted that the American colonists Henry's were entitled to all the privileges, liberties, and resolutions immunities possessed by the people of Great Britain; that the right of the people to tax themselves or to be taxed by persons chosen by themselves was the distinguishing characteristic of British freedom; and, finally, "that the general assembly of this colony have the only and sole exclusive right and power to lay taxes and impositions upon the inhabitants of this colony, and that every attempt to vest such power in any person or persons whatsoever, other than the general assembly aforesaid, has a manifest tendency to destroy 

British as well as American freedom."

With the words of the resolution just quoted, consternation and anger spread through the assembly. Patrick Henry

then delivered a memorable speech, denouncing the tyranny of the Stamp Act, concluding: "Caesar had his Brutus, Charles the first his Cromwell, and George the third " "Treason!" shouted the Speaker, and "Treason, treason," echoed from every part of the house.

Resolutions of the Stamp tives. Act Congress pose of petitioning the crown for relief. By the time this congress met every stamp distributor on the continent had resigned his position and the act had been practically nullified.

The Stamp Act Con gress adopted resolutions worded in loyal and respectful language, but they asserted for the colonists the full rights and liberties of British-born subjects. 

They denied that taxes could be imposed on them except with their own consent or by their representa- They claimed that as the colonies could not be represented in the House of Commons, no taxes could be constitutionally imposed on them except by their respective legislatures. They asserted that the duties imposed by several late acts of Parliament were burdensome and grievous, that, as the profits of the colonists' trade ultimately went to Great Britain to pay for the manufactures which they bought there, the colonists were already contributing to all supplies granted to the crown. In conclusion, they petitioned the king and both houses of Parliament for the repeal of the Stamp Act and of the late acts for the restriction of American commerce. 

These resolutions were read in the House of Commons and precipitated a short debate, but no action was taken. 

It was some time before the new government seemed to realize that the Stamp Act had brought the colonies to the verge of rebellion.

Not only in America but in England itself merchants were opposed to the act. English merchants and manufacturers were suffering from the failure of the colonists Repeal of to pay for the goods they had already bought and the Stamp to give orders for more. Petitions for repeal Act, March, were therefore coming in from many cities and towns of England. George III, in January, 1766, laid the whole matter before Parliament. After one of the most memorable debates that ever took place in that body, the Stamp Act was finally repealed in March, 1766, and the Sugar Act was a little later modified by placing the very low duty of one penny a gallon on all molasses imported into the colonies. 

Along with the repeal of the

Stamp Act was passed the socalled Declaratory Act, which asserted the unlimited right of Parliament to legislate for the colonies.

The news of the repeal of the Stamp Act was received

GEORGE III 

1766 with great rejoicing in America, but the rejoicing was shortlived. Many persons were displeased at the Declaratory Act and some talked of united opposition. But the main trouble arose over the act of 1765 requiring the colonial assemblies to make provision for quartering the king's troops in America.

The New York Assembly was the first to refuse compliance.

In 1766 the British ministry resigned, and it was understood that Pitt would be the real if not nominal head of the new one. He, however, soon entered the House of Lords

as Earl of Chatham, and the loss of popularity which this act entailed, together with bad health, prevented him from taking a very active part in the affairs of the minis- 

The Town shend Acts try. Charles Townshend now became leader of of 1767 the cabinet and, greatly to the surprise of everybody, introduced three measures relating to America which were passed the following year: (1) the New York Assembly was suspended until it should comply with the quartering act; (2) a new board, Commissioners of Customs, was established in America with full powers to enforce the acts of trade; (3) an import duty was laid on glass, red and white lead, paper, and tea. As the opponents of the Stamp Act had emphasized so much the difference between external and internal taxes, Townshend thought that the Americans would have to submit to the new revenue law because it established only external taxes on imports. 

CHARLES TOWNSHEND 

The American colonies did not act on any one political theory to the end, for in each dispute with the home govern- Theoretical ment they assumed a more advanced position. basis of the In the first stage of the controversy they denied Revolution the right of Parliament to impose internal taxes. 

In opposition to the Townshend Acts they denied the right of Parliament to impose external taxes as well, and raised the cry of no taxation without representation. As representation in the British Parliament was an impossibility, the natural and logical conclusion was that the crown was the only connecting link between the colonies and Great Britain.

What was the legal nature of the control exercised by Great Britain over the colonies? Had the British constitution been extended over the colonies? If so, by what acts was it extended over them and in what way did it protect them? Was it the colonial charters that gave the British government its authority? Some of these had been annulled and one of them at least, that of Pennsylvania, expressly recognized the supreme authority of Parliament. 

The American lawyers the real leaders of the Revolution could not find a basis for their arguments on either of these sources of law, so they took their stand on the theory of natural rights. The declaration and resolves of the first 

Continental Congress, in 1774, rested the case on "the immutable laws of nature, the principles of the English constitution, and the several charters or compacts." The Declaration of Independence two years later rested the case solely on "the laws of nature and of nature's God." 

Early American historians pictured the Revolution as a struggle against tyranny embodied in the person of George III. The most that can now be said for this view is that the colonies "made their stand," to use the words of Moses 

Coit Tyler, "not against tyranny inflicted, but only against tyranny anticipated." America had reached the point at which its social and economic development was being hampered by the connection with Great Britain, and the political training that the colonists had received in their long struggle with the colonial governors and the political theories that were current in the latter half of the eighteenth century did not incline them to submit to what they considered injustice. 

John Hancock, a Boston merchant and a leader of the opposition to the acts, in 1768 undertook to land his sloop Liberty with a cargo of wines from Madeira without paying the duty. When the customs officials tried to seize the cargo, the crew resisted, and a riot was precipitated in the

course of which the officials fled to the fort.

Additional British 

When news of this riot reached England, two additional regiments were ordered to Boston. When Parliament met in 

December, they advised that an old statute of Henry VIII empowering the government to bring to England for trial prisoners accused of treason outside the kingdom should be put in force in America. 

The Assembly of Virginia at once adopted a series of resolutions protesting against the Townshend Acts and beseechtroops sent to Boston, 1768 ing the king not to permit his American subjects to be carried over the sea for trial. 

The other colonies were asked to concur in the resolutions. 

Lord Botetourt, the new governor, immediately dissolved the Assembly, but the members retired to the Raleigh 

Tavern, where they signed an agreement that they would not import any more goods from England until the Townshend Acts should be repealed. The Virginia resolutions or similar declarations were adopted by all the Gramstorff Bros., Inc. colonies and nonimportation agreements signed.

As the settlements grew, it became necessary to provide some form of government, but as North Carolina was at this time engaged in the struggle with the Regulators, it was useless to appeal to her for aid in governing the new community. About this time two men of unusual ability, who were destined to figure in history as the founders of 

Tennessee, came to Watauga, James Robertson and John

Sevier. They were both natives of Virginia, and for the next thirty years they played the chief part in the history of the southwest. In 1772 they organized a government under a written constitution known as the Articles of the Watauga Association, thus establishing the first independent community of native-born Americans on the continent. 

The Watauga Association continued as an independent community for four years, but in 1776, at its own request, it was received under the jurisdiction of North Carolina.

The situation became so serious that Lord Dunmore, the governor of Virginia, led an army in person to Fort Pitt, and another was placed under the command of Genmore's War, eral Andrew Lewis. It was agreed that Dunmore should meet Lewis at the juncture of the Kanawha and Ohio. Cornstalk, chief of the Shawnees, had under his command about a thousand warriors, and determined upon a bold piece of strategy. He decided to intercept 

General Lewis at the mouth of the Kanawha, destroy his division, and then return to face Dunmore.

He did this. The battle which followed was more hotly contested than any other Indian battle on record. The numbers engaged were about equal and they Battle of fought from early morning until nightfall. The Point 

Virginians lost seventy-five men. The Indians Pleasant, lost only about half as many, but they finally retired from the conflict sullen and crestfallen. October, 1774 In the meantime Dunmore had already made a treaty of peace with the Indian tribes. Logan alone refused to treat with him. To Lord Dunmore's messenger he delivered a speech which is considered the finest outburst of Indian eloquence recorded. It was soon evident, however, that 

Logan did not intend to continue hostilities, and Dunmore marched home. 

Results of War

The Virginians who were with Andrew Lewis resented Lord Dunmore's failure to join them, and they also objected to his haste in making peace with the Indians, who they thought deserved greater punishment. Dunmore's

Whatever the motives of Dunmore may have been, his campaign had most important results. It kept the 

Indians quiet during the early years of the Revolution and gave the frontiersmen who were pushing over the Alleghenies an opportunity to become well settled in Kentucky.

The Boston "tea party" attracted most attention because the eyes of the ministry were fixed on Massachusetts. 

The five

The ministry at last realized that they had a serious crisis to face. They determined to put down the disorders in 

America and adopted five coercive measures: (1) The port of Boston was closed and the custom- coercive acts house moved to Salem. (2) Many of the powers of self-government which the people of Massachusetts had hitherto exercised were taken away. (3) Crown officers accused of capital offenses were to be sent by the governor of 1774

to some other colony or to England for trial, if he thought that a fair trial could not be had in the province. (4) The quartering of troops upon the inhabitants of the colonies was legalized. (5) By the fifth statute, the territory northwest of the Ohio River was annexed to the province of Quebec.

These measures were carried through Parliament by a very large majority. Chatham in the House of Lords and Burke and Fox in the House of Commons spoke against them in vain. Charles Fox's brother, Stephen, said: "We are either to treat the Americans as subjects or as rebels. If we treat them as subjects, the bill goes too far; if as rebels, it does not go far enough."

The blockade of Boston by a British fleet was drawing the attention of everybody. Washington declared that independence was not "desired by any thinking man in all North America," but he regarded the attack on Massachusetts as an outrage and said: "I will raise one thousand men, subsist them at my own expense, and march myself at their head for the relief of Boston." At the beginning of the blockade General Gage had succeeded Hutchinson as governor and assumed personal command of Boston

During the first two months of the next year, 1775, Chatham introduced his scheme for conciliation and Burke delivered his great speech. In March the restraining act

The strained conditions around Boston could not last indefinitely. On the night of April 18, General Gage sent a small force to destroy the military magazine at The battle of Concord, a village eighteen miles northwest of Lexington, Boston. The secret object of the expedition April 19, leaked out, and Paul Revere made his famous ride to give the alarm. Eight Americans were killed and ten others wounded.

The reason for appointing so many New Englanders to high position was that the army before Boston was made up of men from that section. Washington accepted his commission from the Congress in a modest but dignified speech in which he said that he would not accept any pay, but would keep an account of his expenses, for which the Congress might reimburse him later if it should see fit. On July 3 he arrived at Cambridge and took formal command of the army. 

Congress also made provision for raising troops in the other colonies. During the summer riflemen from Pennsylvania, Maryland, and Virginia joined the army before Boston, the first to arrive being a company from the valley of Virginia commanded by Captain Daniel Morgan. Unsuccessful invasion of Canada, December, 1775 Toward the end of this eventful year an unsuccessful invasion of Canada was made. A force of fifteen hundred men under Montgomery took Montreal, while Benedict Arnold led a force through the forests of Maine to join him in an attack on Quebec. The assault took place during a severe snowstorm, December 

31, 1775; Montgomery was killed and the main attack abandoned. Arnold led the other attacking column and was severely wounded, but Morgan, who succeeded to the command, fought his way into the heart of the city only to be captured through the failure of the main attack. This disastrous expedition was badly planned and not supported by a sufficient force. 

Next spring, Washington seized and fortified Dorchester

Heights, rendering the position of the British in Boston untenable. On March 17 General Howe evacuated the city and embarked his troops for Halifax.

During the years of debate before the beginning of war, there had grown up two opposing parties of Whigs and Tories. 

The English colonial officials were the backbone of the Tory

The Attempt to Coerce Massachusetts 153 party, but many people in every colony were conservative by nature and remained loyal to the British government. It is impossible to determine the number of loyalists in Harsh treatany colony, but New York and Pennsylvania led ment of in the number, and there were many in Connecti- loyalists cut, New Jersey, Delaware, Maryland, South Carolina, and

Georgia. John Adams estimated that about one third of the population in the beginning was opposed to the Revolution. 

New York alone furnished about fifteen thousand enlisted men to the British army and navy and about eight thousand militia.

Naturally the loyalists and patriots were bitterly opposed to each other. Many of the former sought refuge in the 

British lines or fled from their native land altogether. In the early days the Tories were left to the mercies of irresponsible mobs, but later on discriminatory laws were directed against them. They were deprived of the right to vote, hold office, or serve on juries and, in some states, of the right to sue their debtors, or have recourse to law for any injury. As a final measure their property was confiscated and used in support of the Revolution. In a few cases they were tried for treason, but Washington and the other prominent leaders were opposed to this and most of those arrested were treated merely as prisoners of war. The number of executions was very small.

Organiza- revolution- ary state

In every colony the people were taking steps to organize state and local governments. When the royal governors dissolved the assemblies, conventions were organized, in some cases at the call of the committees tion of of correspondence, in others at the call of voluntary meetings of private citizens. The southern governcolonies were being drawn more deeply into the conflict through clashes with the royal governors. Alarmed by the course events were taking, Lord Dunmore removed the powder from the old magazine at Williamsburg. 

Patrick Henry at once marched against Williamsburg with a company of volunteers to recover the powder. The governor in alarm offered to pay for the powder. To this Henry agreed, and having received the £330 which he demanded, disbanded his troops.

Then Governor Dunmore called the Assembly to meet 

June 1 to consider Lord North's proposals, but the House instead began to investigate the conduct of the governor. Taking refuge on the ship Fowey, Dunmore proclaimed Virginia in a state of war, offered freedom to the slaves, and ravaged the shores of Chesapeake Bay and the rivers with armed vessels. 

Opening of hostilities in Virginia

The royal force was defeated in December with considerable loss at Great Bridge about twelve miles from Norfolk. Dunmore burned Norfolk and retired to his ships. Patrick 

Henry, who had raised and was colonel of the First Regiment, desired the command of the militia. But as Henry had had no military experience, the committee of safety selected 

Colonel William Woodford. Henry was so much chagrined that he decided to abandon a military career.

An assembly of citizens in Mecklenburg County, North Carolina, met in May, 1775, and adopted resolutions providing for a temporary local government. The The revoluin North original records of the meeting were later destroyed by fire. The so-called "Mecklenburg movement 

Declaration of Independence," which gained Carolina currency years afterwards, was written from memory and is not supported by contemporary evidence. 

Governor Martin of North Carolina followed the example of Dunmore in August and took refuge on a British man-ofwar. Representing to the British government that the people of the central and western counties were still loyal, he urged that British troops be sent to coöperate with him.

A force under Sir Henry Clinton accordingly left Boston in 

December bound for Cape Fear. Meanwhile the loyalists had collected a force of sixteen hundred men and started for the coast to meet the British, but on February 27, 1776, they were defeated by a patriot force at Moore's Creek, and nine hundred of them taken prisoners.

The scene of war shifted to the Hudson, 1776 

CHAPTER VIII THE ATTACK ON THE MIDDLE STATES 

THE strength of the Tories in New York caused Washington no little alarm and he correctly concluded that this would be the next point of British attack. After the British evacuation of Boston, therefore, Washington left there and arrived in New York City April 13, 1776.

Having failed in the attempt to coerce Massachusetts, the British ministry now had two courses open to them: one was to carry on a naval war entirely, blockade the coast, cut off all trade and intercourse with the outside world, and thus bring the colonies to terms; the other, which was the one adopted, was to conquer the country by military force. The leading military men in England objected to this plan from the first and considered it hopeless, but the ministry persisted in their determination to whip the colonies into obedience. The plan of campaign was to occupy New York City and the line of the Hudson River and thus cut New England off from the support of the middle and southern colonies. Hessian to America

It was difficult to recruit troops in England for this war, as the English people were not very enthusiastic about it. 

Foreign mercenaries were finally procured from troops sent half a dozen petty German princes who were in the habit of hiring out their subjects to pay their debts. Nearly 30,000 soldiers were procured from this source, 12,000 of them being furnished by the Landgrave of Hesse-Cassel. Hence the German troops were usually spoken of in America as Hessians. Over a third of them never returned to their native land. Some were killed, but 160

The Attack on the Middle States 161 most of those who were captured settled down quietly after the war and became American citizens. 

Toward the end of June, General Howe's fleet arrived off 

Sandy Hook. His brother, Lord Howe, arrived from England within a few days in command of a naval Plan of force, and with terms of conciliation which he was campaign to offer the Americans. He sent a letter to "George Washington, Esq." which the latter refused to receive because his proper title was not recog- nized. A few weeks later 

Lord Howe had a conference with three commissioners appointed by 

Congress, John Adams, Rutledge, and Franklin, but negotiations looking to peace were now utterly futile.

The British army landed on Long Island in August, routed the American force under General Putnam, in the battle of Long Island, and drove it back to its intrenchments on Brooklyn Heights. Two days later, under Washington's personal supervision, Putnam's army was successfully withdrawn across the river to Manhattan.

It was impossible for Washington to maintain his position in New York with the British army holding Brooklyn Heights and the navy in both rivers. Certain military critics have even censured Washington for making any attempt to hold either Brooklyn or New

York, but they overlook the fact that he was conducting a political as well as a military campaign, and that he could not afford to give up New York without a fight. On September 15, Howe crossed over from 

Brooklyn, landing at Kip's Bay, and threw a line across

Manhattan Island about where Thirty-fourth Street now runs. Washington had already withdrawn most of his troops to Harlem Heights, but Putnam, who had been left in New York with 4000 men, barely had time to escape.

The British occupation of New York continued until the close of the war in 1783. The Tories at last had a place of refuge and they went there in large numbers not only from 

New York but from the other colonies. Carleton's advance The attack from Canada under Carleton had not made much headway. After the defeat of the Americans at Quebec, Arnold had conducted the retreat, contesting every step of the way. After several checked by desperate fights, Carleton arrived in October before Ticonderoga where Arnold had retired, but he thought that it was too strong to be taken and, as the season was growing late, he retired to Canada, to the surprise of both friend and foe. "These are the times that try men's souls," wrote Tom Paine in The Crisis, the first of the series of pamphlets which he issued in support of the patriot cause. The Crisis came from the press December 

19, when things were at the lowest ebb. It was widely read by the soldiers and reinspired them with enthusiasm for the cause.

The Battle 

The Revolutionary cause was at a low ebb when Washington decided on a brilliant maneuver. On Christmas night he crossed the Delaware amid floating ice, in a blinding storm, with about 2500 men, and in the early morning of the 26th fell upon the British center at Trenton held by a body of Hessians under Colonel Rahl. They were completely surprised and of Trenton, Dec. 26, 1776

Pennsylvania militia also joined him, and, on De- cember 29, he again crossed the Delaware and occupied Trenton. Cornwallis

The "old fox," however, was not to be caught napping so easily, and he formed another bold plan. He knew that 

Cornwallis had left detachments at Princeton and at New Brunswick to guard the military Princeton, Jan. 3, 1777 stores. He determined to overwhelm one or both of these and thus compel Cornwallis to retire toward 

New York. The Americans kept their camp fires burning brightly all night and small parties were kept busy with pick and spade throwing up intrenchments so as to deceive the British. British plan of cam- paign; advance of Burgoyne, 1777

The British ministry, counting on the aid of the New York Tories, determined to make another attempt in 1777 to occupy the line of the Hudson. Three concerted movements were planned. General Burgoyne was to lead an army from Canada against Ticonderoga and, after capturing it, to advance down the Hudson to Albany. Colonel St. Leger was to take a smaller force up the St. Lawrence to Oswego on Lake 

Ontario, attack Fort Stanwix, and march down the Mohawk to meet Burgoyne at Albany. General Howe was to advance from New York up the Hudson to Albany.

Advancing from Canada with an army of 8000 men, Burgoyne easily captured Fort Ticonderoga. The garrison under 

Saint Clair withdrew to Fort Edward, where 

Battle of

Bennington, the main division was stationed under command 

August 16 of General Schuyler. As Burgoyne approached

Fort Edward the latter part of July, Schuyler evacuated that post, crossed to the west side of the Hudson, and retired down the river to Stillwater. Burgoyne's advance was beset with many difficulties. The Americans removed all cattle and supplies out of the way, and, as his supplies were failing, he undertook to seize the American stores at Bennington.

Three weeks later occurred the second battle at Freeman's Farm. Burgoyne again began the movement by advancing against the American left. As the British moved forward, Morgan with his riflemen attacked their right flank, while a strong force assailed them in Freeman's front. The whole line was broken and the British Farm, Oct. tried to form another line farther back. Arnold was quick to seize the opportunity and fell upon them before they could form their line. 7, 1777 Surrender 1777 Burgoyne retreated up the river to Saratoga, and on October 17 surrendered his entire force. By the terms of the surrender, it was agreed that the British should march out of camp with the honors of of Burgoyne war, stack their arms, march to Boston under a at Saratoga, guard and there take ship for England under Oct. 17, promise not to serve again during the American war. The terms of the agreement were not favorably received by Congress and aroused much discussion. Though it was not expressly repudiated, its fulfillment met with so much objection and delay that the British troops were never permitted to return to England. They were kept in camps at various points as prisoners of war until the close of the Revolution, when most of them made America their permanent home. The victory of Saratoga marked the turning point of the war. It strengthened enormously American prestige in Europe, and led to the French alliance.

CHAPTER IX THE ALLIANCE WITH FRANCE 

THE Continental Congress had appointed, late in 1775, a "Secret Committee on Foreign Correspondence," and six months later Silas Deane, a member of Congress Beginnings from Connecticut, was sent in disguise to France of American as the first American diplomatic agent. Deane diplomacy was soon granted a private interview by Louis XVI's foreign minister, the Comte de Vergennes, but most of his negotiations with the French government were carried on through Beaumarchais, a brilliant adventurer who had great influence at court and who is known in literature as the author of Le barbier de Séville and Le mariage de Figaro. In October, 1776, Deane procured through Beaumarchais clothing for 20,000 men, 30,000 muskets, and large quantities of powder, shot, and cannon. Shipments to America were made by Beaumarchais through the agency of a new mercantile house with the fictitious name of "Hortalez et Cie." Lafayette

Early the following year, the Marquis de Lafayette sailed for America to aid the patriot cause. The French government was interested in the Revolution mainly through hostility to England, but Lafayette and and other many other Frenchmen who volunteered their foreign services at this time were moved by their admiration of the political ideas of the Americans, who seemed to be putting into practice the political theories of Rousseau,

Voltaire, and other French writers of the eighteenth century. officers

So many French officers volunteered their services to the American cause that they somewhat embarrassed Congress and Washington, since it was impossible to give many of them 175

commissions. The young Marquis de Lafayette, however, was a man of such prominent connections that, in view of our dependence on French aid, it was considered wise to give him a high commission, and he was appointed major general. 

For several months he was without a command and attached himself to Washington's headquarters. He took part in the battle of Brandywine, where he was wounded, and was later

The French people, already sympathetically inclined, were completely won over to the American cause, and Vergennes was in favor of giving direct aid, but the king delayed mainly for the purpose of getting Spain to join the alliance with America.

France agreed to send troops to America to aid the cause of independence, the possessions of France in the West Indies were guaranteed, and it was agreed that neither party would make peace with England without the consent of the other. 

Crisis in cabinet

The defeat of Burgoyne, followed by the French alliance, precipitated a crisis in the British ministry. On February 

17, before learning of the alliance, Lord North the British had risen in the House of Commons and, to the amazement of everybody, proposed a measure which conceded practically everything for which the Americans had contended and provided for the appointment of commissioners with full powers to treat with the colonies. These measures were adopted, but two days afterward the British government learned of the French treaty and immediately declared war on France. The treaty, together with the death of Lord Chatham, stopped further talk of conciliation.

From a strategical point of view Philadelphia was useless, and, as a French fleet under the Comte d'Estaing was approaching the American coast, Sir Henry Clinton decided to return to New York. He had intended to transport his army by water, but as there was not room on the transports for both the army and the thousands of Tories who had flocked to

Philadelphia, he sent 3000 Tories with their personal effects aboard the fleet, while the army with twelve miles of baggage wagons marched across New Jersey. 

Battle of Monmouth, June 28, 1778 It did not take Washington long to seize the opportunity to inflict a sudden blow on the retreating army. He had 

15,000 men, which was about the strength of Clinton's army. The attack was made at Monmouth, but unfortunately Charles Lee had recently been exchanged and restored to his rank in the American army. His treasonable conduct in this battle completely thwarted Washington's well-planned attack, and, had not the latter come forward at the critical moment, the American army would have suffered severely. 

As it was, Monmouth was a drawn battle. Clinton continued his march to New York. Lee was placed under arrest by Washington and later court-martialed and suspended from his command.

Washington advanced north, crossed the Hudson, and stationed his army at White Plains. The positions of the two armies were now the same as in the autumn of 1776, but the Americans were now the aggressors and Clinton was acting on the defensive. 

During July the French fleet under the Comte d'Estaing arrived off Sandy Hook and held a conference with two of Washington's aides. As there were only six British ships in the harbor, it was planned for Estaing to advance and capture them, but on his pilot's reporting that his two largest ships could not cross the bar which then lay at the mouth of the river, this enterprise was abandoned. 

After the battle of Monmouth there was no more important fighting in the North. Sir Henry Clinton was hemmed in at New York by Washington's army, which extended in a semicircle from northern New Jersey through the Highlands below West Point to Danbury, Connecticut. West

Point had been very strongly fortified and was the key to the

American position. The Tories made frequent raids from the British lines into New Jersey and Connecticut and up the Hudson. In retaliation the Americans performed a few brilliant exploits, which improved their morale. Let us now see what was going on in the West and on the high seas. 

By the Quebec Act of 1774 the territory lying between the Ohio and Mississippi rivers was annexed to the province of Quebec, and soon after the beginning of Conditions the Revolution Colonel Hamilton, the British on the westcommander at Detroit, undertook to organize the ern frontier Indians of the northwest for an attack on the settlers south and east of the Ohio River. Their plan, however, was thwarted by the foresight of a young Virginian, George Rogers Clark, one of the early settlers in Kentucky. Counting on the support of the French inhabitants, Clark was convinced that with a small force he could take possession of this territory. Late in the autumn of 1777 he made his way back to Virginia along the Wilderness Road and laid his plans before Governor Henry.

The governor did not consult the legislature, because of the need of secrecy, but after conferring with Jefferson, Wythe, and Madison, he authorized Clark to raise a force Expedition of 350 men for the enterprise. Clark immediately of George proceeded to the neighborhood of Pittsburgh, Rogers where he began making enlistments nominally for the defense of Kentucky. By May, 1778, he had managed to get together 180 picked riflemen, a flotilla of small boats, and a few pieces of light artillery. With these he proceeded down the Ohio to its junction with the Tennessee and disembarked in what is now southern Illinois. Marching his force over the prairie to Kaskaskia, he surprised the garrison and took possession of the town without resistance. With the aid of Father Gibault, a Catholic priest, he succeeded in winning over Cahokia and other neighboring villages.

Hamilton marched at once from Detroit, with a motley

force composed of 500 men, regulars, Tories, and Indians, to Vincennes on the Wabash and garrisoned that fort. But

The real reason for war, however, was that Holland had just joined the agreement which had existed for several months between Russia, Denmark, and Sweden, known as the "Armed Neutrality." Catherine England at

II of Russia had organized this maritime league great naval for the protection of neutral commerce. England powers denied the doctrine of the league, that free ships make free goods, but she did not care to go to war with Russia. Holland, however, had offended in other ways. Her West

These orders were ruthlessly carried out. England was now at war with France, Spain, and Holland, the three greatest naval powers next to herself, and on the naval situation the independence of America finally hinged. The end was not far off. We shall now turn to the South, where the closing scenes of the Revolution were enacted.

The British attempt to break the rebellion at the center had failed, but the ministry thought that they might at least seize and hold Georgia and the Carolinas, and, if successful in this attempt, Virginia also. After the defeat of the

After the fall of Charleston, General Gates, who had been given undeserved credit for the victory at Saratoga, was placed by Congress in command of the southern department. 

On July 27 he began moving his forces southward, the objective point of his campaign being Camden, South Carolina. Here he met Cornwallis and suffered the worst defeat that befell the Americans during the entire war. The only redeeming feature of the battle was the gallant stand made by the second Maryland brigade under the Baron de Kalb, who fell mortally wounded while trying to save the day. 

Battle of Camden, August 16, 1780 Lafayette had returned to France in February, 1779, to visit his family and to urge that a French army be sent to America.

The treason of Benedict Arnold, September, 1780 Shortly after the depressing news of the battle at Camden the country was startled by the news of Benedict Arnold's treason. Arnold had rendered distinguished services to his country, and Washington had repeatedly recommended him for advancement, but less efficient men had been promoted over his head through political influence. Arnold had married the beautiful Margaret Shippen, a member of one of the leading Tory families of Philadelphia, and this had weakened his influence with the Whigs. In July he had been placed by Washington in command of West Point, which was the key to the American situation on the Hudson.

Arnold soon afterward entered into a treasonable correspondence with Sir Henry Clinton, who finally sent Major André, a member of his staff, to West Point to confer with him. While making his way back to the Vulture with a passport from Arnold, André was arrested by a party of patriots and sent to 

Washington's headquarters under suspicion of being a spy. While not a spy in the ordinary sense, he had come into the American lines under a flag of truce for a purpose not covered by such a flag. He was therefore condemned by a courtmartial as a spy and, in spite of the sympathy which his attractive personality and noble bearing elicited, Washington refused to modify the sentence, and he was hanged. Arnold had made his escape to the British lines.
