Military operations in Virginia, 1779-1781 The major campaigns of the rest of the war were to be fought out in Virginia, which up to now had been free from invaders. Benedict Arnold, now a British officer, landed at Portsmouth on January 2, 1781, and two days later proceeded up the James to Richmond. After destroying everything of value, he fell back down the river to Portsmouth, where he was kept closely within his intrenchments by the militia under Muhlenberg. In view of the helpless state of Virginia, Washington dispatched Lafayette to its aid with 1200 regulars from the main army, hoping through the coöperation of the French fleet to capture Arnold.

Lafayette left his troops at the head of Elk River in Maryland, and hastened to Virginia. The day after his arrival the 

British fleet of Admiral Arbuthnot, having defeated the French fleet of Destouches off the capes, landed 2000 men at Portsmouth under command of Major General Phillips. 

Phillips died at Petersburg and Cornwallis assumed direct command, Arnold returning to New York.

The British in Virginia had now 5000 veteran soldiers. 

The only American army in the state was that of Lafayette, which was stationed at Richmond and numbered 3000 men, two thirds of them raw militia. Lafayette was at this time twenty-three years of age, but he conducted a very skillful campaign, keeping out of 

Cornwallis's reach, while continually harassing him.

CHAPTER X PEACE AND POLITICAL CHAOS 

Peace com- BOTH in Great Britain and in America the surrender of Cornwallis was regarded as the end of the war. Congress had already appointed a peace commission, consisting of John Adams, Franklin, Jay, Lauréns, missioners and Jefferson, so as to be ready to open negotia- appointed by Congress tions at the earliest favorable moment. Their instructions were that the independence of the colonies should be recognized, and that the existing treaties with France should be observed. The commissioners were also explicitly directed "to make the most candid and confidential communications upon all subjects to the ministers of our generous ally, the King of France; to undertake nothing in the negotiations for peace or truce without their knowledge or concurrence; and ultimately to govern yourselves by their advice and opinion." Jefferson declined the mission, Laurens was still a prisoner in London, Jay was occupied for the next year with negotiations in Spain, and Adams was engaged in negotiating a treaty with Holland which was not concluded for more than a year, so that Franklin had the responsibility of conducting the early negotiations alone. 

Lord Shelburne, the head of the new ministry, sent to 

Paris, in April, 1782, Richard Oswald, a retired Scotch merchant, on a confidential mission to Franklin. Preliminary 

Oswald carried back to London a memorandum negotiations of Franklin's views respecting the terms of peace and soon returned to Paris with a commission authorizing him to treat with the "colonies." Franklin and Vergennes thought the commission sufficient to justify negotiations, but Jay, who 197

had lately joined Franklin, objected, insisting that Oswald's commission should mention the "United States."

Jay heard through a confidential source that Vergennes favored giving Spain the territory between the Alleghenies and the Mississippi as far north as the Ohio River, and without consulting Franklin he sent a secret agent to London to confer with Lord Shelburne. Shelburne preferred having the United States in the Ohio Valley rather than Spain and he was pleased at the prospect of breaking the French alliance. Accordingly he directed Oswald to act so as "to regain the affections of America." While Jay and Franklin were divided on the question as to whether they should break their instructions and negotiate independently of France, Adams arrived from Holland and at once sided with Jay. 

Thus, in order to circumvent the alleged schemes of their allies, the American commissioners joined forces with their enemy.

The Americans insisted on three points: first, that the western boundary of the United States should extend to the 

The points 

Mississippi; second, that they should have the at issue right of free navigation to the mouth of that river; and third, that Americans should retain the right to fish on the coasts of Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, and Labrador. 

On the British side two points were pressed: first, that 

American independence should be complete and free from France; and second, that British debts should be secured and the loyalists restored to their rights. It was agreed that other points no impediments should be thrown in the way of agreed on the legal recovery of debts due to British subjects, but the demand that the American Congress should restore to the loyalists their confiscated estates, valued at $20,000,000, or reimburse them with public lands, met with determined opposition. It was finally agreed that Congress should earnestly recommend to the states to restore to the loyalists their confiscated property. It was, however, generally understood that this recommendation would amount to nothing. Great Britain herself later compensated the more active loyalists with pensions or lands in Canada. 

On November 30, 1782, the preliminary treaty was signed. 

Laurens, having arrived two days before, united with

Franklin, Jay, and Adams in signing it. Ver- The treaty gennes was not consulted in the negotiations and signed. Its not informed of the terms of the treaty until after reception it was signed. It took all of Franklin's suavity and tact to appease him. Franklin said to him: "Nothing has been agreed, in the preliminaries, contrary to the interests of France; and no peace is to take place between us and England till you have concluded yours."

Most of the members of Congress felt that the commissioners were not justified in departing from their instructions. 

They were, therefore, thanked for their services, but mildly reproved for their conduct towards France. In England the treaty was regarded as too liberal in its terms and it caused the overthrow of the ministry, but the new ministry signed the final treaty in the exact terms of the preliminary, September 3, 1783. 

Finances of tion

The revenues of the government during the war had been derived from three sources: Continental paper currency, known as "bills of credit"; domestic and foreign the Revolu- loans; and taxes, levied by means of requisitions on the states. The last source produced less than $6,000,000, since the states failed to honor the requisitions of Congress. Over $240,000,000 of paper money was issued between 1775 and 1779, but as Congress was unable to redeem any of it at par, it rapidly depreciated, and finally became utterly worthless. From domestic loans and supplies about $28,000,000 was received. The agents of the United 

States abroad borrowed $6,352,500 from France, $1,304,000 from Holland, and $174,000 from Spain, making a total of $7,830,500. The individual states, besides issuing large volumes of paper money, incurred heavy foreign and domestic debts on their own accounts in carrying on the war. The amount of the state debts was estimated by Hamilton in 

1790 at $25,000,000.

The Articles of Con- federation

The political condition of the country at the close of the war was very bad. Each state was saddled with a heavy debt and the country was held together in a precarious union by a constitution utterly inadequate to meet the demands of the future. During the greater part of the Revolution the only central governing body was the Continental Congress, which exercised only such authority and powers as the states cared to recognize. The 

Articles of Confederation were not finally ratified until 1781,

THE UNITED STATES IN 1783-STATE CLAIMS AND CESSIONS 

90° 25

a few months before the surrender of Cornwallis. They established a weak confederation, with no executive or judiciary, and with a Congress which had no power to regulate commerce or to levy taxes. When it needed money it had to ask the states. It could not proceed against individuals, and if a state refused to pay its share of a requisition, there was no redress, as the coercion of a state was out of the question. In short the government set up by the Articles was a loose federation of independent states. 

One important clause in the Articles, concerning citizenship, was later incorporated in the Constitution. It provided that the free inhabitants of each state should be "entitled to all privileges and immunities of free citizens in the several States." This meant in substance that a citizen of any state was a citizen of the United States. Such was the first government of the United States. When the peace of 1783 removed the danger of conquest, the states paid practically no heed to Congress. Its latter days were redeemed, however, by one measure of consummate statesmanship, the famous Ordinance of 1787. lands 

Four states, Massachusetts, Connecticut, New York, and

Virginia, claimed the Northwest Territory, a wide area north of the Ohio and east of the Mississippi. The Claims to claims of Massachusetts and Connecticut were western based on their colonial charters; the claim of 

New York was based on the theory that she had fallen heir to all the lands over which the Iroquois had held sway; while that of Virginia, which overlapped all the others, was based on the charter of 1609 and the conquest of 

George Rogers Clark. South of the Ohio Virginia's claim to

Kentucky was generally recognized; the remaining territory as far south as the thirty-first parallel was claimed by North and South Carolina and Georgia. The other six states had no western lands and desired to extend the authority of 

Congress over the disputed area.

Northwest Territory ceded to the United States

This was the situation when in 1777 the Maryland delega tion to the Continental Congress proposed that Congress should be given the right to "fix the western boundary of such States as claim to the Mississippi or South Sea; and lay out the land beyond the boundary so ascertained into separate and independent States from time to time as the numbers and circumstances of the people thereof may require." 

Until this was done Maryland refused to ratify the Articles of Confederation. Her territory was limited and she did not care to be overshadowed by the vast empire which Virginia claimed.

The suggestion of Maryland was not received favorably at first, but in 1780 New York, whose claims were vague and shadowy, led the way in offering to surrender her claims. 

Connecticut followed the same year, and the following year Virginia agreed to cede all her claims north of the Ohio on condition that she should remain in undisputed possession of Kentucky. Maryland then ratified the Articles March 1, 1781, and they went into effect. Massachusetts did not cede her claims until 1785, and when Connecticut made the formal act of cession she retained 3,250,000 acres along the southern shore of Lake Erie, which became known as the Western Reserve. Before these cessions the United States consisted of thirteen separate states; now it was composed of thirteen states and a national domain. The existence of a national domain proved to be a potent factor in the development of American nationality.

Massachusetts introduced an ordinance in 1787 concerning the lands which had been ceded north of the Ohio, which was adopted by Congress. Many of its features were borrowed from an earlier law drafted by Jefferson. The Northwest Territory was to be organized immediately by the appointment of a governor, a secretary, and a court of three judges, and as soon as there The Ordi- nance of 1787

should be in the district five thousand free male inhabitants of full age they were to be granted a legislative assembly. 

The territory was eventually to be divided into not less than three nor more than five states, and whenever any one of these states should have sixty thousand free inhabitants it was to be admitted into the Union on an equal footing with the original states. Freedom of worship, trial by jury, and other guarantees of personal liberty were perpetually established, education was to be encouraged, and slavery was excluded. This ordinance was a great state paper and it laid broad and deep the foundations of the territorial system by means of which the United States was enabled to prepare for statehood the vast territories that were later annexed. 

In 1784 North Carolina joined the other states by ceding her western lands to Congress. The settlers of eastern 

Tennessee, the region which had earlier been The "State embraced within the Watauga Association, lin," 1785promptly took steps to form a state government 1787 in order to be prepared to protect themselves against the Indians. They drew up a constitution, took the name of the "State of Franklin," elected John Sevier governor, and applied to Congress for admission into the Union. But 

North Carolina withdrew her act of cession and reasserted her authority over the region. This almost led to civil war. Congress refused to intervene, and when Sevier's term as governor expired, the inhabitants gave up all pretense of independence and recognized the authority of North 

Carolina once more. of Frank Peace and independence weakened rather than strengthened the union, or the "League of Friendship" as it was described in the Articles of Confederation. The Growing second article expressly provided that "Each weakness

State retains its sovereignty, freedom and inde- Confederpendence, and every power, jurisdiction and right, ation which is not by this confederation expressly delegated of the

to the United States, in congress assembled." Even those powers delegated to Congress could not be exercised without the consent of nine of the thirteen states. During the 

Revolution, when portions of the country had been overrun by the British, it was very difficult to secure help from states not immediately threatened. As soon as the danger of conquest was removed the forces of disintegration had full sway. Some of these will now be considered. State sover- Until the Constitution was adopted, it should be remembered, the sovereignty of each state was fully recognized and expressly stated in all important documents, for example, as we have seen, in the Articles of Coneignty federation. The Declaration of Independence announced to the world "That these United Colonies are, and of right ought to be" - not a free and independent state, but -"free and independent States." The treaties of 1778 with France were made with thirteen states, each one being mentioned by name. Finally the British treaty of 1783 acknowledged "the said United States," naming each one, "to be free, sovereign and independent States." Furthermore the gathering of the representatives of the states was not called a parliament, or a legislature, or an assembly, but a congress, a word used to designate a meeting of the diplomatic representatives of sovereign nations, such as the Congress of Vienna, of Verona, and of Berlin. The principle of the equality of states, which governs international congresses, was also recognized in the Congress of the Confederation by giving each state one vote. This was the reason why it was so difficult to secure coöperation. In trying to understand the present government of the United States, it must be remembered that this was the basis on which it grew. 

Sectionalism has always been an important factor in American political life. It first originated with the wide differences in the early colonists and their motives. It persisted with the geographical separation and the conflicting

economic interests of the different sections of the country, such as the manufacturing and commercial states of the East, the agricultural states of the South, and the Sectionearly settlements and later stock-raising states of alism the western frontier.  was a struggle between the sections rather than between the states, and even to-day sectional interests are a serious embarrassment to both political parties and compel them to resort to evasive statements in their platforms on many important economic questions. 

In the critical period of 1781-1788 sectionalism was a strong disintegrating force.

It is difficult for one who lives in the present age of rapid travel and communication by land, sea, and air to imagine the difficulties of intercourse between even near-by sections of the country at that time. Although ties of there was a considerable amount of intercourse travel and Difficultion in sailing vessels up and down the coast and along communicathe big rivers, travel was inconvenient and often dangerous, and communication was slow. Travel by land was tedious and expensive. In the East journeys were made on horseback or in lumbering coaches over rough or muddy roads. In the interior the traveler had to go on foot or in saddle along narrow trails through woods and over streams, and goods had to be carried on pack horses. Judged by slowness of communication, Boston was farther from Savannah than New York is from Peiping to-day. No wonder the states regarded one another with jealousy as foreign nations. 

State control of commerce was perhaps the most disintegrating of all forces. Congress had no power to regulate interstate commerce, or to levy a tariff for rev- State enue. Each state had its customhouses, and control of frequently taxed the products of its neighbors. 

Numerous disputes arose over the navigation of rivers, and some states almost came to blows. When Congress submitted to the states an amendment authorizing it to levy a commerce

small duty of five per cent on imports for the purpose of paying the principal and interest of the public debt, violent opposition was aroused. Why, it was asked, had they opposed the tea duties, if they were now to permit some 

TRAVELING BY STAGECOACH 

The men often had to alight and push the coaches out of mud holes. power outside the states to levy taxes? But after a year's discussion, all the states except Rhode Island gave their consent, and when a similar proposal was made later all but 

New York agreed, but, as unanimous consent was necessary, the proposal came to naught. 

Failure of the states to finance

The states not only refused to grant Congress the power to levy import duties, but also refused to levy on themselves the taxes necessary to meet the requisitions of Congress. It appears that some Americans at least were opposed not only to "taxation. the govern- without representation" but to taxation of any kind. As Congress had no powers of direct taxation, it apportioned the amounts necessary for meeting the expenses of the general government among the states in proportion to land values. These apportionments, or requisiment

tions as they were called, were not fully met by the states during the war, and after the signing of the peace with England, little or no attention was paid to them. 

Congress was thus unable to pay any part of the Revolutionary debt or even the interest. Had it not been for new loans obtained in Holland, it is difficult to see how the government could have continued to exist. France was our principal creditor. In addition to large sums advanced through Franklin as gifts for which payment was never asked or expected, we had borrowed over seven millions of dollars. 

The king generously remitted a large amount of interest that had accumulated, and did not embarrass the new government by pressing for prompt payment of the principal. It was thirty years before the debt was all paid. No steps were taken to pay any of it during the period of the Confederation. The domestic debt was in even worse shape, for the government securities rapidly depreciated in value. There was so little faith in the credit of the country that Congress found it difficult to borrow money either at home or abroad. 

Hard times settled down in earnest with the year in which the treaty of peace with England was signed. The war had upset trade and disorganized business. The gold Paper that had been brought into the country by the money British and French armies and paid out in exchange for supplies soon disappeared, and the people were largely dependent upon paper money. This depreciated so rapidly that the actual prices the farmers got for their produce were low and uncertain. The result was that production fell off and men were thrown out of work. In spite of the sad experiences with paper money during the Revolution, those who felt the pinch of hard times believed that a more abundant supply of money would raise prices, stimulate trade, and lift the burden from the debtor. Seven of the thirteen states yielded to the popular demand for more money, but conditions grew worse rather than better.

Shays' Rebellion, 1786-1787 The demand for paper money caused serious disturbances to break out in New Hampshire, Rhode Island, and Massachusetts. For six months about two thousand men in the western part of Massachusetts were in armed rebellion against the state government under the leadership of Daniel Shays, a captain in the Revolutionary War. They felt outraged by the harsh proceedings of the courts against unfortunate debtors. 

The movement was started by "serious, sober, decent, industrious men," but they were joined later by "the idle, the dissi-

Shays and several of his associates were sent to jail. So widespread was the discontent, however, that in the next election for governor, Bowdoin was defeated by John Hancock, who promptly pardoned Shays and his fellow prisoners.

Under the Articles of Confederation, the government was too feeble to assert its rights in dealing with foreign governments. It was unable to secure control of the territory ceded to it by the treaty of 1783. Great 

Britain still held Niagara, Detroit, Mackinaw, and other important posts on the American side of the northwest frontier. Spain refused to recognize our right to navigate the Mississippi and was encroaching on American territory in the southwest.

Delay in carrying out the treaty of 1783

When the government demanded that Great Britain sur-

render the posts in the northwest, the latter replied that the United States had failed to pay the debts due to British merchants and to satisfy the claims of the loyalists whose property had been confiscated. It is now known, however, that before these questions were raised, the British government had issued orders to the military commanders not to surrender the posts. The real reason for holding them was that they controlled the Indian fur trade of the northwest, at that time the most profitable industry in North America.

Later it was definitely proposed to create a neutral Indian zone which would serve as a buffer between Canada and the United States and exclude the latter from the Great Lakes. In the meantime British officials were continually tampering with the Indians and inciting them to acts of hostility against the advancing American frontier north of the Ohio. This policy, as we shall see later on, led to serious conflicts with the Indians.

The Mis sissippi and West Florida questions Spain had gone to war with England during the Revolution, but not from sympathy for the colonies. She had refused to become a party to the Franco-American alliance, and after the war was over, she very reluctantly recognized the United States. In the peace negotiations of 1782 she tried to exclude the United States from the Mississippi Valley.

Having failed in this, Spain was all the more determined to deny Americans the use of the Mississippi as an outlet to the The right to navigate the Mississippi had been granted to British subjects by Spain in 1763, and Great Britain had transferred this right to citizens of the United States in the treaty of 1783. Spain denied that it was a right at all, but a mere privilege extended to Great Britain which she had no right to transfer to a third party. Another point of dispute was the boundary between the United States and West Florida, which the treaty of peace with England fixed at the thirty-first parallel. Spain claimed as far north as parallel sea.

32° 28', and refused to relinquish her claim until the Pinckney treaty of 1795. 

John Jay, the secretary for foreign affairs, began a long series of negotiations for the purpose of adjusting these disputes, but Spain refused to yield. Jay then asked Congress to authorize him to forego the right to navigate the Mississippi River for a term of twenty-five years in return for liberal commercial concessions. This proposal led to a stormy debate in Congress. The New England and middle states, more interested in promoting commercial relations with Spain than in safeguarding the interests of the southwest, voted solidly for Jay's proposal, while the delegates from 

Maryland, Virginia, the Carolinas, and Georgia strongly opposed it. The proposal was carried by the vote of seven states to five, but fortunately Jay was unable to come to terms with Spain even on the basis proposed. The debate in Congress was a striking illustration of the strength of sectionalism and the conflict of opposing economic interests. 

It was destined to have a far-reaching effect, for a little later the framers of the Constitution, fearing that the new government might by a mere majority vote sacrifice interests vital to some section, provided that no treaty could be made without the consent of two thirds of the Senate. 

One of the main reasons why the united colonies broke away from England was the expectation of an era of trade 

Commercial expansion and unrestricted commerce. They restrictions were doomed to bitter disappointment. After the Revolution England refused for many years to sign any commercial treaty with them, and excluded their ships from the lucrative trade which as colonies they had carried on with the British West Indies. Even their ally France refused to grant them freedom of trade with her West Indian possessions. She allowed American ships of limited tonnage to carry enumerated goods to specified ports and take back rum and molasses. Holland made only slight

concessions in the trade with her West Indian islands, and from the Spanish colonies American ships were absolutely excluded. There was, at times, a considerable amount of smuggling, winked at by the local authorities. In accordance with the prevailing mercantile theory, European powers reserved their colonial trade for their own flags; so the 

United States, the only independent nation at that time in the western hemisphere, found opportunities for trade on this side of the Atlantic exceedingly restricted. 

The Revolution also failed to improve commercial relations with European countries. Franklin, Adams, and Jefferson were commissioned to negotiate liberal commercial treaties with the powers of Europe, but they met with little success. 

Besides the treaties with France and Holland already referred to, the only commercial treaties negotiated during the period of the Confederation were those with Sweden, Prussia, and Morocco, and trade with those countries was not of great importance. Trade with countries with which we had no commercial treaties was hampered by arbitrary regulations and discriminations. British vessels brought the products of the British West Indies to our ports and carried our products back, but American vessels were excluded from the trade and Congress could not retaliate, for the regulation of foreign commerce was reserved to the states. 

From Canada and Newfoundland both our ships and our products were excluded. Although there was no commercial treaty with England, three fourths of all the commerce of the United States was with the British Isles, and over half of it was carried in British vessels. Nine tenths of American imports came from Great Britain, mostly in the form of manufactures. The United States continued to be commercially dependent upon England until the War of 1812. 

Agriculture in New England had not been seriously disturbed by the war, for after the first few months there was little fighting in that section. The British occupation of

Agriculture and manu- New York and Philadelphia and the constant fighting in the middle colonies created a great demand for farm products, and agriculture was stimulated factures by the rise of prices then just as it was during the World War. In the southern colonies British raids resulted in the destruction of crops and the carrying away of slaves. The export of rice, indigo, and tobacco declined, but the growth of cotton was somewhat stimulated. The southern planters as a class suffered severely from the war. After the war agriculture suffered from the decline in prices and the fluctuations of paper 11111

Manufactures were stimulated by the interruption of British and foreign trade during the war. Even the wealthier classes had to depend on local manufactures and home products. 

Many small plants for the manufacture of munitions and other military supplies came into operation, but the demand for munitions was soon met by supplies from France. Luxuries, on the other hand, were provided by privateers who swarmed the seas and brought in richly laden prizes to the home market. With the treaty of peace, however, British goods soon reëntered the American market, so that domestic manufactures derived little permanent benefit from the war.

Although the causes of the Revolution were in no sense of a social or democratic character, it produced marked social and political changes. It greatly increased the number of

small landholders. This result was brought about in two ways. In the first place the large estates of wealthy Tories were confiscated, divided up, and sold to small Social and farmers. In the second place the states adopted a political more liberal land policy than that pursued by the changes British government and granted their western lands on easier terms to settlers. Furthermore, soldiers were granted western lands in lieu of pensions.

The result of the war completely overthrew the fortunes of the Tories, most of whom belonged to the wealthy and conservative classes. They left the country either during or at the close of the Revolution, and political power fell more and more into the hands of the middle class. Within a few years the new governing class abolished quit rents, entails, and primogeniture, and established other reforms of a democratic tendency. Unfortunately the new classes who came into political control in most of the states were opposed to the more conservative planters of the South and the merchants of the eastern cities. They cared little about the foreign debt or the national credit, and were not concerned about giving Congress control over commerce or increasing its powers. disunion In spite of all the forces making for disunion, there were counteracting influences which in the end prevailed. The cession of the western lands to the general gov- Influences ernment, at the stubborn insistence of Maryland, counterhad not only prevented strife over the conflicting acting claims of states, but had also created a national domain. The states could not separate without a revival of overlapping claims which would have led to interstate war. 

The great leaders, fully conscious of the peril, never lost courage or faith in the future. Chief among these was 

Washington, and he proved to be a tower of strength. At the close of the war, when dissatisfaction with Congress ran high, he had spurned the suggestion that he should accept a crown at the hands of the army, and urged his officers not

to resort to force for the redress of their grievances. He had then retired to Mount Vernon to seek a long-deserved rest. 

His correspondence shows that he kept in close touch with the progress of events, and was greatly disturbed at the inability of Congress to cope with affairs either at home or abroad. He was one of the first to realize the need of giving Congress power to regulate interstate and foreign commerce. "One State," he said, "passes a prohibitory law respecting some article, another State opens wide the avenue for its admission. One assembly makes a system, another assembly unmakes it." The need for a national commercial policy was one of the main arguments advanced later in favor of the adoption of the new Constitution. 

Recent writers have endeavored to show that the Constitution derived its main support from and was carried through by the holders of worthless federal and state securities, speculators in western lands, and the capitalistic and commercial classes, who would naturally expect to profit by the establishment of a government able to levy its own taxes and pay the public debt. These classes undoubtedly exercised a potent influence, but without great leaders who took the initiative from the highest patriotic motives, the Constitution would never have been drafted or adopted.

Governor Randolph of Virginia introduced a series of 

The Virginia resolutions early plan in the convention embodying what became known as the Virginia plan.

This plan provided for a national legislature of two houses in which the states should be represented according to the number of free inhabitants. The members of the first branch were to be chosen by the people of the several states, and the members of the second branch were to be chosen by the first from a list of nominations made in each state by the legislature. The plan also provided for a national executive and a national judiciary. The latter was to have jurisdiction over suits in which foreigners were interested, which concerned the national revenue, or which involved the national peace and harmony, and was also to try impeachments. Congress was to be given the right to levy duties on imports and to regulate trade, and the executive was to have the right to coerce a state, or any body of men in a state, who refused obedience to the acts of Congress or to treaties. Patterson held that the basis of the old Confederation was "equal sovereignty," and that the work of the convention was limited to a revision of the Articles of Confederation. The New Jersey plan symbolized a concep-

National Organization tion of the Federal Union later known as the states' rights theory. Those who held this theory believed in giving as little power as possible to the federal government. 

Comparison of the two plans

An excellent comparison of the two plans was made by James Wilson on the floor of the convention. He said: "The only difference between the plan from Virginia and the plan from New Jersey is, in a word, this: Virginia proposes two branches to the legislature, Jersey one. Virginia would have the legislative power derived from the people, Jersey from the States. Virginia would have a single executive, Jersey more than one. 

By the Virginia plan the national legislature can act on all national concerns. By the New Jersey plan only to a limited extent. By the one the legislature can negative all State laws. 

By the other the executive can compel obedience by force." 

In the discussion which followed, Wilson, Madison, and Hamilton attacked the New Jersey plan with great force, and by a vote of seven to three it was finally Jersey plan declared inadmissible. The debate over the power to control commerce also involved the slavery question. The southern states, being exclusively agricultural, were opposed to giving the general government unrestricted control over commerce for fear that the northern states would use this power to enact protective tariffs. Houses. Is it to be expected that they will deliver themselves bound hand and foot to the Eastern States?" Furthermore, South Carolina and Georgia were opposed to giving Congress the power to prohibit the foreign slave trade.

North Carolina came into the Union six months after the new government was successfully organized, but Rhode 

Island remained out until May 29, 1790, when, fearing that her commerce would be excluded by the tariff laws of the Union, she reluctantly accepted the Constitution. Union In after years the nature of the Union established under the Constitution became the subject of violent political controversy. The states' rights school held that Nature of the states had not given up their sovereignty, the new while their opponents held that the federal government was supreme. The former view was universally held at the time that the Constitution was adopted, and it is impossible to produce a single contemporary utterance claiming that the people of the United States regarded themselves as a single political body. The Constitution was adopted by the people of the several states acting as thirteen distinct political entities. The men of that day believed that they were dividing the powers of sovereignty between the state governments and the general government. 

One clause of the Constitution, however, was destined in time to enable the federal government to assert successfully the superiority of its powers. The sixth article pro-

National Organization vides that "This Constitution, and the laws of the United States which shall be made in pursuance thereof; and all 

The germ of treaties made, or which shall be made, under the nationality authority of the United States, shall be the supreme law of the land; and the judges in every State shall be bound thereby, anything in the Constitution or laws of any State to the contrary notwithstanding."

The people of the country were jealous of their liberty and were determined to see it expressly safeguarded in the new Constitution. Pledges had been made in several of the state conventions that amendments embodying a bill of rights would be pushed through Congress and submitted to the states as speedily as possible. 

Patrick Henry and other opponents of the Constitution were now chafing at the delay. Madison finally introduced seventeen amendments, only twelve of which were passed by Congress and only ten ratified by the necessary number of states. These went into effect November 

3, 1791. They are designed to protect the liberty of each citizen, and are usually called the Bill of Rights.

country 

January, Washington made a tour of New England. His visit was without incident save for the question of etiquette raised by John Hancock, governor of Massa- President chusetts, who let it be known that he would wait Washington for the president to make the first call on him. tours the 

Washington took a different view, however, of the relative dignity of president and governor, and Hancock conceded the point and paid the first call. In the spring of 1791 the president made a tour of the southern states, traveling in his own coach. He went as far as Savannah and the journey occupied three months. 

Hamilton submitted the first of his notable reports on the public credit when Congress met in January, 1790. His financial scheme embraced four points: the Hamilton's funding of the public debt, the assumption of the financial state debts incurred in the Revolution, the in- program crease of duties on imports and an excise tax on spirituous liquors, and the establishment of a United States Bank. 

As we have seen, the Confederation had been unable to make the states pay the interest on the Revolutionary debt, which now amounted to $54,000,000, nearly $12,000,000 of which was held abroad. Certificates of the domestic debt had fallen to twenty or twenty-five cents on the dollar.

Hamilton now proposed to refund this debt and pay it off at par in order to make good the public credit.

As soon as his plan was made known, speculators began to buy up the certificates, and they rose rapidly in value. 

Many people, among them Madison, were opposed to paying off this debt at its face value on the ground that speculators and not the original holders of certificates would profit by the measure. Hamilton contended, on the other hand, that the only possible way for the government to establish its credit for the future was to pay its obligations in full. 

His plan was adopted, and the old certificates were exchanged for new bonds bearing interest at six per cent.

National Organization 

The as- Hamilton's reason for wishing the government to assume the debts incurred by the states in the Revolution, amounting to about $25,000,000, was to strengthen the sumption of federal government by winning the confidence state debts and support of the financial interests. Virginia was opposed to this measure, as she had already paid off 

​ALEXANDER HAMILTON 

most of her Revolutionary debt through the sale of western lands, and the southern states, with the exception of South Carolina which still had a large debt, also opposed it. The New England states, on the other hand, favored the measure, while the middle states were divided, the commercial interests favoring assumption and the agricultural interests opposing it. Madison, who had been in close association with Hamilton, now parted company with him and led the fight against assumption. 

Location of capital

Meanwhile there had developed a sharp contest over the location of the national capital. Some favored Philadelphia and others a site on the Potomac. Hamilton now the national proposed to Jefferson, who had just arrived in 

Philadelphia, that he would secure enough northern votes for the Potomac site, if Jefferson would get enough 

Virginia votes for assumption. The details were readily agreed on between Hamilton and Madison at Jefferson's table. The capital was to remain in Philadelphia for ten years and then to be removed to a district ten miles square

on the Potomac to be selected by President Washington. 

State debts to the amount of $18,271,787 were ultimately paid by the federal government. 

The excise Rebellion

Hamilton proposed an increase of duties on imports and an excise on distilled liquors in order to raise a revenue and provide for the enlarged debt. These measures met with strong opposition, but they were and the enacted into law in 1791. The excise especially Whisky created great dissatisfaction among the people in the western counties of Pennsylvania, Maryland, Virginia, the Carolinas, and Georgia. There was a still on almost every farm, and whisky was the one commodity which these frontiersmen could carry over the mountains and readily sell. They naturally regarded the excise as a special tax on themselves. 

The payment of this tax was evaded from the first in western Pennsylvania. Finally, in 1794, a fight occurred with one of the collectors, his house was burned by a mob of 600 armed men, and rioters took possession of the streets of Pittsburgh with the intention of overawing the federal garrison. Washington promptly called for 15,000 militia from 

Virginia, Maryland, Pennsylvania, and New Jersey. General Henry Lee ("Light-Horse Harry") was placed in command of the force and Secretary Hamilton accompanied him.

The troops advanced with great formality and deliberation, so that by the time they reached Pittsburgh the insurgents had dispersed. A few of the leaders were arrested and sent to the federal court at Philadelphia for trial, but only two were convicted and these were pardoned. The federal government had demonstrated its ability and determination to enforce its laws.

Origin of parties under the Constitu- and strict construc- tionists

A great many members of Congress were opposed to the bank, and this led to the first clear alignment of political parties. As the powers of Congress are enumerated in the Constitution and do not expressly include the right to establish a bank or to charter a tion: loose corporation, Jefferson and his followers declared that the bank was unconstitutional. The Constitution contains, however, the so-called "elastic clause," giving Congress the power "to make all laws which shall be necessary and proper for carrying into execution the foregoing powers, and all other powers vested by this Constitution in the Government of the United States, or in any 

Department or Officer thereof." Hamilton held that the right to establish a bank was implied, as a bank was a necessary agency in carrying out the financial powers expressly conferred on the government. 

Washington called for the opinions of the members of the cabinet before signing the bill. Knox upheld Hamilton, while Jefferson and Randolph opposed the measure. Although not clearly convinced of its constitutionality, Washington signed the bill on the ground that where there was an equal division of opinion he would support the officer in whose department the matter arose. Hamilton believed in a loose construction of the Constitution, while Jefferson believed in strict construction. 

Since most of the Federalists favored a strong central government, they became loose constructionists, while the Anti- Federalists and Republicans federalists wished to confine the new government strictly within the limits of the expressly delegated powers. A number of former Federalists like

Madison, however, were perfectly satisfied with the powers conferred on the new government by the Constitution and

therefore sided with the strict constructionists. The name 

Antifederalist was no longer applicable after the adoption of the Constitution, so the new party formed by Jefferson became known as the Democratic or Republican party because it stood for popular rights. When the term democrat came into disrepute on account of the excesses of the democrats of France during the Reign of Terror, it was discarded by Jefferson and his followers, and they took the term Republican.

The name Federalist was still in good repute, so Hamilton and his party who favored an extension of federal control retained the term. They believed in a government controlled by the upper classes and in close alliance with the financial and commercial interests. The Republicans were especially strong in the South and West, where there were numbers of small farmers. The larger planters of South 

Carolina were mostly Federalists, but through the influence of Madison and Jefferson Virginia became almost solidly 

Republican. Patrick Henry's old antagonism to Madison and his dislike of Jefferson finally drove him into the Federalist party.

In July, 1792, Hamilton contributed two anonymous letters to a paper controlled by one of his followers, which charged Jefferson with giving the poet Freneau a government position in order that he might abuse the administration. Freneau replied that his rival's government printing more than offset his own small salary. Relations between 

Hamilton and Jefferson became greatly strained and Jefferson offered to resign, but Washington refused to accept his resignation and wrote letters to both Hamilton and Jefferson with a view to reconciling them. 

At the close of his first term, Washington wished to retire, but Jefferson's party had become so strongly organized that the Federalist leaders feared he would defeat Adams, whom they wished to nominate. Hamilton, therefore, urged

Foreign affairs were always a very important part of the work of the government in the early years of American history, and from the beginning Washington was confronted with foreign problems. As we noted on page 208, Great Britain still held forts in the Northwest which she had promised in the treaty of 1783 to surrender. 

Her excuse for not carrying out the treaty was that the United States had failed to pay the debts due to British merchants and to satisfy the claims of the loyalists. Americans claimed, on the other hand, that the British troops had taken away thousands of slaves in direct violation of the treaty. Relations were now further strained by the open sympathy expressed in America with the new French republic which soon went to war with England. 

War with the Indians Ohio

Three years later, in 1794, Anthony Wayne, who had succeeded him, defeated a large body of Indians at the battle of Fallen Timbers two miles from a British outpost.

Washington also had to face the delicate problem presented by the war which broke out between England and France in 1793. The French Revolution had naturally been regarded with sympathy by the great body and the out- of the American people until the execution of Louis XVI in January, 1793. From this time 

England and on public sentiment was divided. The Federalists condemned the course of events in France and shrank from all political connection with the new government, while Jefferson and his followers still expressed confidence in the ultimate success of the new republic. The 

United States was embarrassed by the treaties of 1778, in which we guaranteed to France her possessions in the West Indies and promised to admit French prizes to American ports in time of war. Hamilton contended that these treaties were no longer binding, as the government which had signed them had been overthrown. Jefferson, on the other hand, contended that treaties survive changes in government and that the United States should live up to its obligations. France

Proclama- tion of neutrality, April 22, 1793 Washington agreed with Jefferson that the treaties were still in force, but he held that the clause in regard to the West Indies did not apply to an offensive war such as France was waging. He also decided that he would have to admit French prizes, but that American ports could not be used as a base for fitting out such prizes for service against England. On 

April 22, 1793, he issued the now famous proclamation of neutrality, laying down a principle of conduct which has guided the policy of the United States toward warring

nations ever since. Writing a hundred years later, W. E. 

Hall, a leading English authority on international law, says: "The policy of the United States in 1793 constitutes an epoch in the development of the usages of neutrality. There can be no doubt that it was intended and believed to give effect to the obligations then incumbent upon neutrals. But it represented by far the most advanced existing opinions as to what those obligations were; and in some points it even went 

E. C. GENÊT 

further than authoritative international custom has up to the present time advanced.

In the main, however, it is identical with the standard of conduct which is now adopted by the community of nations."

Great Britain refused to make any concessions. 

The loss of this trade was a serious blow to American commerce, which found practically every port in North and South America closed to it. When, therefore, at the beginning of the war with England in 1793, France threw open to neutrals the trade with her West India colonies, American ships were quick to take advantage of it. Great Britain promptly ordered the seizure of all ships engaged in this trade and later included all ships carrying the property of French citizens. These orders violated the principle that free ships make free goods, but England had never recognized that rule. 

This policy of Great Britain caused hundreds of American ships to be seized under the most irritating circumstances. 

Jefferson recommended retaliatory legislation against British commerce, but, as seven eighths of our imports were British, the merchants wished to avoid a breach with England. Close of Washington's ad- ministration

Washington had tried to administer the government without recognizing political parties, calling to his aid men of various shades of political belief. Shortly after the beginning of his second term Jefferson resigned, and two years later Edmund Randolph withdrew under a cloud. The cabinet was almost entirely reconstituted and the positions filled with Federalists, but it was with great reluctance that Washington gave up his nonpartisan idea. Washington refuses a third term

When the campaign of 1796 opened, Washington let it be known that he would not accept a third term, and later issued to the public his famous Farewell Address, in which he bequeathed to his countrymen as a political legacy the policy of avoiding European entanglements. He retired to Mount Vernon wearied and worn by the incessant attacks of his critics. He had again carried the country through a trying period and had established the new government on a firm and enduring basis. 

Prosperity had returned, the population was growing rapidly and extending westward, and three new states had been added to the Union: Vermont in 1791, Kentucky in 1792, and Tennessee in 1796.

Congress passed the Alien Act, which gave the and Sedition president power to expel from the country all Acts, 1798 aliens whom he considered dangerous to the peace and safety of the United States, or who he had reason to think were concerned in any treasonable machinations against the government.

Many patriotic men thought that the Federalists had gone too far, and Jefferson prepared a set of resolutions, protesting

National Organization 

The Kentucky and Virginia resolutions of 1798 against the Alien and Sedition Acts. These were submitted to some of his friends in the Kentucky legislature and passed by that body November 16, 1798. After defining the Constitution as a compact between sovereign states and the powers of Congress as delegated and limited, the resolutions declared "that whensoever the general government assumes undelegated powers, its acts are unauthoritative, void, and of no force." In conclusion the resolutions appealed to the other states to unite with Kentucky in requesting the repeal of the objectionable acts at the next session of Congress. 

These resolutions of Jefferson, which were revised by Madison and passed by the Virginia legislature, expounded clearly the compact theory of the Constitution. The appeal of 

Virginia and Kentucky, however, met with an unfavorable response from all the northern states. These states denied that an individual state could pass judgment on the extent of the powers granted to Congress and pointed to the Supreme Court as the constitutional arbiter of that question, but none of them questioned the view that the Constitution was a compact. As the Alien and Sedition Acts were to expire by limitation before the close of Adams's administration, no further action was taken by the Republicans. paign of 1800

Thomas Jefferson was a man of marked individuality. With the enthusiasm of the idealist he combined in large measure the shrewdness of the practical politician. 

With few of the gifts of the public speaker, he was in private conversation convincing and persuasive. No president ever held more complete sway over his associates or over Congress. His intellectual versatility was remarkable. Little that was worthy of note in science or invention, or in religious, social, or political philosophy, escaped the range of his keen intellect. As a writer he had no equal in America, and to the present day no other American statesman has been so widely quoted.

Jefferson withheld the commissions for these "midnight appointments" as Marshall had not had time to deliver them, in spite of the protests of the new judges that they had been confirmed by the Senate and could not be constitutionally deprived of their positions except by impeachment.

Repeal of the Judiciary Act and impeachment

Under Jefferson's influence, Congress repealed the act establishing the new courts. In this the president was clearly right, for it was more than half a century before it was found necessary to increase the number of federal courts. The judiciary, filled with Federalists appointed for life, was nevertheof Pickering less a thorn in Jefferson's side. It was the one branch of the government which had not been affected by the political revolution of 1800. John Marshall, the leading Federalist of Virginia, had just been appointed Chief Justice by Adams, and on every debatable constitutional question his views were opposed to those of Jefferson. and Chase

Congress passed an act limiting the Supreme Court to one term annually, and a little later instituted impeachment proceedings against two judges. The first case was that of Judge Pickering of New Hampshire, who was tried before the Senate in March, 1804. He was found guilty of misconduct on the bench, due to either drunkenness or insanity, and was removed from office. A little later proceedings were instituted against Samuel Chase of Maryland, one of the justices of the Supreme Court of the United States, who in a political harangue to the grand jury at Baltimore declared that the government was sinking into a mobocracy. 

John Randolph, who conducted the impeachment, managed the case badly and Chase was acquitted, but henceforth federal judges conducted themselves with greater circumspection. 

The war

In order to reduce expenditures Jefferson proposed to keep the larger ships of the navy lying idle in the with Tripoli, Potomac, but he was soon compelled to send a 

1801-1804 squadron to the Mediterranean. The Barbary powers, as Morocco, Algiers, Tunis, and Tripoli were called,

Federalists and Republicans 255 had long been in the habit of levying tribute on the commerce of the Mediterranean, and the powers of Europe had tamely acquiesced. The United States had been compelled to do likewise and was at this time paying an annual sum of $83,000 to the ruler of Tripoli. This did not satisfy him, however, as he complained that the rulers of the other Barbary states were receiving relatively more. In May, 1801, he cut down the flagstaff over the American consulate at Tripoli. 

A fleet under Commodore Richard Dale had been sent to the Mediterranean with instructions to disarm any corsair which interfered with American commerce. One of his ships overhauled a Tripolitan cruiser, threw her guns into the sea, and allowed her to proceed home. He also visited 

Algiers and threatened to bombard the town in case of further interference with American commerce.

Two years later (1803) one of the ships of Commodore 

Edward Preble, the Philadelphia, ran aground at the entrance of the harbor of Tripoli. She was boarded by The affair of the enemy, and Captain Bainbridge and his crew the Philadelphia were taken prisoners. Later the Philadelphia was floated and taken into the harbor. Lieutenant Stephen 

Decatur entered the harbor in the Intrepid with a crew of seventy-five men, boarded the Philadelphia, fired her with combustibles which he had brought with him, and made his escape amid a storm of shot from the fort and the ships in the harbor. The next year Preble bombarded Tripoli and made the pasha promise not to demand any more tribute.

The failure of the expedition to Santo Domingo and the prospect of an early renewal of the war with England now made Napoleon as eager to get rid of Louisiana Napoleon as he had been a few months before to acquire it. 

He came to the conclusion that the best thing to do with the province was to give it to the United States, in order to make that country a serious rival of Great Britain. Livingston, who April, 1803 had been negotiating without success for weeks for the purchase of New Orleans and West Florida, was greatly surprised when on April 11, 1803, Talleyrand suddenly asked him whether the United States wished to have the whole of 

Louisiana. He replied that though the United States wanted only West Florida and New Orleans, he 

I would think the matter over and consult Monroe, who was expected in Paris in a few days. Monroe arrived the following day and the terms of the cession were speedily agreed upon.

In 1810 the French inhabitants of West Florida, who wished to come in as part of Louisiana, drove the Spanish garrison from Baton Rouge, and President Madison annexed the territory west of Pearl River to Louisiana. Three years later he order General Wilkinson to occupy the Mobile district. During this time the king of Spain was a prisoner in France, and Napoleon's brother Joseph, who occupied the throne, was not recognized by the United States, so that there was no Spanish minister in the United States with whom President Madison could negotiate. Lewis and Clark's expedition was the first recorded journey ever made across the continent, and it was the basis of our later claim to the Oregon country. The journal of Lewis and

But Jefferson's triumphs were over. His second administration was clouded by factional fights in his own party and by outrageous depredations on American commerce by both England and France, which he was unable to prevent or avenge.

National Organization 

For a purpose which has always remained more or less obscure, Burr began collecting men and supplies on an island in the Ohio River owned by an eccentric man named Blennerhassett, and later proceeded down the Mississippi with an armed expedition. To many of his supporters in the West he represented it as an attack on 

Mexico; to British and Spanish officials he declared his intention of wresting Louisiana from the

Union and organizing a new government in the southwest, but neither of these powers would give him the aid he solicited.

At Natchez the expedition was 

AARON BURR 

stopped by the commander of the garrison, and Burr was later tried for treason before the United States Circuit Court sitting at Richmond. Chief Justice Marshall presided at the trial and John Randolph was foreman of the jury. In spite of 

Jefferson's efforts to secure a conviction Burr was acquitted. 

He lived abroad for several years, and then returned to New York, where he died in obscurity in 1836.

CHAPTER XIV THE STRUGGLE OF AMERICA FOR NEUTRAL RIGHTS 

DURING the long period of the Napoleonic wars, the majority of the powers of Europe were involved the greater part of 

The rule of the time on one side or the other. The United 1756

States was thus the chief neutral power and to her mainly fell the task of upholding neutral rights. Early in the struggle France opened her West Indian ports to American vessels. This action was in conflict with the so-called "Rule of 1756," which had been announced by England during the Seven Years' War, and which was, in effect, that if a country closed its colonial ports to foreign vessels in time of peace, it could not open them to neutral commerce when engaged in war.

As early as 1793 England again announced her intention of enforcing this rule. American ships, however, devised a means of evading it. They adopted the practice of carrying the products of the French, Spanish, and Dutch West Indies to a United States port, unloading the cargo, paying the duties, and then taking these "Americanized" products to a European port. When several ships engaged in this practice were captured and taken before the English admiralty courts, they were released, but after 1803 the British government determined to deal more strictly with the question of neutral commerce and the admiralty courts ruled accordingly. In the case of the Essex, July, 1805, Lord Stowell held that if the products of the French West Indies were shipped to the United States with the intention of being immediately reshipped to Europe, they were liable to seizure and condemnation. This rule became known as the doctrine of continuous voyage, which in a modified form became of great impor- 264

Struggle of America for Neutral Rights 265 

tance in the American Civil War, in the Boer War, and in the 

World War. 

British

England in 1806 declared a blockade of the coast of Europe from the River Elbe to Brest, to be strictly enforced, however, only between Ostend and Le Havre. In French 

November Napoleon issued the famous Berlin decrees and Decree, declaring the British Isles in a state of blockade. This was purely a fictitious or paper council, blockade, since Napoleon's naval forces had been 1806-1807 completely crushed at the battle of Trafalgar and an actual blockade of England was utterly absurd. orders in

The British government retaliated in 1807 by an order in council which prohibited the coasting trade between ports under the control of France. 

A later order issued in November of the same year declared an absolute blockade of all European ports from which 

British ships were excluded.

In December Napoleon issued the Milan Decree, which ordered the seizure of every ship which submitted to British search or which touched at a 

British port.

NAPOLEON BONAPARTE 

We are interested in these decrees and orders because they were directed mainly at the commerce of the United

States. An American ship found it difficult to reach a 

European port without submitting to British search. If, on the other hand, it stopped at a British port and took on British goods, the only condition on which England would allow it to proceed, it rendered itself liable to seizure as soon as it reached a European port.

National Organization 

Search and impress- ment

England did not maintain an actual blockade by stationing her ships before the ports of Europe, but found it easier to station them outside the principal American ports and search American vessels as they started on their voyages. Thus scores of American ships were searched and seized within sight of their own shores. 

But this was not the only outrage against American commerce. The British also inspected the crews of American merchant vessels and seized any deserters from the British navy or any British-born subjects whom they might find aboard. England denied the right of any of her subjects to become naturalized in America. Many British-born subjects who had become naturalized in the United States were thus seized and forced to serve in the British navy.

Even this was not the worst feature of the practice. As it was difficult to distinguish between an Englishman and an American, and as the British officers were not overscrupulous when they were short of seamen, they impressed hundreds of native-born Americans into the British navy. 

Discipline in that service was very severe, flogging still existed, and there were many desertions. Deserters frequently took service on American merchant vessels and occasionally on American warships. 

Number of impress- ments

By 1812 the Department of State had on file 6257 cases of impressed seamen who claimed to be Americans. Lord 

Castlereagh stated on the floor of the House of Commons that in January, 1811, there were 3300 men claiming to be American citizens serving in the British navy. This was obviously a moderate statement. The total number of impressments is estimated by 

Roosevelt in his Naval War of 1812 at 20,000.

It is true that Napoleon's outrages on our commerce were as serious in character as those of England, but Napoleon was confined to Europe, and the impressment of American seamen in sight of our coasts brought the question nearer home and

aroused the people to an intensity of feeling against England which was difficult to restrain.

The fourth had enlisted under an assumed name and turned out to be a British subject. As the Chesapeake was proceeding towards the capes, the British war vessel Leopard approached and fired a gun as a signal that she wished to communicate with the ship. Her captain said that he had dispatches and sent British officers aboard. The dispatches were orders from his commanding officer to search the Chesapeake for deserters. 

Commodore James Barron of the Chesapeake refused to allow his ship to be searched and, as he had not called his men to quarters, tried to gain time, but before the guns could be manned the Leopard fired three broadsides into the Chesapeake. Barron hauled down his flag, whereupon the British boarded the ship, mustered the crew, and seized the four deserters, but refused to receive the surrender of the ship. 

Barron was later tried by court-martial and suspended for five years without pay for neglect of duty in failing to call his men to quarters when the Leopard approached.

The president at once proclaimed American ports closed to British warships and forbade the furnishing of supplies to them. He also called a special session of Congress. The Em-

JAMES MADISON 

It is difficult to follow the tortuous policy pursued by Napoleon at this period, but his object was to deceive President Madison by pretending to repeal his decrees and to force a war between the United States and England. The Non-

National Organization intercourse Act, having failed to bring either England or France to terms, was repealed in 1810, with the proviso that if either one of these powers should withdraw its orders or decrees, the act should be revived against the other. First sugges- tion of an "economic boycott."

The attempt to bring England and France to terms by an "economic boycott" was an interesting experiment and deserved better success. But for its practical nullification by New England it might have succeeded. The idea was one of Jefferson's many contributions to political thought. Fifteen years before, when he was secretary of state, he had made a similar proposal. He wrote to Madison in 1793 that instead of declaring war on England for her violation of neutral rights he hoped Congress would exclude her ships and goods from American ports, adding: "I think it will furnish us a happy opportunity of setting another example to the world, by shewing that nations may be brought to do justice by appeals to their interests as well as by appeals to arms." More than a hundred years later the principle of the economic boycott was introduced in the Covenant of the 

League of Nations.

In spite of all these retaliatory measures, British ships continued to impress American seamen, and in May, 1811, Cap- Encounter between the President and the

Broadsides were then exchanged and the Little Belt was seriously injured. Indians of Tippecanoe, 1811 Another grievance against Great Britain arose out of the aid and encouragement given by the Canadian authorities to the Indians of the Northwest. National Organization 

Madison finally sent a message to Congress, June 1, 1812, which enumerated the following grievances against England: the insolent conduct of British cruisers in searching American vessels on American coasts, the impressment of American seamen, the orders in council, the seizure of 

American ships, and the intrigues with the Indians of the Northwest. 

On June 18 Congress formally declared war. 

Five days later the

British government, acting under pressure of the manufacturing and commercial interests, withdrew the orders in council, but this was before the days of ocean cables, and the news came too late. The impressment question was, moreover, the main cause of the popular feeling against England, and that alone was enough to justify war. Reëlection 1812 

HENRY CLAY 

Madison had already been renominated for the presidency by the Republicans and De Witt Clinton by the Federalists. 

The Federalists still hoped to stop the war and the of Madison, campaign was fought out on this issue. The close alliance of the South and West, aided by the votes of Pennsylvania, carried the day, and Madison was reëlected by 128 electoral votes to Clinton's 89. His majority was much smaller than had been expected and without the votes of Pennsylvania he would have been defeated.

If the war was fought for sailors' rights, as has so often been stated, why were the maritime states of the North and East so opposed to it and the South and West so enthusiastic for it? Historians are not in agreement upon this question. 

The commercial interests were still dependent upon British trade and therefore tended to ignore impressments. The

Struggle of America for Neutral Rights 273 

people of the West, on the other hand, had no such reason to endure British insults to the flag. Moreover, this section had suffered severely from Indian raids encouraged by the British and was eager for the conquest of Canada as the best way of putting an end to them. Furthermore, the West always believed in expansion and had visions of dominating the entire North American continent.

CHAPTER XV THE SECOND WAR WITH ENGLAND 

THE United States realized that it was not prepared to combat the entire military and naval strength of Great Britain. Nevertheless, since the latter was at this unprepared, time engaged in a death struggle with Napoleon, it was generally believed that the conquest of Canada would be an easy task and that a severe blow could be dealt to British commerce. As the American army and navy were both small, much reliance was placed on volunteers for the conquest of Canada and on privateers for the war on British commerce. "On to Canada" was the general cry. The first invading column, of 2500 men under General Hull, crossed over from Detroit in July, 1812, but was driven back and compelled to surrender Detroit. "On to 

Canada "

During that same year two other expeditions against 

Canada failed. One under General Dearborn advanced through New York against Montreal, but met with so many delays that it finally went into winter quarters at Plattsburg without having accomplished anything. The third movement, by way of Niagara, was repulsed at Queenstown with a loss of 1000 men. It was now evident that "on to Canada" was not an easy task for raw recruits and untrained militia. 

The naval warfare of that year was a very different story from that on land. In view of the slim resources of the 

Americans and the tremendous prestige of the the success of the former filled them with pride and attracted the attention of all the world. At the beginning of the war the United States had in commission three forty-four-gun frigates, United States, The war on the sea, British navy, 1812 274

The American coast blockaded,

Not until the early spring of 1813 did Great Britain put forth her full naval strength. Admiral Sir John

Warren took Halifax as the base of operations. 

He had under his command eleven ships-of-theline, thirty-four frigates, thirty-eight sloops, and other vessels, making a total of ninety-seven. His mission 

March, 1813

was partly diplomatic, and he sent to President Madison proposals of peace. The president replied that the abandonment of impressment was an indispensable condition, but, as the British were not willing to concede this, the negotiations came to naught.

Admiral Warren proceeded to blockade the coast from Narragansett Bay to Florida, bottling up naval ships and merchant vessels, and capturing those that were rash enough to venture out. The New England coast was not strictly blockaded until the following year, as the people there were violently opposed to the administration of Madison and were willing to supply the British naval station at Halifax with provisions.

One of the most notable cruises of the war was made by the United States frigate Essex under Captain David Porter. A month after the war broke out she put to sea and The cruise during the remainder of the year she took ten of the Essex, 1812-1814 prizes and 423 men. She next went to the South 

Atlantic and, rounding Cape Horn, captured a number of British whalers off the Galapagos Islands. She was finally captured in Valparaiso harbor in March, 1814. With Porter was David Farragut, then a midshipman thirteen years old. 

These incidents in remote waters had little or no effect on the outcome of the contest, however gratifying they were to 

American pride.

Not only the regular ships of the navy but privateers made brilliant records. Ships were fitted out and armed at great expense to prey on British commerce, and Privateers a successful cruise brought great profits to the and prizes owners and shareholders who had taken stock in the enterprise. Nearly five hundred privateers were granted commissions during the war. Of these Maryland furnished the largest number; New York and Philadelphia came next; the Massachusetts coast towns and Charleston, South Carolina, also sent out a number.

National Organization 

It is almost impossible to give the exact number of captures on either side. During the earlier part of the war the Americans took more prizes, but after the blockade was established the British figures were swelled by bay craft and oyster boats of little value. There were probably as many as 

1700 prizes captured on each side, including the work of both privateers and war vessels. American commerce

After the battle of Leipzig and the capitulation of Paris, general peace was signed in Europe, May 30, 1814, and

Napoleon was sent to the island of Elba. England was now free to direct all her resources against driven from America. Accordingly she ordered a stricter blockade of the American coast, including New England, which had hitherto been largely spared. She was the seas now able to place a strong division, including a shipof-the-line, on blockade before each port. The 

American frigates were thus successfully excluded from the ocean. When the war ended, the only 

American vessels on the seas were the Constitution, three sloops, and one brig.

When, therefore, we consider the effect of the war on the commerce of the two countries, we see that 

England had the over whelming advantage. In fact, American commerce was practically driven from the seas. Exports from the United 

States in 1807, the last year of unrestricted commerce, were $108,000,000; in 1814 they amounted to less than $7,000,000.

The expedition against New Orleans took place later in the same year when a force of over 10,000 men, composed mainly of Wellington's seasoned troops, was sent to the mouth of the Mississippi River. Andrew Jackson, of New who had recently been appointed major general and placed in command of the Southwest, was at Mobile, which had been lately occupied by American troops, when he learned that the British were about to attack New Orleans. Calling on the militia of Kentucky,

Tennessee, and Georgia to follow him, he at once set out for 1815

National Organization the scene of action and threw himself with great energy into the work of preparing the city for defense. 

Jackson fortified himself strongly about five miles below New Orleans. He had with him about 4000 troops, mostly militia, but expert marksmen. The British commander, General Pakenham, advanced cautiously on January 8, 1815,

ANDREW JACKSON 

with a division of 5000 men, and tried to carry the American trenches, but he was repulsed with heavy losses, mainly through the superiority of the American riflemen, who picked off the British with unerring accuracy.

Three of the British major generals were killed among them Pakenham, and their total losses were over 2000, while 

Americans lost only 71. the Jackson's brilliant victory at the battle of New 

Orleans caused great rejoicing throughout the country, but it did not affect the outcome of the war, for the treaty of peace had been signed at

Ghent two weeks before it was fought. Its effect on the course of American history, however, was far-reaching, for it brought the West into greater prominence and made Andrew Jackson the military hero and political leader of that section. 

This portrait, which is in the New York City Hall, shows him as a major general. 

For long weeks the American peace commissioners, John
