CHAPTER XIX OPPOSITION TO SLAVERY IN THE TERRITORIES 

slavery

THERE had been an effort froin the Missouri Compromise to the beginning of the Mexican War to exclude all direct discussion of slavery from the halls of Congress. Early op- 

Outside Congress, however, an active antislavery position to propaganda was being carried on which was now assuming formidable proportions. The first opposition to slavery came from the Quakers of Pennsylvania in the eighteenth century. At the time of the Revolution, Jefferson, Mason, and most of the leading statesmen of Virginia also regarded slavery as a moral and social evil and looked forward to a not far distant emancipation. 

The question which none could solve was what to do with the emancipated slave. The American Colonization

Society, formed in 1816, made an earnest attempt to colonize the free Negroes in Africa. The plan was officially indorsed by Virginia, Georgia, Maryland, Tennessee, and Vermont, and by the United States government, which extended its protection to Liberia, the territory on the west coast of Africa selected by the society as the site for its colony. Several thousand Negroes were sent over to Liberia, but many succumbed to the African fevers, and this would have deterred others from going even had the society been able to raise the necessary funds. The colonization scheme was a noble effort on the part of Southern statesmen and Northern philanthropists to solve the problem. Among the presidents of the society were Monroe, Madison, Marshall, and Henry 

Clay, who was one of its most earnest promoters. 353

The abolition The United States was not the only country with a slavery problem, as the movement against slavery had become world-wide. In 1833, after a long and memorable contest, the British Parliament movement abolished slavery in the British West Indies and appropriated $100,000,000 to compensate the owners. Within the next twenty years most of the other European countries abolished slavery in their colonies. In 1831 William Lloyd 

WILLIAM LLOYD GARRISON 

Garrison founded in Boston the Liberator, a paper devoted to the immediate and unconditional abolition of slavery in the United States, and in 1833 the American Antislavery Society was organized with the same object in view. 

Since the Constitution protected slavery, Garrison denounced the Union as "a covenant with death" and the Constitution as "an agreement with hell."

The abolitionists tried to arouse public opinion in the 

North and to distribute 

South in order to 

Later the "Underpurpose of enabling propaganda among the slaves of the create in them a longing for liberty. ground Railroad" was organized for the slaves to escape from their masters. Secret agents conducted them at night from point to point, supplying their wants and concealing them during the day at appointed stations, until they were safely over the Ohio River or across the border in Canada.

The people in the South were of course indignant at the methods used by Garrison in his slavery crusade, and when,

Opposition to Slavery in the Territories 355 surrection, 1831, and the debate on slavery in a few months after the founding of the Liberator, a slave insurrection broke out in Virginia, it was generally believed that it had been instigated by the abolitionists. In The South- 

1831, Nat Turner, a Negro preacher of Southamp- ampton inton County, with the assistance of a small band of slaves, suddenly began murdering the white people in his community, and before steps could the Virginia be taken to arrest them sixty-one persons, mostly legislature women and children, had been barbarously slain. This was the most serious slave insurrection that had ever been known in the South and it led to a memorable discussion of the whole slavery question at the next session of the Virginia legislature. 

In January, 1832, Thomas Jefferson Randolph, a grandson of

Jefferson, proposed a plan for freeing all slaves born after July 4, 1840, and for removing them beyond the limits of the United States. The debate lasted for weeks and attracted the attention of the entire country, but the committee to whom the plan was referred finally reported against it by a majority of one vote.

The prob- lem of the free Negro

Thousands of slaves in the northern tier of slave states were freed by the voluntary action of their masters. Between the Revolution and the Civil War, more slaves were freed voluntarily in Virginia alone than were freed in the entire North by statute. 

But the presence of the free Negro in slave communities was a serious problem, and most of the southern states had to restrict emancipation, forbidding it altogether unless the freed men were removed beyond the limits of the state. 

John Randolph, who died in 1833, provided in his will for the emancipation of all his slaves and directed his executors to purchase lands for them north of the Ohio. His executors bought a large tract of land in Ohio and took the Negroes on the long journey, but at the border of the county in which the land lay they were met by men armed with rifles who did not allow them to enter. Indiana and Illinois passed laws pro-

hibiting free Negroes and mulattoes from settling within their borders. If the free Negro was considered a menace in the free states, it is not strange that he was so considered in the slave states.

Effects of 

Garrison's crusade north and south

The effect of the abolition crusade was to throw the South on the defensive, and as the Southern members of Congress could not secure legislation excluding abolition propaganda from the mails, the southern states enacted stricter laws regulating slavery, placing the slaves under closer surveillance and forbidding their masters to teach them to read. Garrison's movement met at first with violent opposition in the North. 

Upon one occasion he narrowly escaped death at the hands of a mob in the streets of Boston. Elijah P. Lovejoy, the editor of an abolitionist paper in Illinois, was actually killed by a mob in the town where he published his paper. 

So many antislavery petitions were presented to Congress by the abolitionists that finally in 1836 the House passed a resolution to table all such petitions without a reading. John 

Quincy Adams considered this action a denial of the constitutional right of petition and he soon became the channel through which petitions were presented. Day after day he would rise in his seat and present petition after petition, but the speaker never let him get beyond the words "abolition of slavery." As the number of petitions did not diminish and as the so-called "gag rule" merely gave the abolitionists a standing ground of complaint, it was repealed in 1844. The abolition agitation soon carried the slavery discussion into the churches, and about this time several of the religious denominations became divided into Northern and Southern branches.

The intolerance of the antislavery agitators aroused the sensitiveness of the Southern people and drove them first into an apologetic position and later into an open defense of slavery. William Gilmore Simms wrote in 1852: "Twenty

Opposition to Slavery in the Territories 357 

years ago, few persons in the South undertook to justify Negro slavery, except on the score of necessity. Now, very few persons in the same region question their per- Defense of fect right to the labor of their slaves, and slavery more, their moral obligation to keep them still subject, as slaves, and to compel their labor, so long as they remain the inferior beings which we now find them, and which they seem to have been from the beginning. This is a great good, the fruit wholly of hostile pressure." 

WILLIAM GILMORE SIMMS 

The defenders of slavery presented various arguments.

Some justified it on grounds of economic necessity, others on grounds of the racial inferiority of the Negro, and others on the ground that it was recognized in both the Old and the New 

Testaments. The economic argument became especially popular during the forties. It was in brief that the prosperity of the South was dependent upon staple crops produced by Negro labor and that Negro labor was far more efficient under the slavery system than it would be under the wage system. 

This was doubtless true at that time. To the statesmen and philanthropists of the South, however, the inferiority of the Negro was the main reason for keeping him in bondage. To their minds the Negro problem loomed up larger than the slavery problem. The abolitionist believed that by freeing the slave the problem would be solved. The Southerner, on the other hand, believed that the free Negro would present a far more serious problem socially and politically than the slave.

Calhoun's

The bitterness aroused by the agitation rendered any statesmanlike solution of the problem hopeless. National emancipation, even with compensation to the position slave owners, would have produced an industrial revolution, the outcome of which no one could foresee, besides leaving the race problem unsolved. Calhoun and other 

Southern leaders saw what course the agitation was taking.

In a paper written by Calhoun, signed by forty-eight senators and representatives, and issued in January, 1849, we find these prophetic words: "If [emancipation] should be effected, it will be through the agency of the Federal Government, controlled by the dominant power of the Northern States of the Confederacy, against the resistance and struggle of the Southern. It can then only be effected by the prostration of the white race; and that would necessarily engender the bitterest feelings of hostility between them and the North. 

But the reverse would be the case between the blacks of the South and the people of the North. Owing their emancipation to them, they would regard them as friends, guardians, and patrons, and centre, accordingly, all their sympathy in them. The people of the North would not fail to reciprocate and to favor them, instead of the whites. Under the influence of such feelings, and impelled by fanaticism and love of power, they would not stop at emancipation. Another step would be taken to raise them to a political and social equality with their former owners, by giving them the right of voting and holding public offices under the Federal Government. 

But when once raised to an equality, they would become the fast political associates of the North, acting and voting with them on all questions, and by this political union between them, holding the white race at the South in complete subjection. The blacks, and the profligate whites that might unite with them, would become the principal recipients of federal offices and patronage, and would, in consequence, be raised above the whites of the South in the political and social scale." ...

Opposition to Slavery in the Territories 359

A more accurate picture of what actually took place during the period of Reconstruction would be difficult to draw. 

Calhoun's only mistake was in supposing that the white people of the South would under any conditions submit indefinitely to Negro rule. In Calhoun's mind there were in 

1850 two alternatives open to the Southern people, either to preserve the balance between the sections in the Senate or to form a separate confederacy. 

During the Mexican War, Representative Wilmot of

Pennsylvania had moved as an amendment to an appropriation bill that slavery should not exist in any The Wilmot territory that might be acquired from Mexico. Proviso 

Although this resolution passed the House, it was held up in the Senate and did not become law, but it injected the slavery issue into the debates of Congress once more, and the discussion continued without intermission and with ever-increasing bitterness until the secession of the southern states. 

Calhoun dreaded the reopening of the slavery question in Congress, and for that reason opposed the Mexican War and the acquisition of California and New Mexico, but the great majority of southern Democrats favored the war and territorial expansion.

The question of slavery in California and New Mexico now overshadowed all others. A natural solution would have been the extension of the Missouri Compromise line to the Pacific, but to this the antislavery North was unalterably opposed. By Mexican law this region was free, and the advocates of the proviso held that slavery could not be introduced except by act of Congress, which they proposed to prevent. Calhoun, Jefferson Davis, and other Southern leaders claimed, on the contrary, that the institution of slavery was a part of the public law of the United States, which had been extended over the region by the very act of conquest, and that therefore it must be recognized and protected.

The doctrine sover- eignty"

Lewis Cass of Michigan advanced a third view, later taken up by Stephen A. Douglas of Illinois, which was that Congress did not have the right to legislate slavery either of "squatter into a territory or out of a territory, but that the question should be left for the settlers, or "squatters," as they were popularly called, to decide for themselves. This view was dubbed by its opponents, in derision, the doctrine of "squatter sovereignty," but it was called by Douglas "popular sovereignty." Although this view accorded in general with the doctrine of states' rights, the Southerners were not willing to admit that the inhabitants of a United States territory had the right to exclude slaves or any other kind of property. The presi- dential 1848 As this issue was now becoming both political and sectional, it was difficult for either of the two great political parties to take sides without splitting its followers. And so both Whigs and Democrats ignored in their platcampaign of forms the question of the extension of slavery and tried to conduct the campaign of 1848 along the old lines. The Democratic convention met in Baltimore in May, and as Polk did not seek renomination, Lewis Cass of Michigan was chosen as the candidate for the presidency. This was the first instance of the nomination of a Northern man with Southern principles, a policy which the Democratic party followed until 1860 with the hope of holding its followers in the northern states. The Whigs, on the other hand, who met in convention in Philadelphia in 

June, nominated General Zachary Taylor of Louisiana, a large slaveholder, with the object of holding the Southern wing of their party. Millard Fillmore of New York was nominated for vice-president.

In New York the Democratic party had for some time been split into two factions, one headed by Marcy and the other by Van Buren. The Marcy faction, known as "Hunkers," had the support of the Tammany Society and of the practi-

Taylor and Fillmore were elected, receiving 163 electoral votes to Cass's 127. The Free-Soilers did not carry a state, but they polled nearly 300,000 votes, and in several states they held the balance between the older parties. 

In the meantime California had already called a constitutional convention without waiting for the usual enabling act

The Com- promise of 1850 of Congress and had adopted a state constitution which excluded slavery. President Taylor had given his approval to this proceeding and he now recommended to the new Congress that California be admitted as a state. The admission of California as a free state would upset the balance in the Senate, on which depended the equilibrium of the Union. There were at this time fifteen slave and fifteen free states. The Southern members of Congress refused to allow California to come into the Union until the question of slavery in the rest of the Mexican cession was determined. So intense was the feeling that an acceptable solution seemed a remote possibility. 

A remarkable compromise was suggested by Clay in the 

Senate on January 29, 1850. He proposed that California should be admitted under her free constitution; that territorial governments should be organized in the rest of the Mexican cession without any restriction as to slavery; that the boundary between Texas and New Mexico should be adjusted and that Texas should be paid $10,000,000 for surrendering her claims to the disputed area; that the slave trade should be abolished in the District of Columbia, although it was considered inexpedient to abolish slavery there as long as it continued in Maryland; and that Congress should enact a more stringent fugitive slave law, making it the duty of United States marshals and other federal officials to enforce its provisions.

Mason, of Virginia, because Calhoun himself was too feeble to deliver Calhoun's it, although he was rolled into the chamber in a last speech chair to hear it read. (Before the end of the month he passed away.) In this last speech he declared that the equilibrium between the two sections had been destroyed, that the Union was in danger, and he appealed to the North, the stronger party, to save it. His terms were: "The North must give us equal rights in the acquired territory; she must return our fugitive slaves; she must cease the agitation of the slave question; and she must consent to an amendment to the Constitution, which will restore to the South the power she possessed of protecting herself before the equilibrium was destroyed by the action of this government. The admission of California will be the test question." He did not explain the nature of the amendment, but after his death there was found among his papers a plan for two presidents, one from the slave and one from the free states, each having a veto on the acts of Congress. speech

Webster made a notable speech three days after Calhoun's speech was read. He began by saying: "I wish to speak to-day, not as a Massachusetts man, nor as a Webster's 

Northern man, but as an American." 

After Seventh-ofreviewing some of the historical aspects of the March slavery question he continued, "Now as to California and New Mexico, I hold slavery to be excluded from those territories by a law even superior to that which admits and sanctions it in Texas. I mean the law of nature, of physical geography, the law of the formation of the earth. 

That law settles forever, with a strength beyond all terms of human enactment, that slavery cannot exist in California and New Mexico. . . . I would not take pains uselessly to

reaffirm an ordinance of nature, nor to reenact the will of God. I would put in no Wilmot proviso for the mere purpose of a taunt or reproach." As regards fugitive slaves, he expressed the opinion that the complaints of the South were just and that the North had failed in her duty. A storm of indignation in the North followed this speech, particularly in New England. Webster's position was condemned and he himself severely censured by a gathering in Faneuil Hall. 

Theodore Parker said: "I know no deed in

Webster was compared to Lucifer, the fallen angel, and there was no reaction from this condemnation until his death two years later, but when that event occurred the revulsion of feeling was sudden and complete. "Massachusetts smote and broke the heart of Webster, her idol, and then broke her own above his grave." There can be no doubt in the light of our clearer vision to-day that Webster's speech was prompted by a sincere patriotism and that it was based on wise statesmanship. Yet to such an extent had sectional prejudice been aroused that the antislavery North was as much opposed to compromise as the proslavery South.

The most prominent of the new group were Seward, Sumner, Chase, Douglas, Davis, and Toombs. Uncle

In 1852 the appearance of Uncle Tom's Cabin, a novel by Harriet Beecher Stowe dealing with slavery, created a profound impression. Although neither a true representation of slavery nor a literary master- Tom's piece, this book appealed to the popular imagination on a subject which the politicians in vain tried to Cabin

exclude from public discussion but which "would not down." 

It was read by millions, was translated into various languages, and had a larger circulation than any other novel ever written. 

It made little impression on the older generation, but it was a powerful agency in keeping alive the agitation against slavery, and it molded the opinions of the younger men who elected 

Lincoln president in 1860.

CHAPTER XX ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL PROGRESS 

movement FROM the first settlement at Jamestown to the close of the nineteenth century the most important factor in the economic life of America was the existence of a western The frontier where land was abundant and could be westward had free or at a very small cost. Not until the eve of the Revolution did the population of the Atlantic seaboard begin to push across the Alleghenies. The Mississippi had scarcely been reached when the Louisiana Purchase added the vast area extending to the Rockies, and before a third part of this region was occupied, Texas and the Mexican cession added another million square miles to the territory of the 

United States.

Agriculture was the main occupation in the West. As land was abundant and labor scarce, methods of farming were wasteful. As soon as a piece of land ceased to yield large crops it was abandoned and its owner passed on to new lands. Where there was so much unoccupied land to be had, men were unwilling to work very long for wages. Almost everybody, including the recent immigrants from Europe, looked forward to becoming landowners. The rapid development of the 

West during the period 1830-1860 had a marked effect on both agriculture and manufactures in the East. With the development of means of transportation the East could no longer compete with the West in the raising of corn and wheat. As a result the eastern farmer devoted himself more to dairying and fruit growing and the southern farmer to cotton and tobacco. Though the growth of the West 369

stimulated manufactures to some extent, it also drew laborers from the factories to the land and tended to make wages high. 

In colonial days heavy transportation had been confined to water. Article I, section 8, of the Constitution gave Congress the power "to establish Post Offices and portation post Roads," and this was held by some to authorize the construction of public highways. Trans- The Pike

The Cumberland Road or National Pike was begun in 1811 and completed in 1852. It began at Cumberland, Maryland, and by 1820 had reached Wheeling on the Ohio. 

National It was subsequently extended across the State of Ohio, passing through Zanesville, Columbus, and 

Springfield; across Indiana, through Richmond, Indianapolis, and Terre Haute; and finally to Vandalia, then the capital of 

Illinois. The total length was 834 miles and the cost $6,821,000. A few years after its completion it was turned over to the states through which it ran. Presidents Madison, Monroe, and Jackson believed that internal improvements should be carried out by the states and opposed federal appropriations for any more projects. 

The Cumberland Road played an important part in the development of the West. It was popular from the first, and covered wagons of the Conestoga type, the later "prairie schooner," carrying families and household goods, pressed hard on the heels of the road builders. Steamboats

The steamboat gave a tremendous impetus to western commerce. The earlier pioneers who reached the Ohio by the National Pike usually continued their journey down the river on barges until they reached a desirable place to settle. The products they raised could be easily floated down the Ohio and the Mississippi to New Orleans, but it was a slow and difficult task to bring the barges back, so they were usually sold and the men frequently had to buy horses and ride back home. In 1807 Robert Fulton made his epoch-making trip from New York to Albany in the

Clermont, the first practical steamboat, and four years later he put the first steamboat on the Ohio. In a few years over a hundred steamboats were plying the western rivers, and freight rates were reduced to an amazingly low figure. Until the Civil War the flat-bottom side-wheeler held its supremacy in interior commerce and travel. Many of these boats were luxuriously furnished and equipped, and excited the wonder and admiration of travelers from the eastern states and Europe alike. Life on the Mississippi in the fifties has been 

THE CLERMONT' 

99 (From a model in the National Museum, Washington.) vividly described by Mark Twain, the ablest and most realistic writer that the Southwest has produced. Canals

The steamboat gave the West an outlet to the sea in the South, but it did not solve the problem of transportation between the Great Lakes and the Ohio and Mississippi rivers. The success of the Erie Canal, opened to traffic in 1825, gave a great impetus to canal building, and caused the settlement of the southern shores of Lake Erie and Lake Michigan. Canals were then built across the 

State of Ohio connecting the lake settlements with the Ohio River, and in Illinois a canal was built from Chicago to La Salle on the Illinois River, thus connecting Lake Michigan with the Mississippi Valley.

Other important canals were the one connecting Philadelphia and Pittsburgh, with a portage railway over the mountains, a difficult and expensive link in the chain, and the Chesapeake and Ohio Canal, which was built along the Potomac as far as Cumberland. The construction of the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad, a rival enterprise, caused the abandonment of the original plan to carry the canal to the Ohio. 

The southern states also undertook various canal enterprises. 

A PACKET BOAT ON THE ERIE CANAL 

The panic Most of the canals were built by joint-stock companies, to which the state governments made liberal subscriptions, either directly or through the guarantee of bonds. of 1837 ended many of these undertakings, and by the time the country recovered, the feasibility of railroads had been demonstrated and capital was attracted to this new field of enterprise.

In the forties and fifties railroads were rapidly taking the place of canals as means of transportation, thus spreading the The build- population more evenly over the country and enabling it to leave the rivers and waterways.

Improvements in agricultural implements kept pace with those in transportation. The iron plow, with detachable

Cyrus Hall McCormick of Virginia invented the first successful reaper in 1831. Scores of reaping machines had been invented in this country and abroad, but none of them proved successful. Young McCormick, who had assisted his father in the construction of an unsuccessful reaper at the forge on his farm, finally invented the type of machine which is now used the world over. The reaper, though useful everywhere, was an inestimable boon to the West, for it enabled the farmers to grow vast crops of grain on the prairies which it would have been impossible, where labor was scarce, to gather in by means of the old cradle. The reaper was one of the greatest factors in the rapid development of the West.

During this time most Americans were still engaged in agriculture and transportation, but factories and small in- Industrial dustries were multiplying. As we have already development seen, manufacturing had sprung up during the period of embargoes preceding the War of 1812 and had grown rapidly during that war, but had been unable to compete with English goods after the restoration of peace. The success of the first mill for spinning and weaving cotton, erected at Waltham, Massachusetts, in 1814, led to the establishment of other mills at Lowell, Manchester,

Lawrence, Providence, Fall River, and other points in New England where water power was available for turning the spindles and operating the looms. Cotton manu- Cotton and facturing soon spread to New York, New Jersey, woolen mills and Pennsylvania, where the abundance of coal led to the use of steam engines in running the mills. There were a few small mills in the South in the twenties, but the first mill of any size was built in 1846. Between that date and 

1860 several mills were operated in North and South Carolina and Georgia. The southern mills produced mainly yarn and some coarse cloth.

Because of the supremacy of English woolens and the cheapness of cotton goods, woolen mills were slower in developing. Furthermore, sheep were raised everywhere and woolen articles were extensively produced on the farms. 

Nevertheless, by 1860 the number of woolen factories had grown to over two thousand.

The building of railroads and the development of manufactures gave a great impetus to the iron industry. The demand for iron rails and machinery led to the The iron introduction of improved methods of smelting and industry refining. Iron stoves came into general use, and by 1850 the annual output of stoves was four hundred thousand. Though the Bessemer process was known, the cost of making steel was so great that its extensive use was delayed until the new industrial era that came after the Civil War. Inventions

The inventive genius for which Americans have become noted, especially in labor-saving devices, was doubtless quickened by the scarcity of labor compared with the vast resources of mine, forest, and field. During the second quarter of the nineteenth century the Patent Office found its business rapidly increasing year by year. 

During the single decade 1850-1860 the number of patents recorded was 28,000. Among the important inventions that came into use about the middle of the century, some of which

have already been mentioned, were Cyrus McCormick's reaper, Elias Howe's sewing machine, Richard Hoe's rotary printing press, Samuel Morse's electromagnetic telegraph, and innumerable improvements in factory machinery and farming implements, especially the plow. 

Industrial Revolution is the name given to the change from the old system of household manufactures to the factory system with its problems of labor and capital. It was introduced in England about the time of the American Revolution by a series of inventions in the textile industries and the use of the steam engine. In the 

The Industrial

Revolution 

U. S. National Museum HOWE'S FIRST SEWING MACHINE 

course of a single generation England had been completely transformed and had become the leading manufacturing country in the world. 

In America the Industrial Revolution came a full generation later than in England. The factory system here too began with the cotton mill. As the factory system grew and more capital was required, there came into existence the capitalist class who lived in the cities and had little or no contact with the factory except through the manager or superintendent.

The capitalist was interested mainly in profits, and the factory system soon developed conflict of interests between the laborers and the capitalists. 

At first the cotton mills drew their labor from the country districts. Young women were glad to escape the drudgery of the farm and earn a little ready money. With many of

them work in the mills was regarded as an interesting experience but not a lasting occupation. There gradually developed, however, a class of permanent wage- Organization earners who could look forward to nothing else. of labor 

These people naturally tried to improve their conditions of labor.

At an early date local unions were formed in an attempt to regulate hours of labor and to see that the sick were cared for. In 1827 the Mechanics' Union of Trade Associations was organized in Philadelphia, and during the next ten years the labor movement made notable progress. Strikes were occasionally resorted to, but the leaders were often arrested and tried for conspiracy. Labor parties were organized in at least fifteen states, and political agitation for better laws was begun. The panic of 1837 had a disastrous effect upon labor organizations, but the movement was revived during the forties and fifties. 

During the thirties and forties, foreign commerce showed a steady growth. Imports increased from $70,000,000 to $178,000,000, and exports from $73,000,000 to Foreign $151,000,000. Southern cotton was the basis of commerce exchange. Imports were paid for mainly in cotton, and were received at New York, from which point they were distributed throughout the country. The Southern planter felt that he was paying for these imports and that he did not get his share of the goods or of the profits from handling them. 

In the southern commercial conferences held annually from 1835 to 1860, this was a perpetual subject of discussion, and various plans were advanced for developing southern ports and establishing ship lines of their own to Europe. 

A large part of the cotton crop was consumed in Europe, but there was a growing demand for it in China and other countries of the Orient. Immediately after the Revolution, American vessels had entered the China trade, the Empress of China having made the first trip from New York to Canton

in 1784. That trade had thrived and increased during the early years of the nineteenth century, but a sudden boom came after Great Britain's Opium War with China, which resulted in the opening of the five "treaty ports" to British trade and residence in 1842. Two years later Caleb Cushing negotiated a treaty securing for American citizens "mostfavored-nation" treatment so they became entitled to all the HWC privileges of trade and residence that had been granted to the 

British. Commodore 

Perry's famous expedition to Japan ten years later opened up that country to foreign trade and gave a great impetus to 

THE CLIPPER SHIP "FLYING CLOUD" IN 1851 American commerce in the Orient.

The period we are considering was the golden age of the American merchant marine. From 1820 to 1850 the famous 

Merchant clipper ships could outsail anything on the ocean. marine During these years a greater percentage of American commerce was carried under the American flag than in any other period of our history. But the supremacy of the 

American-built sailing vessel was not destined to last long. 

In 1838 the Great Western, an English steamship, made its first trip across the Atlantic and introduced the era of steam navigation on the ocean. It was, of course, several years before the supremacy of the sailing vessel passed. The iron hull, which was introduced a little later, gave England a great advantage over America, for she could build better and cheaper iron vessels than we could. These changes and the 

Civil War caused the decline of the American merchant marine, and it has never regained supremacy.

Between 1830 and 1860 the population of the United States more than doubled, increasing from 12,866,000 to over 31,000,000. A large part of this increase was due to foreign immigration. Population

In 1842 over 100,000 foreigners came to our shores, and in 1854 the number exceeded 400,000. This movement was due primarily to the famine in Ireland and the revo- Foreign imlutions in Germany, but it was accelerated by the migration rapid extension of the American frontier. Some of the immigrants remained in the eastern states, where they took the place of the native-born Americans who were moving to the West. This was especially true of the Irish. The Germans, on the other hand, preferred going directly to the frontier, and they played an important part in the development of some of the western states. Between 1830 and 1850 six new states were admitted to the Union: Arkansas in 1836, Michigan in 1837, Florida and Texas in 1845, Iowa in 1846, and Wisconsin in 1848.

The years 1828-1848 saw a rapid extension of the suffrage. 

When the new government was organized under the Constitution in 1789, complete manhood suffrage did Extension of not exist in a single one of the thirteen states. the suffrage 

The right to vote was restricted by landholding or other property qualifications, and the right to hold office was similarly restricted. With the election of Andrew Jackson to the presidency in 1828 democracy entered upon a new phase. Within a few years state after state adopted manhood suffrage and abolished property qualifications for holding office. In many of the states the legislatures no longer chose governors and judges, this function having been surrendered to the people, and South Carolina was the only state in which the legislature still chose presidential electors. 

The rapid extension of the suffrage produced political changes of a far-reaching character. Candidates for office had to appeal to the masses rather than to a more limited

group of property holders. In dealing with large masses of voters new political methods were necessary, and we note the appearance of state and national committees, the national nominating convention, political machines, bosses, and other innovations which soon became characteristic features of the 

American party system. versities

As we have seen, several colleges were founded during the colonial period, and academies for boys and schools for girls were quite general in the older communities. On 

Colleges and state uni- the southern plantations tutors were frequently employed. The earlier American colleges, and in fact most of the later ones, were ecclesiastical in origin and partially supported by the churches. Their prime object was the training of young men for the Christian ministry. 

State grants for the encouragement of higher education were sometimes made. The first state university in name was that of North Carolina, founded in 1795, but it was not a real university, and for many years it was only a feeble college. 

The founding of the University of Virginia by Thomas Jefferson, who intended it to be the capstone of a system of public education, was the first great step in secular education. 

The state provided the funds for buildings and maintenance, and the university was opened in 1824 with some equipment and a remarkable corps of professors, some of whom Jefferson brought from Europe. It was the only institution in America before the Civil War which offered a broad curriculum including the humanities, the sciences, history, economics, and politics. The range of studies was so broad that the fixed curriculum which prevailed in other American colleges was modified. The elective system was introduced by Jefferson at the outset. Francis Wayland later borrowed the idea of the elective system and introduced it at Brown University, and still later it appeared at Harvard in a modified form. 

The West enthusiastically adopted Jefferson's idea of a state university. The University of Michigan was the first

important institution in that section. The western state university, supported by land grants, was closely integrated with the public school system, and more nearly approached Jefferson's ideal than did the University of Virginia, which remained aristocratic in tendency, and had little direct influence on popular education until long after the Civil War. 

Though the opportunity for a fairly good college education existed in most of the older states, it was very largely limited

THE LIBRARY AT THE UNIVERSITY OF VIRGINIA 

to young men of family and property. It required great ambition and perseverance on the part of a poor young man to get a college education. 

The idea that it was the duty of the state to provide elementary education developed slowly and encountered strong opposition. At first a small provision was made Public for sending poor but deserving boys to private schools schools at the expense of the community or the state. Later came the demand that public or free schools should be provided for all children whether their parents were able to pay or not. Finally the compulsory feature was added, and

parents were compelled by law to send their children to school up to a certain age.

The first step in the system of public education which now prevails in all the states was taken by Massachusetts, where the first state board of education was created in 1837. 

Horace Mann was appointed secretary of this board, and during the next eleven years under his guidance real prog- Literature

HORACE MANN 

ress was made. He established a normal school for the training of teachers in 1839. 

Other northern and western states followed the example of Massachusetts. Though most of the southern states made provision for the education of poor boys at private academies, comparatively few boys took advantage of it, and no adequate provision was made for public education until after the Civil War. The first American literature of real distinction and permanent value is found in the political writings of the founders of the republic, especially the writings of Franklin, John Adams, Jefferson, Hamilton, and Madison.

Their works will be read as long as men are interested in the history of the American republic and in the problems of government. Political literature kept its hold on the South, and we have a group of later writers from John Taylor, who expounded the agrarian philosophy of Jefferson, to John C. 

Calhoun, who popularized the doctrines of nullification and secession. Political thought colored the writings of Southern writers of romance, such as William Wirt, John P. Kennedy, Nathaniel Beverley Tucker, William Alexander Carruthers, and William Gilmore Simms. The South of this period pro-

duced one poet of immortal fame, Edgar Allan Poe, but his genius was not restrained in any way by sectionalism. 

The first American to achieve a purely literary reputation abroad was Washington Irving, whose Knickerbocker History of New York won immediate recognition. Herman Melville, of New York, won applause with his stories of South Sea islands, and produced one classic of the sea and of whaling, Moby Dick. James Fenimore Cooper, another New 

Yorker, produced stories of frontier life and adventure that enjoyed a tremendous popularity both in this country and abroad. New England produced a group of great writers: Longfellow, Whittier, Hawthorne, Holmes, Emerson, Thoreau, Bancroft, Prescott, and Lowell.

The absence of copyright agreements with England and the existence of a great body

Scott and Dickens enjoyed an immense popularity in this country and were more widely read than American writers. 

Magazines and reviews were few and these were very poor, with a few notable exceptions. The North American Review

Many reform movements began in the thirties and forties. 

The abolition crusade, started by Garrison in 1831, has al- Reform ready been described. Temperance societies were movements organized in Massachusetts as early as 1824, and Maine adopted the first state-wide prohibition law in 1846. 

The long struggle for woman's rights began in the thirties, and in 1848 the first woman's rights convention was held at Seneca Falls, New York. It adopted a "declaration of in-

dependence," demanding the right to vote, legal equality of every kind, including control of their property by married women, equal opportunities for employment, including admission to the learned professions, and equal educational opportunities involving coeducation. These demands were the subject of jest and ridicule for many years, and it took nearly a hundred years to realize them. The early leaders of the movement were Susan B. Anthony, Lucretia Mott, Elizabeth Cady Stanton, and Julia Ward Howe. democracy Fundamental changes in American life occurred in the thirty years following the election of Andrew Jackson to the presidency. Middle-class ideals gained the ascendancy everywhere except in the South, where the aristocratic principle still prevailed. 

The typical America as conceived and described by Europeans, a vast, restless, energetic, crude, and as yet uncultured force, - had come into being.

CHAPTER XXI FURTHER COMPROMISE IMPOSSIBLE 

WHEN President Pierce was inaugurated in 1853, there were surface indications that the slavery issue had finally been settled, or at least removed from national politics. sive foreign The widespread satisfaction with the Compromise policy of 1850 and the falling off in the vote polled by the Free-Soilers seemed to indicate this. The new administration planned a bold foreign policy in order to keep the attention of the nation diverted from this issue. Under Fillmore, Webster and also Everett, who succeeded him in the Department of State, had tried to handle foreign questions in a way to arouse national pride and patriotism, and their efforts had met with success.

The Gadsden Purchase was negotiated with Mexico soon after Pierce came into office. By this treaty (1853) we acquired an important tract of land south of the Gila River in Arizona. In 1854 a Canadian reciprocity treaty was signed with England. During the same year, Commodore 

Perry forced the ruler of Japan to sign the famous treaty which opened up that country to foreign commerce; and a number of other treaties concerning American commerce, neutral rights, and extradition were negotiated with various powers. William L. Marcy, who directed these negotiations, was one of our ablest and most successful secretaries of state. 

Pierce had in his cabinet two other men of great ability, Jefferson Davis as secretary of war, and Caleb Cushing, of

The at- Cuba

Cuba had been coveted in former years by Jefferson, John Quincy Adams, and other farsighted statesmen, and its annexation to the United States was considered only a question of time. Down to the Mexican tempts to 

War the United States feared that Cuba might be acquire annexed by England or France, and our policy was to guarantee the possession of the island to Spain. Clay declared as secretary of state in 1825 that we could not consent to the occupation of Cuba or Porto Rico "by any other European power than Spain under any contingency whatever," and Daniel Webster in 1843, while occupying the same post, assured Spain that, if any attempt were made to wrest 

Cuba from her, "she might securely rely upon the whole naval and military resources of this country to aid her in preserving or recovering it."

American foreign policy assumed a much more aggressive character after the Mexican War. Cuba now was desired not only by the slaveholding population of the South, but by a large part of the nation, on account of its strategic importance, lying athwart the Gulf of Mexico and commanding also the now important interoceanic canal routes. Between the 

Mexican and Civil wars, therefore, repeated efforts were made to purchase the island from Spain. In 1848 Secretary

Buchanan offered Spain $100,000,000 for Cuba, but the offer was indignantly rejected. 

Two filibusters under General López took place in 1850 and 

1851, in which many Americans participated. López was finally captured and executed by the Spanish authorities and about fifty Americans were summarily shot without a trial.

When news of these executions reached New Orleans, a mob attacked and robbed the Spanish consulate. These incidents naturally caused strained relations between the two governments. 

In his inaugural address President Pierce announced that his policy would "not be controlled by any timid forebod-

The "Os ings of evil from expansion." This was taken to refer to Cuba; and the appointment as minister to Spain of Pierre Soulé of Louisiana, a Frenchman by birth and education, tend Mani- who had been exiled for political reasons, created festo," 1854 an unfavorable impression in this country and abroad, for his views on the Cuban question were well known to be of a radical character. Shortly after Soulé's arrival at 

Madrid the two countries were brought to the verge of war when the Spanish authority in Havana harbor seized the Black Warrior, an American ship charged with a technical violation of the port regulations. The ship and cargo were subsequently restored, but the overzealous handling of the incident by Soulé rendered any further negotiations for the purchase of Cuba by him utterly useless.

Accordingly Marcy directed Soulé to confer with Mason and Buchanan, our ministers at Paris and London, on the Cuban question. The three ministers met at Ostend, a watering place in Belgium, in 1854, and drew up a report to Marcy which was subsequently made public and became known as the "Ostend Manifesto." They advised that the United 

States offer Spain a fair price for Cuba, suggesting $100,000,000, and in case of her refusal to sell, that the United States should seize the island, if the welfare and safety of the Union demanded it. Marcy politely but firmly repudiated the recommendations of the report, and Soulé promptly resigned. The manifesto had, however, the desired effect of helping to secure for James Buchanan the Democratic nomination for the presidency in 1856.

We must now once again come back to the slavery question. 

The fugitive slave law had created such intense opposition in the North that it was practically impossible to the fugitive enforce it. The "Underground Railroad" was very active in the fifties, and thousands of slaves were being enticed away from their masters over into the free states. When pursued and arrested they were being rescued slave law

more and more from the hands of the officers of the law and concealed or sent on to Canada.

Still the fugitive slave law was a part of the Compromise of 1850 and public men of both the North and the South had asserted that the life of the Union depended upon its faithful execution. In a speech in Virginia, June 28, 1851, Daniel 

Webster said: "I have not hesitated to say, and I repeat, that if the Northern States refuse, wilfully and deliberately, to carry into effect that part of the Constitution which respects the restoration of fugitive slaves, and Congress provide no remedy, the South would no longer be bound to observe the compact." Every time a runaway slave was arrested and rescued by a mob, hundreds of converts were made to the antislavery cause. 

Men were beginning to fear that after all the compromise was not a finality, when the whole question was suddenly reopened in Congress 

STEPHEN A. DOUGLAS 

by Stephen A. Douglas in a bill which he proposed for the organization of the territory of Nebraska.

The vast region extending from Missouri and Iowa to the Rockies, which went under the name of Nebraska, had never been organized and was still occupied by The Kansas- Indians. It was now proposed to remove the Nebraska 

Indian tribes from a portion of this territory and Bill, 1854 open it up to settlers. The whole of Nebraska was north of the Missouri Compromise line and according to that agreement slavery was forever excluded, but Douglas declared that a new principle had been adopted in the Compromise of 1850,

that is, the principle of popular sovereignty. He therefore questioned the validity of the Missouri Compromise and provided in a bill which he introduced January 4, 1854, that the territory of Nebraska, or any portion of the same, when admitted as a state or states, "shall be received into the Union with or without slavery, as their constitutions may prescribe at the time of their admission." On January 16, Dixon, a Whig senator from Kentucky who was filling Clay's unexpired term, offered an amendment providing in express terms for the repeal of the Missouri Compromise. Douglas at first objected to the amendment, but after conferring with Dixon he finally decided to embody it in his bill. 

Douglas took this step without consulting the Southern leaders, but on Sunday, January 22, he called on Jefferson Davis and got him to accompany him to the White House. 

The matter was discussed at length with President Pierce, who finally gave his approval to the bill. On the following day Douglas offered, as a substitute for his first bill, one which expressly repealed the Missouri Compromise and provided for the organization of two territories instead of one, Kansas and Nebraska. The evident purpose was to make one state slave and the other free. The following reasons were given by Douglas in support of his measure: "The legal effect of this bill is neither to legislate slavery into these territories nor out of them, The debate but to leave the people to do as they please. If on the bill they wish slavery, they have a right to it. If they do not want it, they will not have it, and you should not force it upon them." Sumner, Wade, and Seward made able speeches against the bill, and Chase's speech established him at once as the leader of the antislavery forces. The bill passed the 

Senate March 4 by a vote of 37 to 14 and the House May 22 by a vote of 113 to 100.

This measure reopened the whole slavery issue, and the vote in the House showed that it threatened the disruption of both

political parties. The Southern Democrats were solidly for the bill and the Northern Whigs solidly against it, but the Northern Democrats were divided, 44 for and 42 against, and the Southern Whigs were also divided, 12 for and 7 against. 

Many writers have expressed the opinion that but for the repeal of the Missouri Compromise the Civil War would not have taken place. Whether this view is correct or not, it is undoubtedly true that the Kansas-Nebraska Act introduced a new phase of the slavery conflict which led straight to the 

Civil War.

The bill was carried through Congress by the personal influence of Douglas, a Northern Democrat. What was his motive? Most historians believe that it was a Douglas's motives direct bid to the Southern Democrats for the presidential nomination, which Douglas undoubtedly coveted. 

Recent writers have, however, advanced another explanation. 

The question of a transcontinental railroad was being much discussed at this time and there was great rivalry over the choice of a route. The Gadsden Purchase had opened the way for a road to California along the route later followed by the Southern Pacific, and Jefferson Davis as secretary of war sent a corps of engineers into the field and had this route surveyed. This route would of course be a great boon to 

Memphis and New Orleans. St. Louis and Chicago, on the other hand, wanted the road built west through the Nebraska territory, and the best way to secure the adoption of that route seemed to be to remove the Indians from that territory and open it up as speedily as possible to settlers. The 

Southern leaders wished to delay as long as possible the admission of any more states north of the Missouri Compromise line. If, however, the way were opened for the admission of one slave state and one free state, not only would the Southern opposition be removed, but the rivalry between the sections would lead to a more rapid settlement of the region, which was the thing most desired.

It was becoming more and more difficult to hold the old party alignments. In 1852 many of the Southern Whigs, notably those of Georgia led by Toombs and Reshaping 

Stephens, repudiated General Scott, the Whig of political candidate, and henceforth allied themselves with the Democratic party. In the North many of the antislavery Democrats had joined the Free-Soilers. parties 

The American party came into being between 

1852 and 1854. It was soon dubbed the "Know- 

Nothing" party. This party was based primarily on opposition to foreigners, who were now coming to our shores in increasingly large numbers, and the object of the new party was to lengthen the period necessary for naturalization and to exclude foreigners and Roman Catholics from office. The organization was a secret one, with lodges, countersigns, and symbols, and for a time it made rapid progress and gained control of several states. A great many Southern Whigs went into this movement rather than into the Democratic party. The Know-Nothing party tried to ignore the slavery question, but divided like other parties on the Kansas-Nebraska Bill and soon went to pieces.

ALEXANDER H. STEPHENS 

Another new party, the Republican party, was formed. 

It proved permanent and was by far the most important of the immediate effects of Douglas's measure. The fight

The formation of the Republican party against the bill in Congress had brought together antislavery Whigs, antislavery Democrats, antislavery "Know- Nothings," Free-Soilers, and Abolitionists. On 

July 6, 1854, a convention of anti-Nebraska men was held at Jackson, Michigan, a full state ticket nominated, and the name Republican adopted by the now party. On July 13, the anniversary of the Ordinance of 1787, anti-Nebraska state conventions were held in Wisconsin, Ohio, Indiana, and Vermont.

The bill was the paramount issue in the Congressional elections in the North, and it was overwhelmingly repudiated. 

The House which passed the Kansas-Nebraska Bill had a majority of 84 Democrats; in the House elected after its passage the Democrats were in a minority of 75. Of the 42 

Northern Democrats who had voted for the bill only 7 were reëlected. Douglas tried to show that the result was due to the gains of the "Know-Nothings," but the new Congress was organized by the Republicans, who elected Nathaniel P. 

Banks, of Massachusetts, as Speaker. Thus the Kansas- 

Nebraska bill disrupted both of the older parties and consolidated the antislavery forces into a new party, which from that day to our own, except for a few intervals, has controlled the government.

Meanwhile the principle of popular sovereignty was producing unexpected results in Kansas. It had been 

The struggle generally expected that Kansas would become a for Kansas slave state, and Missouri farmers were soon moving across the border, a few of them carrying their slaves with them. A movement was started in Massachusetts, however, known as the Emigrant Aid Society, for the purpose of sending New England settlers into the territory. The antislavery settlers soon organized an "Underground Railroad," and slaves began escaping from Missouri through the free settlements in Kansas. The Missourians were greatly enraged, and as a measure of self-defense determined to make

Kansas a slave state. When the election for members of the territorial legislature was held March 30, 1855, large numbers of Missourians rode over the border, voted, and returned home.

These methods carried the election for the slavery men, and the legislature adopted a slave code modeled after that of Missouri. The Free-Soilers, however, refused to recognize the election as valid, and without any authorization from the territorial authorities or from Congress, they held a constitutional convention at Topeka, October 23, 1855, framed a constitution prohibiting slavery, and organized a government which applied to Congress for admission as a state. 

There were thus two governments in the territory and conditions were ripe for the border warfare which soon broke out. Meanwhile the Emigrant Aid Society was supplying its settlers with rifles sent out in boxes marked "books." "Beecher's Bibles" was the name popularly given them. Sumner 

President Pierce upheld the authority of the territorial legislature and refused to recognize the legality of the Topeka movement. Douglas took the same view of the Brooks's case and there took place in the Senate the assault on angriest debate that had ever been known in that body. Sumner replied to Douglas in a speech which he gave the title of "The Crime against Kansas." It was prepared with unusual care and sent to the printer before delivery. The special objects of his attack were Douglas and Senator Butler of South Carolina. The speech abounded in personal insults and veiled insinuations which the carefully chosen language rendered all the more exasperating. Sumner himself boasted, with characteristic egotism, that it was the "most thorough philippic ever uttered in a legislative body."

Douglas was present and defended himself with his usual vigor, meeting the personal attacks with counter-attacks. 

But Senator Butler was not present to defend himself, being detained at his home in South Carolina by an illness from

which he never recovered. His nephew, Preston Brooks, a representative from South Carolina, determined to avenge the insult. Entering the Senate chamber after adjournment two days later, he attacked Sumner, who was seated at his desk writing, and gave him a severe beating with a cane. 

A resolution to expel Brooks was introduced in the House, but it failed to receive the necessary two-thirds vote. He promptly resigned his seat, however, only to be returned by the almost unanimous vote of his constituents.

The incident aroused sectional hatred to an extent never before known in the history of the country.

The Supreme Court of the United States was finally called upon, in the famous Dred Scott case, to decide the question of the right of Congress to exclude slavery from 

The Dred the territories. Dred Scott was a Negro slave Scott deowned by an army surgeon, who in 1834 took him cision, 1857 to an army post in Illinois and later to another post west of the Mississippi in territory from which slavery was excluded by the terms of the Missouri Compromise. The Negro made no effort to secure his freedom while residing in free territory, but some years after his master had taken him back to Missouri he sued for his freedom, first in the courts of Missouri and later in the United States courts, on the ground of his previous residence in free territory. 

The Supreme Court first heard the case in February, 1856, and the justices had decided in conference to dismiss it on the ground that Dred Scott was not a citizen and had no right to bring suit in the United States courts. However, Justice

McLean, a candidate for the Republican nomination for the presidency, determined to make political capital out of the case by writing a dissenting opinion reviewing the history of African slavery in America from the Free-Soil point of view. 

The Southern members of the court objected to this, so the decision was deferred and the case was reheard in December, but the court did not deliver its decision until after the inauguration of Buchanan the following March. Meanwhile much pressure was indirectly brought to bear on the court to enter into the merits of the case instead of dismissing it on a technicality. It was thought that the question of slavery in the territories might thus be settled once for all by the highest tribunal in the land.

Chief Justice Taney, who had been appointed by Jackson,

delivered the opinion which held that Dred Scott was not a citizen of Missouri within the meaning of the Constitution and therefore could not sue in the federal courts. Negroes were not included in the term "citizens" by the framers of the Constitution. But the opinion did not rest here. In the course of his argument the chief justice canvassed the question as to whether the Missouri Compromise, under which Dred Scott claimed the right to sue, was a valid enactment. 

He came to the conclusion that the act was not constitutional, that a slave was property and that Congress had no right to exclude this particular kind of property any more than any other kind of property from the common territory of the United States. This decision of course caused deep resentment in the North, and it was many years before the Supreme Court recovered from the odium that was heaped upon it. 

During the Civil War Lincoln ignored the court with impunity, and during the 'years following the war Congress threatened it into silence on the vital issues of Reconstruction. 

No court could settle an issue as deep as the slavery one. 

The Dred Scott decision did not even settle the Kansas 

The Kansas question. question. Robert J. Walker, the former secretary of the treasury, who had been appointed by Buchanan as governor of the territory of Kansas, ordered an election of delegates to a constitutional convention to be held in June, 1857. The antislavery people declined to participate in the election. The convention met at Lecompton, and drafted a constitution recognizing slavery. The slavery question was to be submitted to the people; that is, they were to vote for the constitution with slavery, or for the constitution without slavery. There was no chance to vote against the constitution as a whole, and it contained a clause protecting property in slaves already in the territory. There were only about 200 slaves in the territory. question again

The constitution with slavery was ratified by the people at the polls by a majority of nearly 6000, but again the anti-

slavery people refrained from voting. They, however, now controlled the legislature, which ordered the constitution as a whole to be resubmitted to the people. This time the proslavery people remained at home and the Lecompton constitution was rejected by 10,000 votes. It thus appeared that the antislavery people were in the majority, but the proslavery inhabitants had the advantage of legality on their side. 

Recognizing the legality of the Lecompton constitution, President Buchanan submitted a copy of it to Congress 

February 2, 1858, and recommended the admission of Kansas.

Douglas had from the first advised the president against sanctioning the Lecompton constitution on the ground that it did not represent the wishes of a majority of the people of Kansas, and Governor Walker took the same view. They objected to the form in which it had first been submitted. 

When the bill to admit Kansas under the Lecompton constitution came up in the Senate, Douglas denounced the president's course in strong terms. The breach between him and the administration was complete and henceforth he was denounced by the extreme Southern wing of the Democratic party as a renegade and a traitor, while he regained his hold on the North. His position was apparently bold and sincere. He claimed that he was upholding his favorite doctrine of popular sovereignty, no matter which way it cut. 

The bill failed to pass Congress, but a compromise measure, the English bill, was passed by both houses. It offered 

Kansas a large grant of government lands on condition that the people should ratify the Lecompton constitution. If they rejected it, then the territory was not to be admitted until it had a large enough population to entitle it to a representative in Congress. Kansas overwhelmingly rejected the proposition and was not admitted until 1861, when it came in as a free state.

In 1858 the people of Illinois had to decide whether they would elect a Democratic legislature which would send

Douglas back to the Senate, or a Republican legislature which would choose Abraham Lincoln, who had come forward as a candidate. Lincoln challenged Douglas

Lincoln is addressing an interested audience, while Douglas stands by awaiting his turn. centered on the respective merits of Douglas's doctrine of popular sovereignty in the territories and the Republican doctrine of congressional control. On the outcome of the contest depended in large measure not only Douglas's seat in the Senate, but his chances for the Democratic presidential nomination in 1860.

The plan followed by Lincoln was to force Douglas either to repudiate his doctrine of popular sovereignty or to deny the full application of the Dred Scott decision, for the two were at variance. According to Douglas's doctrine of popular sovereignty a territory had the right either to adopt or to exclude slavery. According to the decision of the Supreme 

Court Congress had no power to exclude slavery from a territory. In the first debate at Freeport Lincoln asked how a territory could forbid slavery when Congress could not. 

Did a territory have more power than the Congress which created it? Douglas answered that legislation by the people of a territory excluding slavery would make the territory free soil in spite of the Dred Scott decision. This view repudiated the Dred Scott decision, and was in direct opposition to the Southern belief that it was the duty of Congress to protect slave property in the territories.

Although Douglas won the senatorial election by a majority of eight votes in the legislature, Lincoln had forced him into a position which cost him the support of the Southern Democrats two years later. The debate brought Lincoln, who was a comparatively unknown man, into national prominence and led to his nomination for the presidency in 1860.

Feverish excitement throughout the country next year followed the announcement that John Brown, a fanatic who had achieved evil notoriety in Kansas, had with The John the aid of eighteen conspirators seized the United Brown raid, States arsenal at Harpers Ferry, Virginia, with 1859 the intention of arming the Negro slaves for a servile insurrection. His scheme was to carry the arms from the arsenal to the neighboring mountains and establish "camps of freedom" to which the slaves could flee.

The government at once rushed United States troops and Virginia militia to the scene, and after a stout resistance in which ten of his followers were killed Brown was captured.

During his trial he displayed extraordinary fortitude and

would make no defense except that he had been commissioned by God to free the slaves of the South. His serene manner and strange words impressed those who heard him and won him thousands of friends in the North. He was condemned and hanged by authority of the State of Virginia. It was found in the investigation that funds and firearms had been furnished him by prominent men of the North, many of

PART V THE CIVIL WAR CHAPTER XXII SECESSION 

At the beginning of the campaign of 1860, Douglas was the leading Democratic candidate, but the Lincoln-Douglas debates had made him unacceptable to the South- The division ern wing of the party. The Democratic national in the convention met in Charleston, South Carolina, Democratic party, 1860 

April 23, 1860. Douglas had a majority of the delegates, but it was soon evident that he could not secure the necessary two thirds. The California and Oregon delegations acted with the South, and so the anti-Douglas men had 17 out of 33 states, and hence a majority of the committee on resolutions. They reported a radical slavery platform which repudiated popular sovereignty, upheld the decision of the Supreme Court in the Dred Scott case, called on Congress to protect slavery in every territory of the United States, and demanded the repeal of the personal liberty laws in the northern states.

The Douglas men presented a report which reaffirmed the platform adopted four years before, upholding the doctrine of popular sovereignty. After a long wrangle, the Douglas platform was adopted by a vote of 165 to 138. Yancey, the chairman of the Alabama delegation, then arose and announced the withdrawal of Alabama from the convention.

Nomination of Douglas by the Northern wing, and of

Breckin- ridge by the Southern wing

On the following day the question was raised as to whether a nomination could be made by two thirds of the delegates remaining in the convention or whether it was advisable to require two thirds of the original membership. The latter alternative was adopted. 

In the next two days the convention cast 57 ballots. On several ballots Douglas received 162 votes, which was a majority but not two thirds.

As there seemed no chance of reaching a nomination, the convention then adjourned to meet in Baltimore. 

When the convention reassembled in Baltimore, an effort was made to bring the two wings of the party together, but as soon as the convention was organized Virginia led another secession, followed by most of the delegates from Tennessee, North Carolina, Kentucky, and Maryland. This time the seceders carried with them the chairman of the convention, Caleb Cushing of Massachusetts. Those remaining then nominated Stephen A. Douglas on the second ballot, reaffirmed the platform adopted at Charleston, and adjourned. 

In the meantime the Southern Democrats who bolted at Baltimore proceeded to nominate John C. Breckinridge, and this nomination was confirmed by the Charleston bolters who had assembled in Richmond. Breckinridge's wing adopted the platform which had been rejected by the 

Charleston convention.

Meanwhile, the Republican convention had assembled in 

Chicago on May 16. Seward had for some time been considered the leading candidate for the Republican nomination, but he had many enemies. When the convention met, Seward and his friends were Republicans quite confident of his nomination, but Lincoln, though not seriously considered in the East, had the support of Indiana, Illinois, Iowa, and a few individual delegates, and was the favorite candidate of the crowds that paraded the streets and filled the convention hall. The principle of the Dred Scott decision, that slaves were not citizens but a form of property, and that therefore Congress had no power to prohibit slavery anywhere, was repudiated by the Re- publican platform. Secession of 

South 

Carolina and the Gulf

When the result of the election became known, the South Carolina legislature immediately called a state convention, which was to decide whether the state should remain in the Union or not. The delegates to this convention were elected on the issue of secession, and when it convened December 20, 1860, it states unanimously adopted an ordinance of secession, declaring that the union subsisting between South Carolina and the other states under the name of the United States of 

America was dissolved.

Conventions were held in all of the Gulf states during the next six weeks, and ordinances of secession were adopted, in most cases by overwhelming majorities. Mississippi, Florida,

Alabama, Georgia, and Louisiana all seceded in January, and 

Texas February 1. In each case the legislature summoned a convention in the usual constitutional manner. 

There was no conspiracy on the part of the political leaders, as was charged at the time. The people knew what was proposed, and they voted overwhelmingly for immediate secession. 

A few prominent leaders stood out in strong opposition to the movement. The most conspicuous of these were Alexander H. Stephens of Georgia, Sam Houston of Texas, and 

James L. Petigru of South Carolina.

Secession considered

The compact theory of government, which, as we have already seen, was almost universally held at the time that the Constitution of the United States was adopted, historically implied the right to secede. The talk of secession, which had been indulged in with increasing frequency during the period of 1850-1860, was by no means new. 

It had been resorted to as a threat by almost every part of the Union in turn, but, before the action of South Carolina in 1860, no attempt had been made to carry the threat into effect. Threats of secession had first been made in New England in opposition to the Embargo

Act of 1807, to the admission of 

Louisiana as a state, and to the 

War of 1812. When the Louisiana 

Bill was under discussion, Josiah 

Quincy of Massachusetts declared in the Senate: "If this bill passes, it is my deliberate opinion that it is virtually a dissolution of the 

Union; that it will free the States from their moral obligation; and, JOSIAH QUINCY 

amicably if they as it will be the right of all, so it will be the duty of some, definitely to prepare for a separation, can, violently if they must." 

An article appeared in the Connecticut Spectator of August 3, 1814, which was copied with editorial approval in the Salem Gazette, in which we find this statement: "State sovereignty excludes the possibility of State rebellion; a sovereign State may infract its treaties, but can never rebel, nor can any citizen of such State when acting under and in pursuance of its authority, be guilty of treason against the 

United States." In 1843 John Quincy Adams declared in an address to the people of the free states that the annexation of Texas "would be a violation of our national compact"

Secession 

415 of such a character "as not only inevitably to result in a dissolution of the Union, but fully to justify it; and we not only assert that the people of the free States ought not to submit to it, but we say, with confidence, they would not submit to it." 

Lodge and Charles Adams

In his Life of Daniel Webster Senator Henry Cabot Lodge made the following statement: "When the Constitution was adopted by the votes of States at Phila- Views of delphia, and accepted by the votes of States in Henry Cabot popular conventions, it is safe to say that there was not a man in the country from Washington Francis and Hamilton on the one side, to George Clinton and George Mason on the other, who regarded the new system as anything but an experiment entered upon by the States and from which each and every State had the right peaceably to withdraw, a right which was very likely to be exercised." Charles Francis Adams in an address on The 

Constitutional Ethics of Secession asks the question, To whom was allegiance due in case of direct conflict between a state and the federal government? And he says: "I do not think the answer admits of doubt. If put in 1788, or indeed at any time anterior to 1825, the immediate reply of nine men out of ten in the Northern States, and of ninetynine out of a hundred in the Southern States, would have been that, as between the Union and the State, ultimate allegiance was due to the State." states

Yet the action of South Carolina appeared precipitate to the majority of people in the upper belt of southern states, as they had no fear of an attack by the federal Attitude of government on the institution of slavery as it the border existed in any state. The border state men generally tried to bring about a compromise between the radicals of the North and South. On December 18, 1860, Senator

Crittenden of Kentucky proposed a constitutional amendment, forbidding slavery north of 36° 30′ and recognizing it

south of that line in all territories then held or thereafter to be acquired. This amendment was practically a revival of the Missouri Compromise. Lincoln expressed himself as strongly opposed to any such compromise, on the ground that it would encourage the South to acquire more territory south of that line. The vote of the committee which finally reported on the amendment stood six for and seven against it.

Between the election of 

Lincoln and his inauguration, there was a period Attitude of of great suspense. Buchanan 

President Buchanan had been intimately associated with the 

Southern leaders. He believed that the states had no right to secede, but he also believed that the Union had no right to coerce them. He refused, therefore, either to recognize a dissolution of the Union and arrange terms of separation with the seceding states, or to take any measure to coerce them, or to protect the property of the United States within their limits. The election of Lincoln had precipitated the crisis and he proposed to let Lincoln meet it.
