Early in the session Congress extended the suffrage in the District of Columbia to the Negro. This was a forewarning of what was coming. 

No large group was able to agree on the constitutional status of the southern states. According to the Southern The con- stitutional theory the states that had attempted secession were still states, all the essentials of statehood remaining unchanged. This was the theory on which Sherman acted when in granting terms of surrender to Johnston he had agreed that the existing status of the southern states

The Reconstruction of the Southern States 499 state governments should be recognized. This agreement was repudiated by the administration, and the state governments were overthrown by the military commanders. 

The presidential theory, as mentioned above, was that the southern states had never ceased to be members of the Union; that their governments had temporarily fallen into the hands of disloyal persons; and that just as soon as loyal governments were reëstablished in these states they could resume their functions as members of the Union. Views of Stevens

The novel theory of state suicide, advanced by Sumner, Iwas that the Confederate States had through treason forfeited their rights as states and relapsed into the status of territories, and therefore were subject like Sumner and the other territories to the exclusive jurisdiction of Congress. Stevens' view was even more radical. He agreed with Sumner as to the effect upon the states of their own disloyal acts, but denied that they possessed even the attributes of territories under the Constitution. He claimed that they were conquered provinces subject to the arbitrary will of Congress, and denied to their inhabitants even the rights enjoyed under the Constitution by citizens of the territories. 

The prevailing theory was that the people in each seceding state had committed a political crime against the nation and forfeited for the time being their political rights; that the constitutional clause guaranteeing to each state a republican form of government makes Congress, and not the president, the final arbiter as to the political status of a state, and that therefore Congress should direct the work of reconstruction and decide when and on what conditions the states should be readmitted.

In February, 1867, the Committee on Reconstruction reported to the House a bill which provided for state governments on the basis of Negro suffrage. It set aside Radical rethe reorganized state governments in the late Con- construction federate States, with the exception of Tennessee, and divided

Senate amended the bills so as to provide that the military governors should be appointed by the president, instead of by the general of the army. It was considered beyond the powers of Congress to deprive the president of his position as commander-in-chief of the army. The bill was finally passed with an amendment excluding from the suffrage and from office those persons who were excluded by the Fourteenth 

Amendment. On March 2 the president vetoed the bill, but it was passed over his veto the same day. Thus two years after the war was over the work of restoration carried on by Lincoln and Johnson was undone and the South thrown back under military rule. "Carpet- baggers wags

It is difficult to get a fair picture of Johnson's character, as no president of the United States has fared so badly at the hands of historians. Only in recent years, with Character of the publication of the diary of Gideon Welles and Andrew Johnson the acquisition of Johnson's papers by the Library of Congress has the verdict of his contemporaries been set aside. Sprung from the "poor whites" of North Carolina, he moved early to Tennessee and became a tailor. He did not learn to read and write until taught by his wife after their marriage. His strong intellect, positive convictions, and

ready speech, crude but forceful, enabled him to make his way to the front, but to the last his character was marred by marks of the hard conditions of his youth. At several of the critical moments of his public career he gave way to unseemly outbursts of passion, and once or twice to his fondness for strong drink, though his excesses in this matter were greatly exaggerated. He was placed on the ticket with Lincoln as

Republican. He was despised by the South because he had the poor white's jealousy of the Southern aristocrat and wanted to make treason odious by hanging Jefferson

Confederacy, and he was distrusted by the North because he had the poor white's contempt for the Negro and wanted to deny him civil and political equality. Yet no one who makes an impartial study of his career can deny to him the two great virtues of patriotism and moral courage.

Negro vote. Amendment

All the southern states except Virginia, Mississippi, and 

Texas had ratified the Fourteenth Amendment by June, 1868, and been readmitted to representation in The Congress. It was soon evident that the second Fifteenth section of that amendment would not assure the vote to the Negro, for the southern states would prefer to have their representation in Congress reduced rather than submit to Negro rule. The Fifteenth Amendment was, therefore, proposed, declaring that "The right of citizens of the United States to vote shall not be denied or abridged by the United States or by any State on account of race, color, or previous condition of servitude." The ratification of this amendment was made a further condition of readmission in the case of Virginia, Mississippi, Texas, and Georgia.

In 1870 this amendment was declared in force and the remaining states were readmitted. rule

Carpetbaggers and scalawags now dominated public affairs in the South through the manipulation of the Negro vote. 

The agents of the Freedmen's Bureau played The South leading part in organizing the Negroes against their under Negro late masters through means of the Union League and its secret ritual. The reconstruction conventions and legislatures contained numbers of Negroes and the extravagance of the governments knew no bounds. The public debts of several states increased at an alarming rate without any corresponding benefit to the people. Vast sums were spent

in the purchase of mahogany desks, costly carpets, and other furnishings for legislative halls and the offices of public officials. In the capitol at Columbia, South Carolina, the legislature maintained a free restaurant where its "black and tan" members could satisfy their desires for meat or drink at any hour free of charge.

The Ku- 

Klux Klan

A secret organization known as the Ku-Klux Klan was organized in Tennessee in 1867 to check these abuses, and within two years it spread over the entire South. 

With masks and white coverings for horse and rider its members dashed along the country roads at night or through the streets of villages terrorizing the Negro and keeping him from attending the secret meetings of the Union League. At first the Klan played mainly upon the superstitions of the Negro, but it did not hesitate to visit serious offenses with prompt punishment even to the point of taking life. The rule of this "invisible empire" naturally led to excesses, and after a congressional investigation in 1871 an act was passed empowering the president to use the army in suppressing the Klan. It had, however, put a damper on the political aspirations of the Negro and had done much to reëstablish white supremacy in the South. 

Grant's first tion

Having had no experience at all in civil administration, President Grant made poor selections of advisers and officeholders. To make matters worse, thousands of administra- men who had helped to save the Union were clamoring for government patronage. The result was that Grant's administration was one of the most corrupt in the history of the government. In 1869 James Fisk and 

Jay Gould, two of the most unscrupulous stock speculators in Wall Street, planned a deliberate scheme to secure a corner in gold, and through indirect influence they succeeded in getting Grant to instruct the secretary of the treasury to sell no more gold, as he had been doing from time to time in order to keep the price from soaring too high. Their plan came

The Reconstruction of the Southern States 507 

very near succeeding, and Friday, September 24, 1869, has ever been known as "Black Friday" in Wall Street. The plot was revealed to Grant in time to prevent the complete success of the scheme, but not until a number of banking firms had failed and others had suffered severely. movement

A Liberal Republican movement began early in his administration in opposition to the president. When it became evident that he would be renominated, the Liberal Liberal Republicans decided to place a candidate in the Republican field. They held a national convention at Chicago in May, 1872, and nominated Horace Greeley of New York. Among other things, the new party demanded "the immediate and absolute removal of all disability imposed on account of the rebellion which was finally subdued seven years ago, believing that universal amnesty will result in complete pacification in all sections of the country." The 

Democratic convention decided to indorse Greeley, and to adopt the platform of the Liberal Republicans. 

Grant was nominated by acclamation at the Republican convention in Philadelphia. In the election Grant received 

3,597,070 votes, and Greeley 2,834,079. Greeley Grant carried only six states, Georgia, Kentucky, Mary- reëlected land, Missouri, Tennessee, and Texas. He was heartbroken at the result and died a few weeks after the election. 

On the last day of Grant's first administration, March 3, 1873, Congress passed the so-called "Salary Grab" Act increasing the salaries of the president, vice-president, and Supreme Court justices, as well as raising the salaries of members of Congress from $5000 to $7500 a year. The worst feature of the act was that it was to be retroactive and to date from the beginning of the Congress which was just closing. This meant, of course, that the members of Congress voted themselves each a bonus of $5000. The act raised a storm of protest and was repealed by the succeeding Congress.

Within a few hours after the closing of the polls it was known that Tilden had carried New York, New Jersey, Connecticut, and Indiana, and on the morning after election nearly every newspaper in the country announced his victory, but there were two notable exceptions, the New York Herald and the New York Times, which said that the result was in doubt. As it turned out, Tilden had 184 undisputed votes and Hayes 165, while there were in dispute 7 votes in South 

Carolina, 4 in Florida, 8 in Louisiana, and 1 in Oregon. 

Hayes needed every disputed vote in order to win.

The con- returns Since one of the three Republican electors in Oregon was a postmaster, and constitutionally ineligible, the governor gave a certificate of election to the highest elector on the Democratic ticket. The secretary of state, how- tested ever, issued a certificate to the three Republican electors. In Florida, where the vote was very close, the 

Democratic member of the returning board gave the certificates to the Democratic electors, while his two colleagues declared the Republican electors chosen.

The spectacle of two governors and two legislatures was seen in Louisiana and South Carolina, the Republican gov-

ernment in each case upheld by Federal bayonets and the Democratic government claiming to be the choice of the people. In Louisiana the Republican board of state canvassers in a recount threw out several thousand Democratic votes in order to give Hayes a majority. James Ford Rhodes says in this connection: "As a matter of fact, Wells (the chairman of the board) and his satellites in secret conclave determined the presidency of the United States, but, before returning the vote of Louisiana for Hayes, there is little doubt that he offered to give it to Tilden for $200,000." 

With disputed returns in four states, the Constitution was ambiguous as The electoral commission to who should decide their validity.

RUTHERFORD B. HAYES 

The twenty-second joint rule adopted by Congress in 1865 provided that if either House refused to accept the vote of any state, the vote of that state should be thrown out.

In 1873 the votes of Louisiana and Arkansas had been excluded under this rule. Tilden had a popular majority of 

264,000 and a good chance to win, but he did not manage his case well.

To cut the Gordian knot, Congress passed an act creating an electoral commission with full power to determine the cases in dispute. The act named, as members of the commission, five senators, five representatives, and four members of the Supreme Court: seven Republicans and seven Democrats. 

The four justices were to select a fifth member of the court as the fifteenth member of the commission.

The Reconstruction of the Southern States 511 elected The justices were expected to name as the all-important fifteenth member Justice Davis, an independent in politics, but just before the bill was passed Davis was Hayes elected to the United States Senate by the legis- declared lature of Illinois and resigned from the court. 

Justice Bradley, a Republican, was finally put on the commission, which was thus composed of eight Republicans and seven Democrats. In every important case that came before them the vote stood eight to seven. As a result, all the votes in dispute were given to Hayes, and he was declared to have been elected president of the United States. This result was not reached until March 2, 1877, two days before the day set for the inauguration of the new president. Restoration South

This was the most serious election crisis that ever faced the country, and another civil war was narrowly averted. The 

Democrats, however, offered no resistance, and it is now known that assurances were given to the of home Democratic leaders through some of Hayes's rule in the friends, that in case they would acquiesce in the decision of the commission Hayes would immediately withdraw the troops from the South. As this was one of the main objects of the Democrats, they accepted the compromise. Hayes did not help the situation when he rewarded 

Wells, the chairman of the Louisiana Returning Board, and his friends by appointing them to good positions under the federal government. The Republican governors of Louisiana and South Carolina who had certified the Hayes returns were unable to maintain themselves without federal aid and withdrew with the troops, leaving the field to their Democratic opponents, who were promptly recognized by Hayes.

PART VI THE NEW INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION CHAPTER XXVII "BIG BUSINESS" AND ORGANIZED LABOR 

ALTHOUGH the Industrial Revolution, as we have seen (page 378), took place in England in the second half of the eighteenth century, the factory system made comparatively little progress in the United States before the Civil War. We were mainly an agricultural people and dependent to a large extent on foreign manufactures. In fact it was not until 1880 that the value of domestic manufactures exceeded the value of farm products.

 introduced a new industrial era in this country. The demand for munitions, iron and steel, clothing and food was a tremendous stimulus to industry. The revolution It was met by erecting furnaces and factories, economic introducing new processes and inventions, and improving agricultural machinery. The high tariff of the war fostered these industries in the North and was continued for their protection after the restoration of peace. The few manufactures that were developed by the necessities of war in the South disappeared with the fall of the Confederacy, and the South, destitute of capital, continued to be almost exclusively an agricultural community for another generation. 

The economic revolution that took place in the North during the same generation was in some ways more fundamental even than the English industrial revolution of the eighteenth century. The new industrial revolution in 513

America introduced a new civilization, so far as all the material conditions of life are concerned. It is a civilization based on science and invention, on steel, oil, and electricity, and the end is not yet. We are living in the midst of stupendous changes.

By the end of the nineteenth century this industrial upheaval had made the United States the greatest manufactur- Manufac- ing nation of the world. We were not only supplying most of our own needs, but also exporting manufactured products to the ends of the earth. The rapid tures growth of American in- dustry was due to several causes, chief among them being the vast natural resources of mine and forest, producing raw materials in abundance, and the wide distribution of water power, used at first for turning the wheels of mills and now used for producing electric power which is distributed to factories over wider areas. 

The existence of cheap land on the frontier tended to divert labor from the factories, but the demand for labor was met in part by immigrants and in part by American inventive genius, which has developed labor-saving machinery to an amazing extent. 

As a result, American industry has become noted for standardized machine-made products and large-scale production. 

A BESSEMER CONVERTER IN OPERATION 

The steel industry, the fundamental basis of the economic revolution, made rapid strides in the years directly following the Civil War. This came about as the result of a new

Steel soon replaced iron in The iron and machinery, tools, agricultural implements, loco- steel motives, and rails. Another factor in the rapid industry growth of the steel industry was the abundant deposits of coal. 

Pittsburgh, in the center of the anthracite region, became the principal seat of iron and steel manufactures. Petroleum and natural gas also contributed their part in developing the gigantic industries of this city and region. In more recent Cleveland

It was not until the Civil War that the vast mineral resources of the country were fully explored. Improved means of transportation and communication was another vital part of this economic revolution. Railroad Transportation and communi- cation mileage, about 30,000 in 1860, had nearly doubled by 1870, and by the end of the century it had risen to 193,000 miles, considerably more than that of all the countries of Europe combined. Pullman sleeping cars and steel rails were introduced before 1870. 

Locomotives were being constantly improved. The telegraph system was also greatly improved and extended, so that it became a valuable adjunct to business.

As the result of years of persistent effort on the part of 

Cyrus W. Field, cable communication with Europe was finally established in 1866.

The mail service, too, was brought to a high state of efficiency. Free delivery and money orders were both introduced before the close of the Civil War. In 1885 the postage rate on letters was reduced to two cents an ounce, the rate which stands to-day.

CYRUS W. FIELD 

On the great plains of the Middle West, where the grain ripens over wide areas at the same time and has to be har- Agricultural vested within a few days, production was at first machinery seriously limited by the scarcity of labor. This situation was met by the invention and development of agricultural machinery. The McCormick reaper, as we have

"Big Business" and Organized Labor

Labor 519 seen, was invented in 1831, and came into general use in the West during the decade preceding the Civil War. It enabled the North not only to feed its armies but to export a large surplus of wheat, mainly to England. The great development of agricultural machinery, however, took place after the Civil War. The processes of cutting, binding, and threshing were finally combined in one huge "harvester." 

M'CORMICK DEERING A MODERN CORN HARVESTER 

Improved machinery was likewise applied to plowing and harrowing, to corn-harvesting, and to almost every process of farming. Along with these inventions came the change from horse power to the use of steam and finally of gasoline. At the same time there was great advance in scientific methods of farming, particularly in the use of fertilizers, the preservation of the soil, and the adaptation and variation of crops. 

As a result of these revolutionary changes in agriculture, farmers now required capital, and farming in many ways

resembled large-scale production. The man without means could no longer take up a small piece of land and with a horse or mule and a few simple implements make a living for himself" and his family.

One of the most significant results of the economic revolution has been the drift of population to the cities. In Jefferson's day we were an agricultural people, and his system of democracy found its support in the ranks of the small independent farming class. As late as 1860

The chief artificial stimulus to manufactures has been the tariff. Before the Civil War the national government was largely dominated by statesmen from the agricul- The tariff tural South. The tariff question became a subject of political agitation after the War of 1812 and precipitated the nullification controversy of 1832, but after the compromise reached at that time the principle of protection made little headway until the Civil War, when the system of high protective tariffs became firmly established. It might 

CHICAGO TO-DAY 

P. & A. Photo have been expected that the high duties adopted to meet the exigencies of war would be lowered after the restoration of peace, but such was not the case. The exclusion of Southern representatives from Congress enabled the manufacturing North through the dominant Republican party to maintain the protective system. The Liberal Republicans of 1872 demanded a revision of the war tariffs, but this demand made little impression on the regular wing of the party and the panic of 1873 overshadowed the question and caused it to be dropped.

In 1882 President Arthur pointed to the treasury surplus and suggested a reduction of the tariff rates. The tariff was "revised but not changed." Five years later President 

Cleveland forced the issue.

To-day a surplus would not be an embarrassment to the government, for the people have grown accustomed to large Surplus and expenditures, but in the eighties the public attitude pensions was different. A large part of the Civil War debt had been paid off and the rest funded in long-term bonds. 

Most of the emergency taxation of the Civil War period had been repealed, but the high tariff continued to roll up a large surplus in the treasury and this surplus invited extravagance in appropriations. The annual River and Harbor Bill had grown to enormous proportions, and both Arthur and Cleveland had found it necessary to interpose the veto. 

The politicians, however, discovered a new means of disposing of the surplus. Pensions had been granted hitherto for disabilities received in the service. In 1887 Congress passed a bill granting pensions for incapacity and dependence of every kind, and Cleveland promptly vetoed it. A bill of the same character was, however, passed under Harrison in 1890, which in the course of ten years took out of the public treasury $1,350,000,000. Pensions were later granted to all who had seen three months' service, so that during the next decade the appropriations were even larger, and they still continue. 

As the South has paid its share of this enormous sum, which has been distributed mainly in the North and West, the pension system has had the effect of imposing on the South one of the heaviest war indemnities that any conquered people have ever been called on to pay. The system has not only impoverished the South, but also won thousands of supporters for a high tariff.

President Cleveland had other ideas as to the method of reducing the surplus. In his annual message of 1887 he gave almost bis entire attention to the topic of tariff reform. In

"Big Business" and Organized Labor 523 1888 a tariff bill led to a great debate in the House. Cleveland, in his plea for lower rates, had the solid support of the Democratic party. The Republicans were The tariff equally united against the measure, and thus for becomes a the first time in more than twenty years the two party issue great national parties were lined up on a definite, clear-cut issue. The bill passed the House of Representatives, but with the Republicans in control of the Senate it was not allowed to come to a vote in that body. 

Tariff Act 

President Cleveland had thus staked his political fortunes on a single issue. He was again the Democratic nominee and it was expected that Blaine would again oppose The him, but on the eve of the Republican convention McKinley 

Blaine withdrew his name and Benjamin Harrison of Indiana was nominated. Probably no presidential campaign in American history has been confined more closely to one issue than the tariff campaign of 1888. Although

Cleveland received a popular majority of over 100,000 votes, Harrison had a majority of the electoral votes. Notwithstanding the closeness of the vote, the Republicans proceeded to enact the McKinley Tariff Bill of 1890. The duties were raised to an average about fifty per cent higher than any level ever reached before. The McKinley Act was regarded by its advocates as the triumph of protection, but it proved unpopular. In the congressional election held a few months later the Democrats sent a large majority to the House, and in 1892 Cleveland was returned to the presidency.

Cleveland hastened to carry out the party pledges, and a tariff bill embodying his views was put through the House under the leadership of William L. Wilson. Gorman of Maryland. Cleveland was revision

so chagrined at the failure of a Democratic Senate to carry out the party pledges that he let the bill become a law without his signature.

The system of high protection, originating during the Civil War, has become so strongly intrenched that no political party is likely again to advocate a "tariff for revenue only." 

All that the Democratic party advocated in its platform of 1928 was the correction of abuses. It declared that a tariff should not be framed solely for the purpose of amassing profits for manufacturers, but that it should have regard for the

"Big Business" and Organized Labor 525 It needs of industry, agriculture, workers, and consumers. admitted that the rates should be high enough to cover the difference between the cost of production abroad and at home. 

It recognized furthermore the fact that foreign trade is a matter of give and take, that we cannot continue indefinitely to exclude foreign products from our markets and expect to increase the sale of our goods abroad. 

CELEBRATING THE COMPLETION OF THE UNION PACIFIC RAILROAD 

grown construction

As already noted, one of the most striking features of the industrial development of the United States has been the building of railroads. In 1860 we had 30,000 Railroad miles of track. By 1910 the mileage had to 250,000, which was about one third of that of the entire world. Since the beginning of the World War new construction has practically ceased. This was due not so much to war conditions as to other causes. Railroad building had been overdone, most of the roads were in financial straits, and they were beginning to feel the competition of motor cars and trucks.

The first transcontinental line, the Union Pacific, was chartered by Congress in 1862 and completed in 1869. Its construction was made possible by land grants and govern-

The great transcontinental lines ment loans. The Northern Pacific was chartered in 1864, but as a result of the failure of Jay Cooke, its chief promoter, in the panic of 1873, it was not completed until 

1883. The following year the Atchison, Topeka, and Santa Fe opened a southern route to California along the old Santa Fe trail. A little later James J. Hill completed the organization of the Great Northern system. 

By 1890 the trans-Mississippi region was well supplied with railroads and the western frontier was fast disappearing.

Consolida tion of eastern roads While all this construction was going on in the West, there was a rapid consolidation of short lines in the East. Cornelius 

Vanderbilt was the leader in this movement. In 

1865 he sold his steamboats, from which he had amassed a fortune of ten millions, and devoted his energies to organizing a through railway line from New York to Chicago. He started with the Hudson River line to 

Albany, acquired the New York Central in 1867, and leased the Lake Shore and Michigan Southern in 1873. When he died in 1877 at the age of eighty-three, he left what seemed then a fabulous fortune of over a hundred million dollars. 

Some of this was derived from legitimate profits, but the greater part came from the manipulation of railroad stocks.

The consolidation and extension of other roads quickly followed. The Pennsylvania and the Baltimore and Ohio extended their systems westward, finally reaching Chicago and St. Louis. In the southern states the process of consolidation took place more slowly. 

With the development of railroads, river and canal transportation has declined. Traffic on the Mississippi has fallen off steadily since the eighties, until it is now relatively insignificant. Many canals have been canal traffic abandoned, and canal mileage to-day is less than half of what it formerly was.

The farmers were at the mercy of the railroads, being dependent usually on one line. A farmers' organization "Granger " formed in 1867, known as the Patrons of Huslegislation bandry, made the first demands for state regulation. It was made up of local groups of farmers known as "granges" and the movement which it inaugurated to regulate railroads and improve general farming conditions was known as the "Granger Movement." As a result of its efforts several states in the Middle West passed laws which undertook to establish maximum rates, to prohibit a greater charge for a short haul than for a long one, to prohibit the consolidation of competing lines, and to put a stop to the issuing of free passes. The railroads contested these laws in the courts on the ground that the fixing of rates deprived them of property and was therefore in conflict with the Fourteenth Amendment. They failed to make good this contention, but in 1886 the Supreme Court held that state regulation interfered with interstate commerce and that the regulation of roads which crossed state boundaries was exclusively a federal function.

The Inter- merce Act

The next year Congress passed the Interstate Commerce Act. It created a commission of five members, not more than three of whom should belong to the same state Com- political party, and gave it power to investigate and prevent unfair discrimination in rates. The courts interpreted the act very narrowly and thus deprived the commission of many of the powers which Congress had intended to give it. The railroads were not disposed to recognize the public character of their business and did everything they could to evade the law. The creation of the commission was, however, a step in the right direction, and it

"Big Business" and Organized Labor 529 rendered valuable services in collecting and publishing statistics.

In 1903 James J. Hill and J. P. Morgan had tried to effect a merger of the Great Northern and Northern Pacific railroads through the Northern Securities Company, The case formed for the purpose of holding a majority of the Northern stock of both roads. President Roosevelt had Securities them prosecuted for violation of the Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890, and the federal courts ordered a dissolution of the Northern 

Securities Company. This decision failed to restore competition between the two roads, but it convinced the public that competition could no longer be relied upon to regulate rates and that governmental control of some kind was necessary. The powers of the Interstate 

Commerce Commission were greatly enlarged by the Hepburn Act of 1906, and the railroads were brought under closer control.

The trust form of organization was adopted by other industries and we soon had a Sugar Trust, a Whisky Trust, Antitrust and a Tobacco Trust. Meanwhile the unfair agitation methods employed by the Standard Oil Company had thoroughly aroused the public. The American people were still wedded to the idea of competition as a fundamental economic principle and were strongly opposed to monopoly in any form. During the late eighties many state legislatures adopted measures to prevent combinations or agreements in restraint of trade, but as long as states like New Jersey, Delaware, and West Virginia took no action, corporations and trusts could secure liberal charters from them and carry on their business without restraint in other parts of the country.

In response to a widespread popular demand Congress passed the Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890, which declared 

The Sherman Anti- trust Act illegal "every contract, combination in the form of trust or otherwise, or conspiracy, in restraint of trade or commerce among the several States, or with foreign nations." The courts hesitated to interpret literally such sweeping language. Did the act apply to railroad combinations as well as industrial? Did it apply to labor organizations? Was a strike a conspiracy in restraint of trade? Should a distinction be made between acts in restraint of trade that were reasonable and fair and those that were unreasonable? These and other questions led the courts to construe the act rather narrowly. Nevertheless the Standard Oil and other trusts had to change their form of organization. It was, however, a change in form rather than

The opposition to a national bank had never died out, but in order to curb the New 

York "money trust" and to afford banking facilities for the rest of the country, a compromise was reached in the 

Federal Reserve Act of 1913. The act revised radically the financial system that had grown up under the 

National Banking Act of 1863. It divided the country into twelve districts and established a reserve bank in each to act as a clearing house for member banks. 

The federal reserve banks were also given the right to issue notes secured by commercial paper as well as notes secured by a deposit of government bonds. The new system has made the currency more elastic and greatly diminished the danger of financial panics to which the old system frequently gave rise.

In social conditions the industrial revolution has had a profound effect. Under the old system employers worked with 

Capital and laborers or personally superintended them. With the growth of factories conflicts between capital and labor arose. The workmen came in contact only with superintendents and agents employed by the corporations. 

The capitalists and stockholders who owned the factory or mill frequently lived in distant cities and were interested mainly in profits. 

The labor

The panic of 1837, as we have seen, put an end to the first labor movement in America. During the fifties the movement was revived and several national trade movement unions came into existence. With the industrial development that followed the Civil War the number of wage-earners increased rapidly, and one labor organization after another was formed, each one growing in experience and strength. First came the National Labor Union, a loose federation of local unions, formed in 1866, but it did not meet with much success and was eventually eclipsed by the Noble Order of the Knights of Labor. The new organization had its beginning in a small group of Philadelphia garment workers in 1869. Its aim was to combine all toilers, skilled and unskilled, whether they belonged to trade unions or not, in one great organization which could present a solid front to capitalism and agitate for industrial reforms, such as an eight-hour day, the abolition of child labor, and the arbitration of disputes. It operated at first as a secret order and

"Big Business" and Organized Labor 537 made little progress. In 1881 it came out in the open and within five years increased its membership to 700,000. It engaged in a number of strikes and boycotts and attracted to its ranks many socialists and radical agitators who advocated extreme measures. Internal dissensions resulting from its heterogeneous membership were the main reasons for its decline, which was as rapid as its rise. 

The American Federation of Labor had been formed in 1881 as a national federation of trade unions. Its chief' tion of Labor promoter and directing genius was Samuel The Ameri- 

Gompers, an English Jew, who came to New York can Federa City during the Civil War and soon became the leading spirit in the Cigar Makers' Union. He was the first president of the Federation and held this office almost continuously until his death in 1924. Under his wise leadership the membership increased from 150,000 in 1886 to 3,000,000 at the time of his death. Gompers pursued a conservative policy, refusing to let the Federation become identified with socialism or enter the field of politics as a labor party. He always worked for practical ends and succeeded in securing from the two major parties a large body of labor legislation, both state and federal, such as the eight-hour day, childlabor laws, workingmen's compensation, and the restriction of immigration.

The American Federation of Labor includes only members of unions, thus excluding the unskilled and unorganized laborers. The four great railway brotherhoods Independent engineers, conductors, firemen, and trainmen— organizahave refused to join the Federation. Organized tions originally as mutual insurance associations, they have a membership of half a million, have accumulated large reserves, occupy a strong independent position, and have nothing to gain by becoming affiliated with the Federation. 

Another unaffiliated group, which has attracted great attention, is the Industrial Workers of the World. This

organization was formed in 1905 by the more radical agitators who did not find much encouragement in the Federation. Its membership was recruited mainly from 

The I.W.W. unskilled workers in the Far West and it never numbered over 75,000. Its unpatriotic activities during the World War caused the government to adopt repressive measures from which it has not fully recovered. 

Conflicts be The main conflicts between labor and capital have grown out of disputes over wages and the right of laborers to organize. Some idea of the extent of industrial contween labor flicts may be gained from the statistics of the and capital

United States Bureau of Labor, which records over 

34,000 strikes between 1881 and 1905, involving losses exceeding half a billion dollars. Many of these strikes resulted in bloodshed and untold suffering.

Some of these strikes have become historic. The first to attract nation-wide attention was the great railroad strike of 1877, brought about by a general reduction of wages on the 

New York Central, Pennsylvania, and Baltimore and Ohio railroads. Rioting, destruction of property, and loss of life occurred in Baltimore, Martinsburg, Pittsburgh, Chicago, and St. Louis. The state militias were unable to control the strikers and President Hayes was finally called upon to send federal troops to restore order.

Another strike, which attracted the attention of the entire country, occurred at the plant of the Carnegie Steel Company The Home- at Homestead, Pennsylvania. Three hundred stead strike Pinkerton detectives were employed by the company to protect the plant against the strikers. Their arrival precipitated a fight in which ten men were killed and sixty others wounded. The idea that industrial barons should be permitted to hire men to fight their battles, instead of relying on the laws and the public police force to protect them, was utterly repugnant to most Americans. The conquest and settlement of this region constitute one of the most thrilling and romantic stories in American history.

The Mormon community was a highly developed economic unit as well as a religious one. Brigham Young was an able business man. There was little or no money in Mormon incirculation then, and people were paid for their stitutions services in orders on stores for food, clothing, and household wares. Notwithstanding his efforts to compel the faithful to deal exclusively with these, he was unable to shut out competition completely. So widespread and autocratic was Young's influence that the federal governors of Utah, appointed by the president after the organization of territorial government in 1850, found it difficult to assert their authority. 

From the first the Mormon settlements grew rapidly and prospered greatly. Their missionaries carried the gospel of 

Mormonism all over the United States and into foreign countries. Converts from the older states and from the

The Indians of the West, despite their lack of numbers and organization, stubbornly opposed the advance of the The Indians white man. At the close of the Civil War there of the plains were about 250,000 Indians on the Great Plains and in the Rocky Mountain region, and nearly 50,000 on the Pacific coast. Although widely scattered, the warriors moved with such rapidity on their swift ponies that small parties of whites bound for the mining regions of the West were always liable to sudden and unexpected attacks. The Indians of the plains were a strong and vigorous race, expert horsemen, and they displayed great skill and courage in their encounters with the whites. They paid little attention to agriculture, had little property except their ponies and their weapons, and spent their time in hunting. Their life was dependent upon the great herds of buffalo that roamed over the western prairies. From these they derived their principal food and clothing.

The inrush of miners and settlers during the Civil War started hostilities which kept up almost incessantly until 1886. The most intensive periods of the con- 

Indian wars flict were the years 1865-1867 and 1875-1876. It was a life and death struggle between two types of civilization, and of course the Indian was doomed. In 1864 the Cheyenne and allied tribes went on the warpath and began attacks on the settlers in Nebraska and Colorado which soon developed into a regular war. The Sioux tribes of the north soon grew restless and began attacks on the route from Minnesota to Montana. The years 1866 and 1867 presented an alarming situation. The government had 25,000 troops in the field

stationed at strategic points extending all the way from Minnesota to New Mexico, but this force was unable to afford adequate protection. Settlements were destroyed, stagecoaches robbed, trains held up, and men, women, and children killed. The atrocities were not all on one side. 

In fact, some of the worst were committed by the whites. 

Such was the Sand Creek massacre in which an unoffending Cheyenne village was suddenly attacked by a regiment of Colorado volunteers and its population of five or six hundred men, women, and children slaughtered. This incident sent a thrill of horror through the East, but was applauded by many of the western settlers, who believed that the only solution of the question lay in the extermination of the Indian and that the sooner it was over the better. To General 

Sheridan was attributed the saying: "There are no good 

Indians but dead Indians." reservations Congress finally decided that it was cheaper to feed the Indian than to fight him. A series of treaties was signed in 1867 and 1868 with a number of tribes, which The Indians established two large reservations. The south- assigned ern branch of the Cheyenne and other tribes along the route of the Union Pacific Railroad were moved to Indian Territory, and the Sioux were assigned a large reservation in western Dakota with the Black Hills in the center. 

The object of these arrangements was to separate the northern and southern tribes and open a way for the completion of the Union Pacific Railroad.

Relations with the Indians improved for a time, but sporadic outbreaks continued. Finally in 1876 the Sioux again took the warpath under the last great Indian The Sioux leader, the famous Sitting Bull. During the seventies and eighties young men went west to seek their fortunes, workingmen and their families to build homes on their own land, immigrants from Europe to start life anew in this wonderful land of opportunity. 

Land was plentiful and cheap, but not always as productive as its purchasers had been led to believe, and many of the settlers were wholly unfitted for the hard conditions of life on the frontier. Many of them were unable to pay for their lands and lived under the burden of heavy mortgages without much hope of being able to lift them. These conditions gave rise to unrest and political agitation.

The advance of the white man and the building of railroads were accompanied by the wasteful and ruthless slaughter of the great herds of buffalo that lived on the western plains. Estimates of the number of buffalo when railroad construction began run as high as fifteen millions. Within twenty-five years they had been practically exterminated in the United States, and the only ones left were found on the plains of Canada. With the building of the Union Pacific, buffalo robes and hides were shipped east and were soon in great demand. By 1875 the herd which ranged the southwestern plains had been exterminated. This was mainly the work of professional hunters who took the hides and left the meat to waste, though sportsmen from various parts of the world came to take part in the hunt. The northern herd up in Montana and the Dakotas survived a little longer, but was killed off in the late eighties. The destruction of the buffalo, depriving the Indian of his most important occupation and means of livelihood, was one of the main causes of his discontent. 

He naturally hated the white man, who deprived him of his big game and his hunting ranges. 

Mining in California and The incoming settlers developed three great industries in the West: mining, cattle raising, and agriculture. At first the chief interest was in mining. The discovery of gold in California had laid the economic foundations of that state. The placer deposits in the sand and gravel of streams could be worked by individuals and did not require the outlay of capital necessary to extract gold from quartz, but these deposits were exhausted in a few years and the gold hunters rushed Colorado

to other fields. In 1859 gold and silver were discovered in 

Colorado, and in a short time 100,000 people were attracted to that region. The Colorado deposits were embedded in quartz and prospectors who had come without capital soon departed. Denver sprang up as a thriving town and was the main source of supplies for the mines as well as the abode of 

A PIONEER WASHING FOR GOLD 

the wealthy miners. The permanent population of Colorado increased slowly, and it was 1876 before the territory was admitted as a state. 

While the rush to Colorado was still in progress, the richest silver deposit in the world, the famous Comstock Lode, was discovered in Nevada, then the western part The silver of Utah. Virginia City, which sprang up almost mines of over night, was one of the marvels of the age. 

Miners from California and Colorado and adventurers from Nevada

distant parts of the earth hastened to Nevada. By 1864 the population was so large and increasing so rapidly that Nevada was admitted as a state. In twenty years the Comstock Lode yielded silver bullion valued at over $300,000,000, but in the late seventies it suddenly ran out, and no other such rich deposits were discovered. The population rapidly declined, but, having been admitted to statehood, Nevada continued to have one representative and two senators at Washington. It became a sort of pocket borough represented by silver senators who maintained nominal residences in Nevada but had their palatial homes on Nob Hill in San Francisco. 

Mining in 

Idaho and Montana

Idaho and Montana gained their first population as the result of discoveries of gold and silver made during the Civil War. There was the usual rush of miners, prospectors, and adventurers, but after the exhaustion of the placer deposits the population rapidly declined. Not much attention was paid to the baser metals until William A. Clark, of Montana, began smelting the copper which he found mixed with the silver ore in the mining district of Butte. In 1881 he opened the Anaconda mine, out of which he made an enormous fortune. 

Cattle raising: the "Long

Drive " The destruction of the buffalo and the pushing back of the Indians left the great plains stretching from the Kansas frontier to the mining frontier open for the development of stock raising, and the building of the railroads provided the means of shipping cattle to the eastern markets. The raising of cattle had already become well established in Texas, but Texas was a long way from the markets. The Texas cattlemen discovered that cattle could be driven north to points on the Santa Fe and Kansas Pacific and fatten on the superior pasturage of the northern ranges, reaching the railroads in good condition to be shipped east.

In 1867, 35,000 cattle were driven north to Abilene on the Kansas Pacific. Soon the drive was continued still

further to Kansas, Nebraska, and Colorado, whence they were shipped east on the Union Pacific. The "Long Drive" became an annual event, starting about the first of March each year, and between 1869 and 1879 fully 4,000,000 beeves were driven up from Texas. The cowboys who drove the cattle found it an exciting adventure. They had to ford great rivers, fight off roving bands of Indians and marauders, round up the cattle to keep them from becoming too widely

The years 1889 and 1890 saw the admission of six new western states to the Union. Before the expiration of Cleveland's term the Democratic House and the The last of Republican Senate passed a bill admitting North the frontier 

Dakota, South Dakota, Montana, and Washington. As these states were likely to be Republican, the Democrats had not been disposed to admit them, but after the election of 1888, when it became evident that the Republicans would control all branches of the national government, the Democrats had no reason for further delay, and admitted these states. Idaho and Wyoming were not included in the bill, but they were admitted by the Republicans in 1890. 

The Republicans, on the other hand, prevented Arizona and New Mexico from coming in in 1889 and 1890 because they would naturally be Democratic. They were not admitted until 1912. With the admission of Idaho and Wyoming there was for the first time a continuous belt of states from the Atlantic to the Pacific. The frontier had at last disappeared; most of the public land that was suitable for cultivation had been occupied. If the population of the 

West was to continue to increase, irrigation and more intensive methods of cultivation must be introduced. As a nation we had been lavish and wasteful in the use of natural resources, because the necessity of conserving them had not been apparent.

With the settlement of the trans-Mississippi region and the admission of new states the West became an important factor in national politics. As already noted, the Agraria settlement of the West had been overstimulated unrest by the railroads, and the farmers had operated on borrowed

Their farms were heavily mortgaged and interest rates were high. Overproduction of agricultural products and the efforts of Congress to deflate the currency and return to specie payments caused a general decline in prices. The panic of 1873 proved the ruin of many farmers who found it impossible to meet their obligations, and caused general unrest. The effects of an inflated currency , like all wars, had been attended by an inflation of the currency and a general rise of prices. At an early stage of the contest specie payments had been suspended and the country had become dependent on paper currency. This had been supplied in part by national bank notes, secured by a deposit of government bonds, and in part by legal-tender notes, or "greenbacks," issued on the general credit of the government. As the treasury did not have enough gold to redeem all of the greenbacks, they declined rapidly in value, in 1864 reaching the low mark of thirty-nine cents on the dollar. At the close of the war the government adopted a policy of deflation, that is, it undertook to withdraw some of the greenbacks from circulation and to accumulate a sufficient supply of gold in the treasury to redeem the others when they were presented. In order to carry out this policy Congress passed the Resumption Act of 1875, which directed the secretary of the treasury to begin the redemption of greenbacks in gold on the first of January, 1879. The greenbacks at once began to rise in value. The effects of this on the debtor classes are readily seen. farmer who borrowed money in greenbacks when they were worth sixty cents in gold had to repay in greenbacks worth ninety or ninety-five cents, he would be ruined. 

If a

The farmers of the West, therefore, opposed the retirement of greenbacks and the resumption of specie payments. The same position was taken by the debtor classes back party in other parts of the country, and in 1875 there was organized the National Greenback party, which de- 

The Green-

clared that money derived its real value from the stamp, or "fiat," of the government, and that Congress could stabilize prices by increasing or decreasing the amount of paper money. 

The Greenback party nominated candidates for the presidency in 1876, 1880, and 1884, but the advocates of an inflated currency finally united forces with those who favored the free coinage of silver. The ratio of 16 to 1 for the coinage of silver and gold had been fixed by law in 1834, but as silver was undervalued little or none was brought to the mint. As the silver dollar had been practically out of circulation for a generation, Congress in 1873 dropped it from the list of coins. This demonetization of silver, which attracted very little attention at the time, was later referred to as "the crime of 1873." currency With the development of the silver mines of the West there arose a demand for the recoinage of silver, and in 1878 Congress passed over the president's veto the The demand Bland-Allison Bill, which directed the secretary for a silver of the treasury to purchase from $2,000,000 to $4,000,000 worth of silver bullion each month and to coin it into standard silver dollars. The Bland-Allison Act did not satisfy the demand for "cheap money" and in 1890 Congress passed the Sherman Silver Purchase Act, directing the secretary of the treasury to purchase 4,500,000 ounces of silver each month and to issue in payment thereof treasury notes redeemable in gold or silver at the discretion of the secretary of the treasury. At the same time Congress declared that it was the intention of the United States to maintain the two metals on a parity. 

The silver purchase acts were supported by two distinct interests: the mining interests whose object was to raise the price of silver by making the government purchase monthly most of the output of the mines, and the agricultural interests whose object was to inflate the currency and keep prices up. The currency, however, was not the only

difficulty the farmers had to contend with. In 1889 the rainfall was decidedly below the normal and crops failed over large areas, causing widespread dissatisfaction. The farmer felt that the government was run in the interests of Eastern merchants and manufacturers. There was little difficulty in convincing him that the McKinley Tariff had been framed in the interest of the capitalistic classes. 

The Farmers' Alliance had become a national organization in the eighties, superseding the Granger movement of The rise of the seventies. In December, 1889, the Farmers' the Populists Alliance held a national convention at St. Louis and took the first step in the organization of the People's party. The leaders of the movement, convinced of the hopeless conservatism of the two older parties, hoped to combine in one radical party organized labor and organized agriculture. The labor leaders regarded the new movement with favor, but, as the event proved, the new party did not succeed in winning the labor vote. The decline in agricultural prices and the increasing cost of manufactured articles created a demand in the West and South for cheaper money, and the demand for the free coinage of silver, stimulated by the mining interests of the West, became one of the chief tenets of the new party. 

In the congressional elections of 1890 the House became Democratic. In many of the western states there was a combination of Democrats and Farmers' Alliance men, and in the new House there were 236 Democrats, 8 Populists, and only 88 Republicans. The Republicans retained control of the Senate by a narrow margin. 

The cam Harrison and Cleveland were again the candidates in 1892. 

They were both conservatives and the platforms on which they ran agreed in making the tariff the main paign of 1892 issue of the campaign. The People's party, which met in convention at Omaha, July 2, boldly denounced what was termed "a sham battle over the tariff," and put

forth one of the most radical and significant platforms ever placed before the American people; it contained most of the important reforms which were the subject of political agitation for the next twenty-five years. Among other things it advocated the free coinage of silver at the ratio of 16 to 1, a graduated income tax, postal savings banks, government ownership of telegraph and telephone lines, the Australian ballot, the restriction of immigration, an eighthour day on all government work, the initiative and referendum, and the popular election of United States senators. 

The contest between the two older parties centered on the tariff. The McKinley Act had reduced the revenue and caused a rise in prices; the Republicans were on the defensive and the Democratic party posed as the champion of the consumer. The result of the election was a surprise to everybody. Cleveland carried not only the solid South and all the doubtful states by large majorities, but also the Republican strongholds of Illinois, Wisconsin, and California. 

One of the surprises of the election was that General James B. Weaver, the Populist candidate, received over 1,000,000 popular votes and the electoral votes of five states, Colorado, Idaho, Kansas, Nevada, and North Dakota, as well as one of the three votes of Oregon.

With the inauguration of Cleveland the Democratic party came into full control of the government for the first time since 1860. It had to face unexpectedly the The panic of most serious financial crisis in the history of the 1893 country. For fourteen years the country had enjoyed uninterrupted prosperity. Financial disturbances abroad, beginning with the failure of Baring Brothers, had before the close of Harrison's administration started a heavy exportation of gold, the stock of which in the treasury had already been considerably reduced through the operation of the McKinley Tariff and the expenditures for pensions and river and harbor improvements.

Meanwhile the operation of the Sherman Silver Purchase

Act had greatly increased the amount of credit money. 

Furthermore, there had been overspeculation and inflation of values. When Cleveland came into office the gold reserve in the treasury, on which the value of silver and paper money depended, was rapidly dwindling. Neither party had expressed itself unequivocally on the silver issue, but Cleveland was outspoken in his support of the gold standard and, summoning Congress to meet in extra session in August, he urged the immediate repeal of the Sherman Act. The 

House promptly repealed the act but the Senate debated the matter until the last of October, when the repeal was carried through that body with the aid of Republican senators. 

The failure of banks, the closing of factories, and the general business depression that ensued from the financial crisis Labor threw hundreds of thousands of workmen out of troubles employment and produced during the winter of 1893-1894 the most serious labor disturbances that the country had ever witnessed. Mobs of the unemployed threatened to coerce city councils and state legislatures, and a widely advertised band known as "Coxey's Army" was organized in Ohio and marched to Washington for the purpose of demanding relief from the federal government. 

The split in the Demo The Democratic party was now hopelessly divided on the question of finance. The president had driven the advocates of free silver into close alliance with the Populists. He had antagonized organized labor. cratic party Business depression was attributed by the advocates of free silver in the South and West to the president's maintenance of the gold standard, and by the Republicans of the East to the Wilson tariff. The failure of the Supreme 

Court to uphold the income tax helped to increase the deficit in the treasury. In the congressional elections of 1894 the 

Republicans secured control of both House and Senate. 

President Cleveland had apparently been repudiated by the

country as well as by his own party. His further efforts to maintain the gold standard through the sale of bonds and the agreement made in February, 1895, with J. P. Morgan, to protect the gold reserve in the treasury against further raids, caused him to be denounced in the harshest possible terms by the silver wing of his party.

In 1892 the Democratic and Republican parties had both tried to dodge the silver issue. In the preconvention campaign of 1896 the Republicans again tried to The silver avoid committing themselves on this issue. Their issue principal candidate, William McKinley of Ohio, had openly advocated free silver, but as he was also the author of the tariff bill of 1890 and as the Republicans intended to make the tariff the main issue of the campaign, he seemed to be the strongest candidate. His campaign for the nomination was managed by Marcus A. Hanna, a successful business man of Cleveland, who now introduced effective business methods into politics. During the preceding winter Hanna had gone south and through the free use of money among the Negroes had secured for McKinley the Southern delegates to the Republican convention. He did his work so thoroughly and systematically that when the convention met at St. Louis, June 16, the nomination of McKinley was secured on the first ballot. The question of the platform was not so easily decided. The advocates of the gold standard finally prevailed and thirty-four silver Republicans withdrew from the convention.

When the Democratic party met in Chicago early in July, no candidate had the lead, and the attention of the whole country was centered on the question whether the convention would pronounce in favor of free silver or not. The silverites controlled from the start, and the platform demanded "the free and unlimited coinage of both silver and gold at the present legal ratio of 16 to 1 without waiting for the aid or consent of any other nation."

In the debate on the silver plank William J. Bryan of Nebraska captivated the convention by a brilliant speech in 

Nomination advocacy of free silver, closing with the now famous words: "You shall not press down upon the brow of labor this crown of thorns; you shall not crucify mankind upon a cross of gold." of Bryan

Before the next presidential election the Gold Standard Act was put through Congress by the Republicans, committing them unequivocally to the policy of maintaining a sufficient gold reserve in the treasury to keep the country on a gold basis. The alliance between the Republican party and "big business" was thus firmly cemented, and the Spanish War and the new questions that it raised obscured for several years the radical tendencies that had appeared in the campaigns of 1892 and 1896. CHAPTER XXIX THE NEW INDUSTRIAL SOUTH 

THE rise of the South from the economic ruin and political demoralization of war and reconstruction to its present posi- Economic prostration of the South at the close of the Civil War tion of industrial prosperity is an achievement that has few parallels in history. It is almost impossible for the present generation to realize the utter destitution of the Southern people at the close of the Civil War. The following incident will serve as an illustration of the poverty of even the richer classes. When the board of trustees of Washington College at Lexington, Virginia, decided to offer the presidency of that institution to General Lee, they asked Judge Brockenbrough, a former federal judge, to go to a distant part of the state to convey the invitation. After a moment's embarrassment, the latter replied that he had no clothes except the suit he was then wearing and that it was not fit to travel in, much less to wear in General Lee's presence. Another member of the board relieved the situation. He said that one of his sons, who had gone north and secured work, had sent him a suit of clothes which had arrived that day, and he would gladly lend it to Judge Brockenbrough. The judge thanked him, but said there was still another difficulty. He had no money to meet his traveling expenses and the college had none.

An embarrassing silence ensued. Finally one of the trustees said he knew of a lady in Lexington who had just received some money from the sale of tobacco on a plantation in another county and he thought she would be willing to lend some of it to the college. Thus equipped, Judge 564

Brockenbrough set out on his mission. It was successful; 

General Lee accepted the presidency of the college at a salary of $1500 and a house. 

The defeat of the South in the Civil War deprived it of political power and destroyed its wealth. The ruthless reconstruction policy of Congress delayed its eco- The Solid nomic recovery for a generation. It also had the South effect of creating the "Solid South," for the whites were welded together in the effort to save what was left of their civilization. In order to deprive the Negro of the political power so suddenly thrust upon him, which he was not fitted by training or intelligence to wield, the whites resorted to the purchase of votes and to fraud and intimidation at the polls. With the withdrawal of federal troops by President Hayes white supremacy was speedily reëstablished. 

The South in self-defense became solidly Democratic and remained so for half a century. ery of the

The Democratic party, which had lost control of the federal government in 1860 through a factional split, recovered ground rapidly after the Civil War, and in the elections of 1874 regained control of the House of Rapid recov- Representatives. In fact, in eight of the eleven national 

Congresses convened between 1875 and 1897 the Democratic House had a Democratic majority, though in all but two of these Congresses the Senate was Republican. In four of the six presidential elections held during these years the party in power was defeated. It was a period of political change and uncertainty. party The cam- During the whole of Hayes's administration the House was Democratic, and during the second half the Senate also was Democratic. The Democratic party was thus encouraged to look for success in the presidential paign of campaign of 1880. The leading candidates in the

The Democrats nominated as their candidate General

The Democratic orators made undue use of "the crime of 1876," by which their party had been deprived of the presidency. Garfield and Arthur were elected.

On July 2, 1881, less than four months after his inauguration, President Garfield was shot in a railroad station in Washington by a disappointed office seeker who was probably insane. He hovered between life and death for weeks, and finally, on September 19, died in a cottage on the Jersey coast where he had been taken by the advice of his physicians. The presidency now devolved upon Arthur, who, contrary to general expectation, filled the office with great credit to himself and with general satisfaction to the country.

nomination, but was soon confronted by a revolt of prominent Republicans and party newspapers. Although "purity in poliwas the watchword of the Independents, probably no campaign in American history had been fought so largely on personalities. Scandalous reports concerning the morals of the two candidates were circulated. Blaine made an open play for the foreign vote, but an incident which occurred on the eve of the election probably cost him the State of New York and the presidency. 

A clergyman, who headed a delegation which met him in New York as he was returning from a campaign tour, said in the course of his remarks that the Democratic party was the party of "Rum, Romanism, and Rebellion." The phrase was taken up by the press and erroneously attributed to Blaine. It cost him thousands of votes throughout the
