THE ELECTORAL VOTE IN 1884 

Grover Cleveland was the first Democratic president inaugurated since Buchanan, and his election naturally created tremendous enthusiasm in the South. The people of that section rejoiced that they were once more to have some influence in national affairs. Their expectations, however, were not fully realized. Throughout the whole of Cleveland's first administration the Senate was Republican, so it was impossible for the president and the Democratic House to carry out the pledges of the party platform. 

Cleveland was a man of great force of character and independence of judgment. Although he had had no experience in national politics, he possessed qualities which quickly won him the confidence of the people.

The Solid South was a thorn in the side of the Republican party, and in the campaign of 1888 that party pledged itself to the enforcement of the Fourteenth and Fif- The Lodge teenth Amendments. As the result of Harrison's Force Bill election a Force Bill, which aimed to place the control of Southern elections in federal hands, passed the House. It was championed by Henry Cabot Lodge of Massachusetts. 

However, it was defeated by a combination of Southern senators and Republican senators from the silver states of the West. This combination was destined to have an important influence on national politics a few years later, when the Southern senators supported the demands of the Western senators for the free coinage of silver. 

Meanwhile, the growth of the Populist party in the South was dividing the whites and threatened to give the 

Negroes the balance of power.

GROVER CLEVELAND 

It therefore became necessary to find some method of depriving them of the suffrage. In this significant movement 

Mississippi led the way. The new state constitution of 1890 prescribed for all voters the payment of a poll tax of two dollars by the first of February of the year in which the election was held, and ability to read any section of the state constitution or to understand and interpret it when read. 

It further disqualified from voting all those who had been convicted of "bribery, burglary, theft, arson, obtaining money or goods under false pretenses, perjury, embezzlement or bigamy," offenses which were common among the Negroes.

While these requirements excluded a large percentage of the Negro voters, they also excluded a large number of whites. 

In order to meet this difficulty the Louisiana constitution of 1897 adopted the famous "grandfather clause,” which The "grand- father clause " provided that no male person who was entitled to vote on January 1, 1867, and no son or grandson of any such person over twenty-one years of age at the time of the adoption of the new constitution should be denied the right to vote by reason of his failure to possess the necessary educational or property qualifications. 

This clause restored to the electorate the poor and illiterate whites who would otherwise have been excluded. This, or some similar device for disfranchising the Negro, was adopted within a few years by most of the southern states. The grandfather clause was, however, only temporary, because voters could register under it only before a certain date. 

After that date new applicants for registration had to meet the educational or property test. 

Several cases designed to test the validity of the new Southern constitutions were carried to the Supreme Court of the United States, but the court rejected the cases on technical grounds and failed to pass on the merits of the question. The new Oklahoma constitution of 1910, however, undertook to make the grandfather clause of permanent duration. In a decision handed down June 21, 1915, the Supreme Court held that the exemption from the literacy test of persons who voted in 1866 and their descendants was contrary to the Fifteenth Amendment, as it perpetuated the conditions which that amendment was intended to destroy. The disfran- The effect of the new Southern constitutions has been to eliminate the Negro to a large extent from politics. During the days of reconstruction and for some years chisement of afterwards, he was deprived of political power through intimidation, fraud, and bribery. The necessary resort to such measures lowered the political the Negro

morale of the South and created unfortunate conditions in many of the southern states. The present method, although an evasion of the Fifteenth Amendment, is effective and renders unnecessary a resort to fraud and intimidation. 

Under the new constitution of Mississippi only 8615 out of 

147,000 Negroes of voting age were registered. In Louisiana the number of Negro voters fell from 127,000 in 1896 to 5300 in 1900. In 1900 there were over 350,000 adult male 

Negroes in South Carolina and Mississippi, yet the total Republican vote in both these states was only 5433, of whom probably 2000 were whites.

The North and West have to a large extent acquiesced in this condition. This attitude of mind has been brought about partly by the realization that the giving of full suffrage to the Negro was a stupendous error, and partly by the development of the industrial South with the aid of Northern capital. During the last forty years industries which were undreamed of in the days of cotton and slavery have been developed with amazing rapidity. With the production of timber, coal, iron, and the manufacture of cotton the South has entered upon an era of industrialism, and has problems not differing essentially from those that face the other parts of the country.

Economically, the South, once the most prosperous section of the country, was left by the Civil War the poorest. Little was left but the land, the buildings, and the popu- Land and lation. The land and buildings were suffering population from neglect, and the population had been depleted by the ravages of war. The greatest loss was that of the young manhood that had perished. War always takes its toll of the best. Casualties are greatest among young men of energy, initiative, and daring. This loss could not be repaired, and it was made greater by the number of young men of enterprise who, unable to find a means of livelihood in the disorganized condition of things at home, went north and west to seek

their fortunes. There was no compensating immigration to the South. Foreign immigrants have largely avoided the 

South on account of the presence of the Negro, and there has been little migration from other parts of the Union except to Florida, Arkansas, Oklahoma, and Texas.

The break- up of the plantation

One of the greatest changes that followed the war was the break-up of the plantation into small farms or its subdivision among tenants. The plantation owner no longer had slaves to raise his crops, he had no funds from which he could pay wages, and he had no credit on which he could borrow money. Some of the larger plantations were broken up and sold. Others were subdivided and rented to white or Negro tenants. The form of tenancy varies in different communities, but in general there are two types of tenants: (1) those who pay a fixed rental in money or a fixed amount in produce, so many bushels of corn or wheat or so many pounds of cotton or tobacco, after the crop is gathered, and (2) the so-called "croppers," who cultivate the land on shares and turn over to the owner a fixed proportion of the crop. In some cases the landlord furnishes the horses and mules, the seed and implements; in others the tenant furnishes these, in which case, of course, he retains a much larger share of the crop. 

The tenant and the country merchant Very few Negro and not many white tenants save enough money to live on while the crop is being raised. Consequently they have to get their supplies on credit at the country store. The country merchant takes a lien on the crop and furnishes them with groceries, clothing, and other necessities while the crop is growing. He does not charge them direct interest, but he sells his goods at an advance, which in reality amounts to a very high rate of interest. When the crop is gathered, the tenant has to sell it to the merchant who holds the lien and not in the open market. The disadvantages of the system, due to the shiftlessness and improvidence of the tenant, are

that the merchant requires the cultivation of a staple crop, such as cotton or tobacco, and that the tenant or "cropper" spends his crop before it is made and thus frequently reduces himself to a condition little better than peonage. It is sometimes charged by outsiders not familiar with the conditions that the system is the result of a general and deliberate effort to keep the Negroes in a state of peonage. As a matter of fact, the merchants frequently lose heavily through the failure of crops or the abandonment of the land by the tenant. Some merchants refuse to sell on credit and the landlord has to furnish supplies and assume the risk in order to keep tenants on his land. In many cases the condition of the white tenant is little better than that of the Negroes. culture There is ample opportunity for a reliable and industrious man, white or black, to buy land on easy payments, and many take advantage of it, thus rising from tenant Diversificafarmers to owners. About sixty-five per cent of tion of agrithe agricultural land of the South is cultivated by owners. Many of these, however, are in debt and carry mortgages on their farms. The Department of Agriculture, through its county demonstrator, is doing much to improve the condition of the farmer by telling him what to plant on different soils, how to cultivate and care for his crops, and how to market them. The result is an increasing diversification of agriculture. The farmer is getting away from the one-crop idea and engaging in the cultivation of fruits and vegetables, the raising of poultry, hogs, and cattle, and dairying. One of his greatest difficulties is the scarcity, high cost, and unreliability of labor. Young men are easily drawn off to the towns and cities.

Truck-farming is successfully carried on around all the larger towns and cities, and refrigerated cars carry fresh produce to distant markets. Florida supplies the markets of the 

East with grapefruit, oranges, melons, and a great variety of vegetables the year round. Georgia, the Carolinas, Virginia,

and Maryland have the advantage of being able to ship their spring and early summer products to the great eastern cities before the truckers of the eastern states, where the season is later, are ready with theirs. A farmer who is dependent upon a single crop is in constant danger of being ruined by a temporary fall in the price of his particular commodity. 

HARVESTING PINEAPPLES IN FLORIDA 

Diversification of crops has improved immensely the condition of many farmers. It has, of course, its limits, for some lands are adapted to only one crop. 

When we turn from agriculture to manufactures, we find that the textile industries, especially cotton mills, hold the Textile man- first place both in the value of the output and in ufactures the number of the wage earners. The South has always had a few woolen and cotton mills. The modern development of cotton manufactures dates from about 1880. 

It is a mistake, however, to overlook the earlier history of this

industry. It had made considerable progress before the 

War of 1812. It is stated on good authority that in 1810 the value of the products of North Carolina was greater than that of Massachusetts. This was the result of household industry rather than the output of mills. Every plantation had spinning-wheels and looms which produced "homespun," 

A COTTON WAREHOUSE IN NEW ORLEANS 

This receiving shed is one of the biggest in the United States, having a capacity of 400,000 bales. out of which the clothing of the slaves and all but the finer clothing of the whites were made. The families of the small farmers and mountaineers also made their own cloth. After the War of 1812 British goods flooded the American market and interfered seriously with home manufactures. From that time until the Civil War the South devoted itself more and more to the production of raw cotton, which was sold to the New England mills or exported.

Effects of the Civil

Cotton mills had been established in North Carolina and Georgia as early as 1810, and the manufacture of cotton was never abandoned. In fact, the number of mills increased. In 1860 there were 160 mills in the 

War on the southern states, running 300,000 spindles, with a yearly output worth $8,000,000. During the war these mills were run to their full capacity. 

Many of them were destroyed by the invading armies and others were completely worn out. By the close of the war the industry had almost disappeared, and it was not until 1880 that it regained the position it held in 1860. cotton industry Expansion of the cotton industry since 1880

Before the expansion of the industry in the eighties the Southern mills were small and they turned out only yarns and the coarser grades of goods. Between 1880 and 

1900 fully 240 new mills were established and the "poor whites" of the mountain regions were drawn upon for labor. The new mills were generally larger and during this period the number of spindles increased from 561,000 to 4,368,000. Southern towns vied with one another in securing the location of mills. Local capital was not always sufficient and the mill organizers went north to secure funds. Commission agents and manufacturers of machinery took shares of stock in part payment. 

Most of the mills were located near water falls, but where water power was not available they used steam. 

The Southern mills had many advantages over their New England rivals. Their cotton cost them less and came to them in better condition; wages were lower; the hours of labor were longer; and laws regulating the employment of women and children did not exist or were laxer than in the older mill communities of New England. The number of children employed soon attracted attention and gave rise to a very bitter controversy. All the southern states now have laws forbidding the employment of children under fourteen years of age, and the percentage of children in the

Southern mills is not larger than in other parts of the country. 

Most of the Southern mills provide houses for their workers at moderate rentals and make ample provision for their general welfare and recreation. A competent authority states that "the operative in the South is the beneficiary of the most complete program of welfare work provided anywhere in 

American industry." 

The South land

Since 1923 the South has forged ahead in the cotton industry, while many of the New England mills have closed down. In 1926 there were 814 cotton mills in the South and the value of the product was over outstrips half that of the entire country. The leading New Engsouthern states in the manufacture of cotton are, in the order named, North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, and Alabama. North Carolina is still second to Massachusetts. South Carolina and Georgia stand third and fourth in the entire country. Though a good deal of New England capital has been put into Southern mills, it is estimated that over eighty per cent of the capital invested is owned in the South. The South is now producing finer grades of goods and is also dyeing and finishing its products. 

The South has within the past few years gone extensively into the manufacture of silk and rayon. During the years

Cottonseed was formerly considered useless and thrown away. In fact it was a problem to know how to dispose of it. 

Shortly before the Civil War it was discovered that it contained a valuable oil, but it was not until the eighties that

oil the production of cottonseed oil became an established industry. To-day this by-product yields about $500,000,000 

Cottonseed annually. The oil is used as a substitute for lard in cooking; it is sold as salad oil, either pure or mixed with olive oil; and it enters extensively into the manufacture of oleomargarine and soap. The cottonseed cake, which remains after the oil has been pressed out, is dried and ground into meal. This is fed to cattle, and, as it is rich in nitrogen, it is also used in the manufacture of fertilizers. 

From the earliest days tobacco was prepared in a crude way on the farm for smoking and chewing. Later small factories 

Tobacco grew up in various parts of the South. Before manufacture the Civil War Richmond and Lynchburg, Virginia, and Louisville, Kentucky, had become centers of the manufacture of tobacco. The war popularized smoking in both the 

Northern and the Southern armies and increased the demand for tobacco. The soldiers of Sherman's army liked the quality of the tobacco they found in the barns of North Carolina, and when the army disbanded and they returned to their Northern and Western homes, they spread the demand for 

Southern tobacco. The Duke family of Durham, North

Carolina, took advantage of this demand and laid the basis of their great fortune. 1 Cigarettes were not much used in America until the late seventies, and smokers usually rolled their own cigarettes. In the early eighties James Bonsack, a Virginian, invented the first cigarette machine. The Dukes adopted the machine and went into the production of cigarettes on a large scale. In 

1890 young James B. Duke organized the American Tobacco 

Company, the "Tobacco Trust," and after a fierce "tobacco war" with rival manufacturers north and south finally forced most of them to enter the combination. 

The South manufactures mainly cigarettes, smoking tobacco, and snuff. The leading states are North Carolina, Virginia, and Kentucky. Florida makes cigars and ranks

next to Pennsylvania and New York, which have long had the lead in cigar manufacture. Winston-Salem, North Carolina, is the largest tobacco manufacturing center in the world. 

The value of the annual output of the North Carolina factories in 1925 was over $340,000,000. That of Virginia, which comes next, was $144,600,000.

dustry

Efforts to establish the iron industry in America date back to the early days of the Virginia colony. Governor Spotswood's interest in the early part of the eighteenth The iron and century is well known. Later small blast fur- steel innaces became quite numerous in the piedmont and mountain regions of the South. They rendered indispensable service during the Revolution and the Civil War. The modern industry dates from the founding of Birmingham, Alabama, in 1870. The proximity of coal and iron ore accounts for the rapid rise of Birmingham as a center of the iron in-

dustry. At first only pig iron was produced. In 1888 the first steel was made. Between 1890 and 1897 the pig iron industry suffered as a result of the coming in of the Lake Superior ores and the financial panic. The Southern industry was almost ruined, but, with the sudden rise in the price of pig iron in 1899, it revived. The Tennessee Coal, Iron and 

Railroad Company began making steel on a large scale and acquired control of a large number of Southern plants. The panic of 1907 seriously embarrassed the Tennessee Company, and it was purchased by the United States Steel Corporation for $35,000,000.

Until the beginning of the present century most of the pig iron produced in the South was shipped to the North and West to be worked up into manufactured products. At the present time over eighty per cent of it is used by Southern foundries, which make water and gas pipes, stoves, radiators, car wheels, machinery, and agricultural implements. 

The manufacture of furniture is one of the South's important industries. North Carolina leads, with a production in Other Southern industries 1925 valued at over $51,000,000. Virginia came second with products valued at nearly $19,000,000. 

Furniture is also manufactured in Tennessee and Georgia. This industry is growing rapidly. In 1921 the furniture produced in the South was valued at $41,000,000; in 1925 the production reached $89,000,000. 

The lumber industry is still important. A few years ago the South produced nearly half the lumber used in the United States. Hard woods are being rapidly exhausted, but waste has been greatly reduced, and the Southern furniture factories consume a large percentage of the production. Louisiana is second in the value of its timber production. 

Cottonseed and the phosphate deposits of the southern Atlantic states give the South a natural advantage in the manufacture of fertilizers. In this industry Georgia and Maryland lead.

As industries have become well established, they have shown a healthy tendency to develop the higher processes of manufacturing and to turn out products that can compete with those of the older manufacturing centers. CHAPTER XXX INTELLECTUAL AND SOCIAL CURRENTS 

POPULAR belief in education, as a means of individual advancement and social and economic progress, impresses foreign visitors to the United States as one of the greatest ex- most significant features of American democracy. periment in We are engaged in the gigantic experiment of education offering to all people of all classes education of every kind, elementary and secondary, college, professional, and technical. We are spending far more money for public education than any other nation, and gifts and bequests to private foundations greatly exceed those of other countries. 

This remarkable development has taken place within the last fifty years.

Education finally recognized as a duty of the state

The public school system, dating back in Massachusetts to the colonial period, had become fairly well established in the North and Northwest before the Civil War.

Several of the southern states had "free schools," mainly for the children of the poor. People of means were expected to send their sons and daughters to private academies and seminaries, or to employ tutors. With prophetic vision Jefferson had advanced the view that education was the main safeguard of democracy and therefore a public function. He believed that political power could be safely intrusted to the people if they were educated, and he planned an elaborate system of public education for Virginia with the state university as the capstone. He devoted the later years of his life to founding the University of Virginia, but the rest of the system 582

was delayed until after the Civil War. For a long time there was a deep-seated prejudice against "free schools" in Virginia and in many other states. Jefferson's state university, however, set an example for the state universities that grew up later in the West. 

A MODERN HIGH SCHOOL 

tension of the public school sys- The public school system developed rapidly after the Civil War throughout the entire country. In the western states the expenses of public education were met in large Rise and expart from the sale of public lands, in the eastern states and the South by taxation. By 1870 all of the southern states had taken steps toward the tem establishment of public school systems. At first, as a result of the extreme poverty of the South, progress was slow, and the problem of Negro education presented many difficulties. 

In most of the states of the Union education of boys and girls between certain ages was made compulsory. Laws against child labor, passed about the same time, helped much to make the new system a success. During the past twentyfive years the most notable feature of our educational system has been the development of high schools. In every town of

any size and in many rural districts high school buildings have been erected, some of them of imposing architectural design and many of them better equipped with libraries and laboratories than the average small college of half a century ago. 

The high school has, in fact, become the peoples' college, offering academic, business, and technical training. The most recent developments in public education have been the junior high school and the junior college. 

Increase of school ex- This great development of our public schools has caused expenditures for finer buildings and better equipment, salaries of teachers, and administrative expenses to increase enormously in recent years and to add penditures a heavy burden to the taxpayer. In 1880 there were 9,867,000 pupils enrolled in the public schools of the entire country and the total expenditures amounted to $78,000,000. In 1926 the enrollment had increased to 

27,741,000 and the expenditures to $2,016,000,000. The amount paid in teachers' salaries during the same period increased from $55 942,000 to $1,061,000,000. The amount now spent annually for new buildings and equipment is about $500,000,000. So common, however, is the belief in the value and importance of education that these huge expenditures are borne with very little complaint from the taxpayers. 

The development of higher education during the past halfcentury has been no less striking. In 1870 college education 

The Ameri- was at a low ebb. The colleges were small, poorly can college endowed, poorly equipped, and the curriculum had undergone little change in two centuries. It was narrow, and designed mainly to prepare men for the three learned professions of law, medicine, and theology. Most of the colleges were sectarian in origin, and with the exception of the state universities they were still more or less under church control. 

Jefferson had broadened the curriculum at the University of Virginia and introduced the elective system, so that a student had some choice in the selection of the subjects he wished

to study. This system in a modified form was later adopted at Brown, Harvard, and Columbia, and eventually spread throughout the country. 

So poorly equipped were American colleges that in the decade following the Civil War a young man who wished to pursue advanced studies had to go to Europe, The rise of usually to the German universities, to find what universities he wanted. The opening of the Johns Hopkins University in 

1876 was a turning point in higher education in this country. 

About seven million dollars had been left by Johns Hopkins, a successful Baltimore merchant, to found a university and a hospital. This was the largest single benefaction that had at that time ever been made in America for education. 

Daniel C. Gilman, who was chosen by the trustees as the first president of the university, persuaded them to devote their resources to the development of higher scholarship and research. Charles W. Eliot at Harvard, Andrew D. White at

Cornell, and James B. Angell at Michigan had already entered upon their notable careers as university presidents and were trying to transform colleges into universities, but Gilman undertook to create a real university in which undergraduate studies should hold a subordinate place. He gathered around him a brilliant group of young scientists and scholars and gave them opportunities for research not before available in America. The new university soon attracted as students young men who would otherwise have gone abroad to continue their studies. Other universities soon developed graduate work and diverted the stream of students formerly directed to Germany. 

The devel- With the development of universities more attention was paid to the physical sciences. Laboratories well equipped for research replaced the meager apparatus that had been used mainly to illustrate classroom lec-opment of tures. America had already produced some scien- scientific tists of international repute, but very few, and these labored under great handicaps. Chief among them studies

were Gray and Agassiz in botany, Dana in geology, Joseph

Henry and Willard Gibbs in physics, and Maury, the "Pathfinder of the Seas," in oceanography. The results of scientific research have been applied to industry, and America has become noted for inventions in the field of practical or applied science. All large industries now maintain scientific staffs, THE GENERAL ELECTRIC COMPANY'S RESEARCH LABORATORY

During this same period (later nineteenth century) great progress was also made in professional and technical training. 

Professional Though the law schools of the University of training Virginia, Harvard, and Michigan had set high standards and trained many students, probably the majority of candidates for admission to the bar read law in the offices of practicing attorneys. The standards for admission to the profession have gradually been raised, and the better law

schools now require either a college degree or at least two years of college work for entrance. The course of study has been lengthened and the "case system," first employed at Harvard, has now been generally adopted. 

Medical education fifty years ago was very backward. 

Young men were admitted to most medical schools with little or no preparation and degrees were conferred by some schools after a year's study on young men who were utterly incompetent to practice medicine. Medical education is now very severe and exacting, probably more so than the preparation for any other profession. The standards set for the licensing of physicians are so high that only heavily endowed schools can give the training necessary to meet them and medical schools of the older proprietary type have practically disappeared. schools Before the Civil War there were also very few technical schools in the United States. Some of the colleges gave general courses in civil engineering, but thorough Agricultural training in this subject was given only at a few and mechanic places, such as the United States Military Academy at West Point and the Virginia Military Institute. 

A great impetus to technical training was given by the Morrill Act of 1862, which provided for a college of agriculture and the mechanic arts in each state. Each state was granted thirty thousand acres of the public domain for every member it had in Congress. It could sell or lease this land and use the proceeds for agricultural and mechanic training, either in connection with the state university or by establishing a separate college.

The advance of education in America has been accompanied and aided by large private benefactions. The first American to give large sums for this cause was George George Peabody, a native of Massachusetts. He founded Peabody's a Peabody Institute for the promotion of the study gifts to eduof literature and the fine arts in his native town in Massachusetts and another in Baltimore. In 1866 he cation

gave $2,000,000 for the promotion of "intellectual, moral, or industrial education among the young of the more destitute portions of the southern and southwestern States of the Union." Before his death three years later the sum was increased to $3,500,000. This trust was wisely administered.

American journalism has undergone many changes since the Civil War. More attention is paid to the news columns and less to the editorial comments. The business American of advertising has grown to such enormous pro- journalism portions that it dominates the policy of many newspapers. 

As a consequence the personal element in journalism has declined, that is, editorial policy is determined largely by the

corporation which owns the paper or chain of papers and not by a dominating personality such as Greeley, Bennett, Bowles, Bryant, Dana, Whitelaw Reid, Henry Watterson, and other editors of the older school. Accurate reports of events all over the world, sensationalism, the comic strip, and the illustrated Sunday supplement are the leading features of the modern newspaper. Coöperation in gathering news wrought a great change in the character of newspapers. The Associated Press and the 

The gather- Western Union Telegraph Company formed the ing of news first combination for supplying news to the daily press. Other press associations later came into the field and

The big metropolitan dailies maintain their own special correspondents at Washington and at the more important capitals of the world. Most of the great industrial corporations and propagandist organizations have publicity departments which supply the press with well written articles on matters in which they are interested, interpreted from their point of view.

The modern editor thus finds on his desk far more material ready for the press than he can use. He chooses what appeals to him and rejects the rest. 

An astonishing amount of this material gets into the news columns of our daily papers and the average reader has no means of knowing what is impartial news and what is propaganda.

The beginning of this period of cultural development found no public art galleries of any value. A few wealthy men had 

Art galleries private collections, but these contained few works of real merit. In 1869 W. W. Corcoran, a wealthy banker, founded and endowed the art gallery in Washington which bears his name, giving his own collection as a nucleus. The first building of the Metropolitan Museum of Art (New York) was erected in Central Park and opened to the public in 1879. The movement soon extended to other large cities and to-day no city feels that it is entitled to first rank unless it can boast of an art museum. Most of the large cities now have also art schools, though New York attracts the more promising students and the more ambitious of these find their way sooner or later to Paris, Rome, or other art centers of the Old World. Life in the South, on the contrary, assumed a more somber hue. Before the war the reverse was the case. The Southerners were more given to pleasure-seeking, gayety, and such sports as horseback riding

and hunting. At this time athletics and sports in the modern sense were unknown. Most of the population lived in the country, and life on the farms of the North and West was very exacting. By the time the day's work was over there was not much energy left for sport of any kind. Young men who went from the country to the cities enjoyed freedom from the physical labor to which they had been accustomed on the farm, and as a consequence their health suffered. The bicycle In the eighties and nineties bicycling became the most popular of all outdoor exercises. The old bicycle, with one high wheel over which the rider was mounted and a small wheel behind, was too dangerous and too difficult to be generally used, but the "safety," with two wheels of the same size and pneumatic tires, came into use in the eighties and was quickly taken up by men, women, and

Attention to exercise and The Young Men's Christian Association did physical much to encourage and popularize indoor gym- outdoor life nastics and outdoor athletics, and the later becomes organization of the Boy Scouts, and finally of general the Girl Scouts with their summer camps, brought thousands of city-bred boys and girls in close contact with

The public schools now devote much care to the physical development of their pupils, and practically all of our cities provide public playgrounds, shower baths, and swimming pools. President Roosevelt by both his example and his writings did much to encourage outdoor life, love of nature, and manly sport. The wealthier classes found their recreation in country clubs, yachting, polo, and golf. Golf made its appearance in the nineties and was slow in gaining popularity, but its spread in recent years has been amazing. It is no longer a fad of the idle rich. The establishment of public golf courses in most of our cities has brought the game within the reach of thousands of citizens of moderate means.

Develop- and suburban life

The amazing growth of cities and the resultant suburban life during the past thirty or forty years have wrought great changes. About half of our population now lives ment of city in cities, including small ones. When James 

Bryce published his American Commonwealth in 

1888 he startled many Americans by calling attention to the fact that, though we had achieved great success in working out the problems of national and state government, our one notable failure was in city government. Most of our cities were in the hands of corrupt political rings which squandered the public revenues and gave the people poor service. Bryce's book started the movement for municipal reform, and while there has been much improvement, much remains to be done. Our large cities present many problems which are still far from solution. Material comforts On the material side there have been many improvements. 

Streets are well paved and lighted, sewer systems and water supplies have been installed, and exand conven- tensive public parks opened for the use of the iences people. More attention is paid to hygiene and public health, houses are equipped with better plumbing and

with central heating plants. The electric light and the telephone have added greatly to the convenience of life. chitecture

One of the most striking features of city and suburban development has been the improvement in the architecture of homes. Architects had little scope for origi- Suburban nality in the construction of city blocks, but the and city ardetached house on a suburban lot afforded opportunity for variety and beauty of design. The architecture of the seventies and eighties (mid-Victorian) was the worst in American history. Even the large and costly houses of the wealthy were monstrosities of gloomy formality, mixed styles, and poor taste, and most of the public buildings were equally bad. Recent architecture has reverted to simpler styles, in which the American colonial prevails. City architecture has created the "skyscraper," a new and distinctive American type. The construction of huge office buildings and apartment houses has presented difficult engineering and architectural problems, which are being worked out in some cases with fine artistic results. There are few streets in the world more imposing than Fifth Avenue, New York. 

Street railways, drawn by horses until the late eighties, were revolutionized by the introduction of the electric motor and the overhead trolley. During the nineties the new Electric system spread rapidly in all parts of the United railways States. The introduction of this system of rapid transit has made possible the remarkable suburban development of recent years. People of even moderate means have been enabled to move from crowded city blocks to the outlying districts where they can enjoy grass and trees, gardens and tennis courts of their own, and still retain their contacts with the city. In interurban traffic the trolley car became a serious competitor of the railroads.

The invention of the gasoline engine and the development of the automobile brought about even greater changes in American life. At the beginning of the century the auto-

The invention of moving pictures affords daily amusement to millions of people. The screen has become more popular than the legitimate stage, and many leading actors have become "movie stars." The production of "movie" films has become one of the most important American industries. 

The moving picture and the radio

Of all scientific achievements the radio is the most wonderful, and it is capable of affecting profoundly the daily lives of millions of people. The possibilities of its use in the diffusion of education and culture appear to be illimitable. Already the families of farmers on the distant plains, as well as the inhabitants of small towns and great cities, sit in their homes and listen daily to musical concerts, public lectures, sermons, and political speeches. In the presidential campaign of 1928 the radio was the most important agency of publicity. Television, the sending of pictures over the air, has recently been accomplished. Its future as yet remains uncertain. 

The first quarter of the twentieth century saw the adoption of many political and social reforms, chief among which are Woman woman suffrage and national prohibition. The suffrage suffrage movement dates back to the middle of the last century. It encountered the opposition not only of men, but of many women as well. In 1869 the National Woman 

Suffrage Association was formed with Elizabeth Cady Stanton as president, and a vigorous fight for the ballot was begun in most of the states of the North and West. Women were first granted restricted suffrage in elections involving school questions, bond issues, or other local matters by Kansas, Iowa, Minnesota, and Montana. They were first given full suffrage by Wyoming in 1890, then by Colorado in 1893, by Utah and Idaho in 1896, by Washington in 1910, and within

the next four years by California, Arizona, Kansas, Oregon, Illinois, Nevada, and Montana.

The important work performed by women in the World War led to a demand that suffrage be conferred upon them by action of the national government, and under the The Nineleadership of Mrs. Carrie Chapman Catt and with teenth the cordial support of President Wilson Congress Amendment was induced in June, 1919, to submit the Nineteenth Amendment to the states. The Volstead Act, providing the machinery for the enforcement of prohibition and defining intoxicating liquors, was vetoed by President Wilson on the ground that it went further than the amendment warranted, but Congress passed it over his veto. In February, 1933, Congress proposed the Twentyfirst Amendment to make repeal a part of the Constitution.

By December of the same year, the thirty-sixth state had ratified the Amendment, which went into effect at once. (See page 28 of the Appendix.) State conventions rather than the legislatures acted on the Amendment, making it the first to be so ratified.

The care of the sick and wounded in time of war had always been left to the medical staff of the army until the Crimean 

War, when an Englishwoman, Florence Nightingale, organized a corps of women nurses. She encountered much

opposition from the medical staff and from the public at large, who thought that army hospitals were not fit places for women, but she overcame all obstacles and revolutionized army nursing. During the Civil War the same sort of work was organized in the Northern army by Clara Barton. In 1864 the International Red Cross Society, with national societies in different countries, was organized at Geneva. A treaty or 

The Red 

Cross and other humanita- rian agen- cies convention was signed by twelve nations, and later acceded to by many others, guaranteeing protection to

Red Cross hospitals, ambulances, doctors, and nurses engaged in attending the sick and wounded. They were to be regarded as neutral and not to be fired upon. The 

United States did not send a delegate to the Geneva conference and declined the invitation to accede to the convention for fear that it might prove to be an "entangling alliance." Clara

Barton became the great champion of the Red Cross in this country, and it was largely through her efforts that the Senate, after eighteen years' delay, finally consented to ratify the Geneva convention. She organized and became first president of the American Red Cross Society.

Red Cross work, limited at first to war, was later extended to the relief of suffering caused by fire, floods, earthquakes, famines, pestilence, and anything in the nature of a public disaster. Though the Red Cross is an official agency of the government, its funds are derived from voluntary subscrip-

tions. During the World War the American Red Cross raised and distributed hundreds of millions for the relief of the war sufferers of Europe.

One of the earliest political reforms in the period under consideration was Civil service that of the civil reform service. As we noticed, it had been the uniform practice since the days of Andrew

Jackson for the party in power to turn out officeholders of the defeated party and fill the federal offices with its own adherents. It was also a general practice to levy contributions on all officeholders to meet campaign expenses. Reform of the civil service had been agitated for several years without success, when the question was forcibly brought to the attention of the public by Garfield's assassination at the hands of a disappointed office-seeker. 

His successor, President Arthur, who had been regarded as a spoilsman, urged upon Congress remedial legislation in his first and second annual messages. In 1882 the Democrats elected governors in a number of normally Republican states and won a majority in the House of Representatives. After the election the Civil Service Act of 1883, introduced in the 

A RED CROSS POSTER

Senate by an Ohio Democrat, George F. Pendleton, was passed by both houses. It provided for the appointment of a Civil Service Commission of three members, which was to establish competitive examinations to test the fitness of applicants for office. The act applied at first to only about one tenth of the federal office-holders, but the president was authorized to extend the system to other groups of employees from time to time. Persons in the "classified service," as those appointed under the civil service rules were designated, could not be removed without cause. The unclassified service was still at the mercy of the spoilsmen. Almost every succeeding president has brought new groups under the merit system until now over sixty per cent of federal office-holders are on the classified list. 

The Sixteenth (in- come tax) Amendment

The first attempt at a federal income tax was the Wilson- Gorman Tariff Act of 1894, which levied a tax on incomes to make up for any losses in revenue that might result from the lowering of the customs duties. 

The following year the Supreme Court, by a vote of five to four, declared that this tax was a "direct" tax and, therefore, unconstitutional, because it was not apportioned among the states according to population as required by Article I, Section II, of the Constitution. 

This decision by a closely divided court raised a storm of criticism. The question was finally settled by the Sixteenth 

Amendment, proposed in 1909, and, after ratification by the necessary thirty-six states, proclaimed in February, 1913. 

This amendment authorized Congress to levy an income tax without apportionment among the states. Over forty years had elapsed since the adoption of the Fifteenth Amendment and the belief had become general that it was impossible to amend the Constitution. Reformers now took courage. 

The Seventeenth Amendment, providing for the direct election of United States senators by the people instead of

by the state legislatures, quickly followed. This amendment, which had passed the House half a dozen times within the preceding twenty years, was finally adopted by The Seventhe Senate in 1911 and proclaimed May 31, 1913, teenth shortly after the beginning of Wilson's administration.

Changes in tive government

Much dissatisfaction with representative government had been voiced during the twenty years preceding the election of 1912, and many new forms of democracy were tried. The initiative and referendum in legisla- representation were adopted by South Dakota in 1896, and by 1912 fourteen other states, mostly western, had adopted it. The recall of elective officers, adopted by Los 

Angeles in 1903 and Seattle in 1906, was widely advocated throughout the West, and it was proposed to extend it to state judges. The movement for greater popular control over party machinery found expression in the enactment of a state-wide primary law by Wisconsin in 1903, by Oregon in 1904, by Illinois in 1905, and by other states in turn. 

The commission form of city government, doing away with the familiar city council and placing municipal affairs in the hands of a small board of administrative officers, was first adopted by the city of Galveston, Texas, after the destructive tidal wave of 1904, to meet a temporary emergency, but proved so satisfactory that it was continued as a permanent form of city government. The same kind of city government, with varying modifications, was later adopted by Des Moines, Iowa, and other cities. The appearance of these new institutions of democracy was due to a deep-seated distrust by the people of state legislatures, party organizations, and city councils. 

With the rapid settlement of the West private interests had secured control of a large part of the mineral lands, forests, and water rights. These vast natural resources were being rapidly squandered, and in 1891 Congress passed an act

Roosevelt also withdrew from entry many millions of acres of oil and mineral lands, and also barren lands which could be made productive by irrigation. The reclamation of arid lands was authorized by the Newlands Act of 1902, which began the work of national irrigation. By this act all moneys received from the sale of public lands in certain western states were to be set aside as a special fund in the treasury to be used for the construction and maintenance of irrigation works. Conservation of natural resources was the most characteristic of the Roosevelt policies and the one on which he laid greatest emphasis. In 1908 he invited the governors of all states to a conference at the White House and urged them to coöperate with the national government in this important work. 

Pure Food

Acts Roosevelt extended governmental supervision to the manufacture of foods and drugs. His attention was called by 

Upton Sinclair's novel, The Jungle, to the unsanitary conditions prevailing in the Chicago slaugh- and Drug terhouses. After a thorough investigation by a committee, Congress passed, on the recommendation of the president, the Meat Inspection Act of 1906. Roosevelt also succeeded in forcing through Congress a bill to prevent the manufacture, transportation, and sale of "adulterated, or misbranded, or poisonous, or deleterious" foods and drugs. 

This measure met with determined opposition from the manufacturers concerned.

The population of the United States is nearly all derived from European immigration, but the character of that immigration underwent great changes in the last Foreign imquarter of the nineteenth century and the early migration part of the twentieth. Before 1880 three fourths of all persons who migrated to America came from the Celtic and Teutonic countries of northern and western Europe, mostly from Great Britain, Ireland, and Germany. About 1880 the numbers from southern and eastern (Latin and Slavic) Europe began to increase and soon assumed formidable proportions. In the year 1882 the number of immigrants entering the United States was 788,992, but this figure was not equaled again for twenty-one years. Because of differences of race, religion, and standards of living, the new groups of immigrants were less easily assimilated than the old and

tended to congregate in the slums of the larger cities, giving rise to problems that were new to American experience.

The restriction of immigration by legislation has been adopted but still presents many practical difficulties. The first restrictive acts were directed against the Chinese, but in 1885 Congress prohibited the importation of laborers under contract, and various other acts excluded convicts, prostitutes, lunatics, idiots, paupers, polygamists, anarchists, and persons suffering from contagious diseases. Chinese

With the settlement of California Chinese laborers were welcomed to our shores, and they played a large part in the development of the coast states, particularly in exclusion building the Pacific railroads. The trade in coolies, a form of peonage, was prohibited by act of Congress in 1862. By 1880 the opposition to the Chinese on account of their lower standards of living was general among the other laboring classes of the United States, and a commission was sent to China to arrange for the restriction of Chinese immigration. The result was the treaty of 1880, by the terms of which the government of China consented to the exclusion of laborers, provided that teachers, students, merchants, and travelers should be allowed to come and go of their own free will, and that return certificates should be issued to laborers already in the United States for the purpose of allowing them to visit China. Congress promptly passed exclusion laws which were later made more stringent. 

The alleged fraudulent transfer of the return certificates to new immigrants led Congress in 1888 to suspend the privilege, a measure which was not only harsh, but in violation of the treaty of 1880. The Chinese exclusion laws have been administered with undue severity, and overzealous officials have too frequently subjected Chinese gentlemen of culture and refinement to unnecessary hardships and indignities.

After the exclusion of the Chinese there was an increase in the immigration of Japanese laborers and an anti-Japanese agitation began on the Pacific coast. Matters Japanese reached a crisis in 1905 when the San Francisco immigration school board undertook to exclude Japanese subjects from the schools attended by American children and children of European nationality, and assigned them to a special Oriental school. President Roosevelt brought about an adjustment of this question, but the school incident was evidence of a strong feeling of opposition to Japanese immigration. In view of 

Japan's position as a world power and of the remarkable progress made by the Japanese people, Congress hesitated to legislate against the admission of Japanese while we were admitting freely the subjects of the other great powers. The 

Japanese government relieved the situation by agreeing informally not to issue passports to Japanese laborers to come to the United States. This "gentlemen's agreement" was scrupulously kept by Japan. 

The highwater mark of immigra- tion Immigration reached a high-water mark in 1905, when over a million foreigners reached our shores. President Roosevelt called attention to the fact that the number of immigrants who arrived in this single year exceeded the entire number of colonists who came to the colonies during the one hundred and sixtynine years that elapsed between the first settlement at 

Jamestown and the Declaration of Independence. At the outbreak of the World War it became evident that the "melting pot" was not working as satisfactorily as had been sentimentally imagined and that our population of foreign birth had not been fully assimilated and Americanized. Organized labor had for years advocated a restriction of immigration, and at the close of the war it appeared that the country was in danger of being flooded with refugees from the disorganized and debt-burdened countries. of Europe.

Congress, therefore, passed an act in May, 1921, limiting immigration and establishing the quota system. The number of aliens admitted each year from any given

CHAPTER XXXI FOREIGN RELATIONS, 1865-1897 

IN foreign affairs two outstanding problems were left as heritages by the Civil War, one with France over the presence of her troops in Mexico and the other with 

England over the "Alabama claims." As vic 

French from tory began to turn more and more definitely to the North, Secretary Seward's protests against the continued intervention of France in Mexico became more and more emphatic. Finally, in December, 1865, he declared to France that friendly relations would be seriously jeopardized by a continuance of her Mexican policy and a little later he demanded to know when the military occupation would come to an end.

Not desiring to risk a war with the United States, Emperor Napoleon III on April 5, 1866, announced that the French troops would evacuate Mexico in three detachments, covering a period of eighteen months. When the time came for the first detachment to withdraw, no action was taken, but Napoleon explained to the United States that he had decided to withdraw all his troops in a body the following spring. The success of Prussia in the Austrian War of 1866 was a serious blow to Napoleon's prestige, and in order to prepare for the conflict with that power which he now regarded as inevitable, he decided to leave Maximilian to his fate. After the departure of the French troops that unhappy prince was soon overthrown by Juárez and summarily shot. 618

On the first demand of the United States for reparation for the damage inflicted on American commerce by the Alabama and other Confederate cruisers, the British gov- The ernment disclaimed all liability on the ground Alabama that the fitting out of the cruisers had not been completed within British jurisdiction. Even after the close of the war the British government continued to reject all proposals for a settlement. claims

Later the American nation, flushed with victory, was bent on redress, and so deep-seated was the resentment against England that the Fenian movement, which had for its object the establishment of a republic in Ireland, met with open encouragement in this country. In 1866 several thousand 

Irishmen undertook to invade Canada from the United States, and were driven back by the Canadian authorities. 

At the same time numbers of Irishmen who had been naturalized in this country returned to their native land and conspired against England. Many of them were arrested and the American government felt called upon to ask for their release. The House of Representatives encouraged the 

Fenian movement to the extent of repealing the law forbidding Americans to fit out ships for belligerents, but the 

Senate failed to concur.

Uneasiness in England was being caused by the success of Prussia against Austria in 1866, which disturbed the European balance and foretold the Franco-Prus- The convention sian war.

For this reason England became more Johnsonconciliatory, fearing that if she were drawn into Clarendon the conflict the American people might take a sweet revenge by fitting out "Alabamas" for her enemies.

In January, 1869, Lord Clarendon signed with Reverdy Johnson, who had succeeded Adams as minister to England, a convention providing for the submission to arbitration of all claims which had arisen since 1853. The convention did not specifically mention the Alabama claims, and it

failed to contain any expression of regret for the course pursued by the British government during the war. The 

Senate therefore refused by an almost unanimous vote to ratify the arrangement. 

The treaty of 

Hamilton Fish, who succeeded Seward as secretary of state, renewed the negotiations through Motley, the American minister at London, who managed to get things in a bad tangle. Fish then transferred Washington the negotiations to Washington, where a Joint High Commission appointed to settle the various disputes with Canada convened in 1871. The main obstacle in the way of a settlement was now Sumner, the chairman of the 

Committee on Foreign Relations of the Senate. 

Sumner insisted that England should pay not only damages for the property actually destroyed by the Confederate cruisers, but also indirect damages for the increased rates of insurance, for the loss sustained through the transfer of American shipping to foreign flags, and for the prolongation of the war resulting from England's hasty recognition of belligerency and subsequent encouragement of the Confederates. Realizing that the sum total of these claims would be too vast even for England to pay, he suggested that the least she could do would be to withdraw from this hemisphere, leaving Canada and her West Indian possessions to be annexed by the United States. President Grant, who had lost all patience with Sumner for having opposed his pet scheme for the annexation of Santo Domingo, caused him to be dropped from the Committee on Foreign Relations. Motley was recalled from London, and on May 8 the treaty of Washington was signed.

The treaty of Washington, in addition to providing for the settlement of questions that had arisen with Canada in The Geneva regard to commerce, navigation, inshore fisharbitration eries, and the northwest boundary, provided that the Alabama claims should be submitted to an arbitra-

tion tribunal composed of five members, one appointed by England, one by the United States, and the other three by the rulers of Italy, Switzerland, and Brazil. When this tribunal met at Geneva the following year the United States, greatly to the surprise of everybody, presented the indirect claims as well as the direct, and Great Britain threatened to withdraw.

Rising to the occasion, the American member of the tribunal, Charles Francis Adams, decided against the contention of his own government. The indirect claims were rejected by unanimous vote and on the direct claims the United States was awarded the sum of $15,500,000. Although the British member of the tribunal dissented from this decision, his government promptly paid the award. This was the most important case that had ever been submitted to arbitration, and its successful adjustment encouraged the hope that the two great branches of the English-speaking people would never again have to resort to war. 

The purchase of Alaska

The first addition to the United States outside the limits of the country proper came with the purchase of Alaska from Russia in 1867. It came as a great surprise to the public. There was no demand for this frozen zone and the idea that it would ever be of any value was openly ridiculed. But Seward, who negotiated the purchase, was the greatest of all American expansionists. 

As early as 1846 he declared that our population was destined "to roll its resistless waves to the icy barriers of the North, and to encounter oriental civilization on the shores of the Pacific." He also believed that we would expand to the South and predicted that Mexico City would be "the ultimate central seat of power of the North American people." 

Learning in 1867 that Russia was willing to sell her American possessions, he quickly opened negotiations. The price finally agreed upon between him and Baron Stoeckl, the

Russian minister, was $7,200,000. The treaty was promptly

ratified by the Senate with only two dissenting votes and proclaimed June 20, 1867. The House, which was bitterly hostile to the administration, did not so readily consent to vote the appropriation, but finally did so the following year. 

It was charged at the time, and later investigations seem to confirm the charge, that a part of the purchase money was used in bribing members of Congress to vote for the appropriation. The United States thus secured for a trifling sum a vast area of nearly 600,000 square miles immensely rich in unsuspected minerals. From the fur seals alone the government has received double the amount of the purchase price. 

The navy, after its Civil War experience, impressed on the government the need of securing coaling stations and naval bases in the West Indies. The Danish islands of St. Thomas, St. John, and Santa Cruz had been a favorite resort for the war vessels of the United States, most of the other West Indian islands being favorably disposed to the Confederates. In December, 1865, Secretary Seward started on a cruise for his health, in the course of which he visited St. Thomas and also Santo Domingo. On his return he immediately opened negotiations with the Danish minister, who was authorized to sell the Danish group for $15,000,000. 

Seward thought this too much, but the following year a treaty was signed at Copenhagen by which Denmark agreed to sell two of the islands, St. Thomas and St. John, for $7,500,000, provided the inhabitants should agree to the transfer. Negotiations for the purchase of the

Interest in the Atlantic-Pacific canal contemplated by the Clayton-Bulwer treaty was sidetracked during the Civil War, and the construction of the Union Pacific Railroad rendered the enterprise for the time being of secondary importance. Attention was, however, suddenly drawn to the subject in 1878 by Colombia's concession of a right of way through Panama to a French company under the presidency of Ferdinand de Lesseps, the builder of the Suez Canal. The prospect of the speedy construction of a canal under French auspices led to a sudden and radical change of policy on the part of the United States. In a special message to Congress March 8, 1880, President Hayes declared that any canal connecting the Atlantic and Pacific oceans would be "virtually a part of the coast-line of the United States," and must be under 

American control. 

Efforts to modify the Clayton- Bulwer treaty In his inaugural address Garfield commended the policy of his predecessor, and Secretary Blaine soon began his famous correspondence with the British government for the purpose of securing modifications of the Clayton-Bulwer treaty. His argument that the United States had outgrown the treaty, and the declaration of his successor, Frelinghuysen, that it was really voidable at the pleasure of the United States, made little impression on the British government, which simply announced its intention of adhering to its rights under the treaty. President Cleveland in 1885 admitted that the agreement reached in the Clayton-Bulwer treaty was still valid. Eleven years later Olney declared that the only way to modify the stipulations of 1850 was through a direct appeal to Great Britain for a reconsideration of the whole matter. Meanwhile the failure of the

French enterprise postponed the construction of the canal until after the Spanish War. relations

While he was secretary of state in 1881, Blaine undertook to extend the influence of the United States in Central and South America by sending out a general invita- Latintion to a conference to be held the following year American in Washington, "for the purpose of considering and discussing methods of preventing war between the nations of America." This was the beginning of the modern 

Pan-American movement, a revival of Bolivar's cherished scheme, to secure coöperation among all the republics of the new world. The war between Chile and Peru caused a postponement of Blaine's plan, but in 1888 President Cleveland approved an act of Congress providing for the International American Conference, which was held in Washington during the winter of 1889-1890. 

Blaine was again secretary of state when the conference assembled, and presided over its opening session. The delegates declared that arbitration was "a principle of American international law," and outlined a general plan for the settlement of international disputes, which their governments, however, failed to ratify. The conference resulted, nevertheless, in the organization a few years later of the Bureau of American Republics, now known as the Pan American Union, and housed in a beautiful building in Washington. 

The second conference was held in Mexico City in 1901, the third at Rio de Janeiro in 1906, the fourth at Buenos Aires in 1910, the fifth at Santiago, Chile, in 1923, and the sixth at Havana in 1927.

The highest grade in the diplomatic service of the United States was for more than a century that of minister. Ambassadors were supposed to represent the "person" of the sovereign rather than the state, and the diploit was not considered in accordance with demo- matic cratic ideals to send or receive persons of ambassadorial rank. The growing importance of the United 

States in international affairs and the repeated recommendations of some of our representatives abroad led Congress in 1893 to authorize the higher grade, and Thomas F. Bayard was appointed as the first American ambassador to England. Our representatives to the principal European and 

Latin-American countries and to Japan were subsequently raised to the new grade and the representatives of those countries to the United States were given corresponding rank.

The higher rank was not accompanied by an increase of pay or allowance for the more expensive scale on which ambassadors are expected to live, so that it has had the effect of restricting our highest diplomatic posts to men of great

wealth. Notwithstanding this fact, the change was probably inevitable and it has been on the whole beneficial. 

American interests in the Pacific received attention during Harrison's administration. In 1878 the United States had acquired a coaling station in the Samoan interests in islands, and in 1889 serious trouble with Germany arose over the attempt of that power to control American the Pacific the government of the group.

England also had interests there, and the dispute was adjusted by a treaty establishing a joint protectorate of the three powers over the islands. In 1899 the powers agreed upon a division of the islands, the United States receiving Tutuila. American missionaries and traders had gone to the 

Hawaiian Islands early in the nineteenth century, and their descendants, having grown wealthy and influential, favored annexation to the United States. In 1893 this party, with the connivance of the American minister and the aid of United States marines, overthrew the reigning queen and established a provisional republic. A treaty providing for the annexation of the islands was soon signed and submitted by President Harrison to the Senate. Before a vote on the treaty was taken, President Cleveland came into office, and a commission was sent to Hawaii to conduct an investigation. As a result the flag of the United States was hauled down and the marines withdrawn. The provisional government was strong enough, however, to prevent the restoration

of the queen, and the next year President Cleveland recognized the Republic of Hawaii. Annexation was, however, delayed until Dewey's victory in Manila Bay made it inevitable.

The dispute with Canada over the treaty rights of Americans to engage in the inshore fisheries became acute during Cleveland's first administration, and a number The Bering of American vessels were seized for alleged vio- Sea conlation of the treaty. England and the United troversy
