Serious trouble with England was also threatened about the same time by another controversy the right of Canadians to take seals in Bering Sea. The habits of the seal are interesting and peculiar. During the breeding season the herds occupy for a period of several months islands belonging to the United States. When the young are strong enough to put to sea, they all start on the long annual voyage out into the Pacific. They return to the same breeding grounds at the

proper season.

The United States government could regulate the catching of seals by its own citizens both on the islands and at sea, but the question arose as to its right to prevent Canadians from taking seals beyond the three-mile limit. In other words, were the seals the property of the 

United States and did the American government have a right to protect them on the high seas? In 1886 some Canadian sealers were seized by the United States revenue cutters at a distance of more than sixty miles from land and were condemned by the district court at Sitka. President Cleveland, however, ordered their release.

The feeling in Canada over both the northeastern and the seal fisheries prevented Great Britain from coming to an The fur seal agreement. At the beginning of Harrison's adarbitration ministration seizures of Canadian sealers were renewed. Secretary Blaine undertook to defend the action on the ground that the indiscriminate killing of seals in the open sea was rapidly exterminating the herds and was therefore contra bonos mores, and on the further ground that Russia had exercised exclusive rights in Bering Sea and that these rights had been ceded to the United States with Alaska.

These questions were finally arbitrated at Paris in 1893, after a treaty to arbitrate them had been signed. The tribunal refused to recognize the claim of the United States to property right in the seals and declared that Bering Sea was & part of the high seas and not subject to the special jurisdiction of the United States. The arbitrators suggested, however, certain regulations for the protection of the seals, which were put into effect by the two governments. These regulations proved inadequate, and the seals were being slowly exterminated when, after lengthy negotiations, the question was adjusted on a more satisfactory basis by the treaty of 1911, to which Russia and Japan as well as England were parties.

The Monroe Doctrine had been taken less seriously after Blaine's failure to get Britain to renounce her canal rights. 

It was now suddenly revived in a striking and The sensational way by President Cleveland in the Venezuelan famous Venezuelan boundary controversy. Ven- boundary dispute ezuela had never been able to get England to agree on a boundary line between her territory and British Guiana, and the British government had from time to time en- Venezuela larged its claims. repeatedly urged arbitration, but Great Britain refused to submit the question to a third party unless her claim to a large part of the disputed area was first recognized. 

LORD SALISBURY 

Diplomatic relations between the two countries had been severed after a dispute of fifty years, when President 

Cleveland decided to take up the case for Venezuela. On 

July 20, 1895, Secretary Olney dispatched a note to the

British government in which he reviewed the question at length, reciting the willingness of Venezuela to arbitrate and the refusal of Great Britain to do so. He claimed for the Monroe Doctrine a place in international law as an American statement of the well-recognized right of a state to intervene in a dispute between other states when it considers its interests affected. He concluded by asserting that the United States regarded the controversy as one in which both its honor and its interests were involved. To this dispatch Lord Salisbury replied at length, refuting Olney's arguments and denying

that the Monroe Doctrine was a principle of international law.

President Cleveland laid the correspondence before Congress that year in a vigorous message. He stated even more President Cleveland appeals to Congress emphatically the interpretation of the Monroe 

Doctrine advanced in Mr. Olney's dispatch and asked for an appropriation for the expenses of a commission, to be appointed by the president, which should make the necessary investigation and report upon the true boundary with the least possible delay. "When such report is made and accepted," he continued, "it will, in my opinion, be the duty of the United States to resist by every means in its power, as a willful aggression upon its rights and interests, the appropriation by Great Britain of any lands or the exercise of governmental jurisdiction over any territory which after investigation we have determined of right belongs to Venezuela." Lest there should be doubt as to his meaning he added, "In making these recommendations I am fully alive to the responsibility incurred and keenly realize all the consequences that may follow." The public on both sides of the Atlantic was amazed and stunned. While only a few government officials knew that there was any serious cause of dispute, the two countries were suddenly brought to the verge of war. Congress promptly voted the appropriation and the president appointed the boundary commission. 

War averted 

Indignation followed the first surprise in England, but before Lord Salisbury could decide upon a course of action, public attention was unexpectedly drawn to another quarter of the globe. Before the year was out, the Englishman Dr. Jameson made his unsuccessful raid into the Transvaal, and a few days later the German 

Emperor sent a telegram of congratulation to President

Kruger for having suppressed it. The wrath of England was diverted from America to Germany. A few days later

Lord Salisbury offered to place at the disposal of the boundary commission the British records relating to Venezuela and Guiana, and before the report of the commission was completed, Great Britain signed a treaty with Venezuela submitting the case to arbitration.

Both in the United States and abroad President Cleveland's message was widely criticized, but his position has since been approved by most American writers on diplomacy. 

It turned out to be a most opportune assertion of the intention of the United States to protect the American continent from the sort of exploitation by Europe to which Africa and Asia have fallen a prey. Cleveland's bold assertion of the United States policy had a clarifying effect on relations with England, whose attitude has since been uniformly friendly. In fact, before two years had elapsed, Olney signed with Sir Julian Pauncefote a general arbitration treaty, which, however, was rejected by the Senate in the closing days of the Cleveland administration. 

By no means new, the Cuban question had finally reached an acute stage toward the close of the Cleveland administration. From the days of Thomas Jefferson The Cuban many Americans had coveted this important question island, but until the Mexican War the main object of our Cuban diplomacy was to prevent its acquisition by Great Britain or France. During this early period the United 

States repeatedly offered to guarantee Spain's possession provided she would not cede the island to one of the larger European powers. Lying athwart the Gulf of Mexico and controlling the outlet of the Mississippi Valley as well as the more important approaches to the proposed isthmian canal, Cuba was too important a prize to pass into the hands of a strong naval power. If we could not get it ourselves, we preferred seeing it remain in the possession of a weak power like Spain.

We have read how after the Mexican War the United

States made several unsuccessful efforts to purchase the island, while Cuban "patriots" with the aid of adventurous

Americans made repeated efforts to annex it to the United States by means of filibustering expeditions fitted out in this country. These latter were a serious strain on peaceable relations with Spain and several times almost led to war. 

American diplomacy in Cuba after the Civil War aimed at extending commercial relations and protecting American The "Ten interests there. In 1868, at the time of the over- 

Years' War" throw of the monarchy in Spain, a formidable insurrection against Spanish rule broke out in the island. 

The "Ten Years' War," from 1868 to 1878, during which a succession of governments in Spain attempted to suppress the insurgents, was characterized by great cruelty, the destruction of property, and a general disregard of the interests of foreigners, especially Americans. Early in the struggle President Grant wanted to extend belligerent rights to the insurgents, but was prevented from doing so by Secretary Fish.

In 1873 the Virginius, a vessel bearing the American flag and carrying men and military supplies for the insurgents, was captured on the high seas by a Spanish war vessel and carried into the port of Santiago. Here fifty-three of the passengers and crew, including some British and a number of Americans, were summarily executed. As neither Spain nor the United States had recognized the insurgents as belligerents, Spain had no right to seize the vessel outside her own territorial waters, and the execution of Americans without the formalities of a legal trial was in open violation of treaty rights. The incident caused great excitement in the United States and for a time war seemed unavoidable, but the matter was finally settled by the payment of an indemnity and the surrender of the captured vessel. 

The long and cruel struggle in Cuba, the persistent neglect by Spain of treaty obligations, and her refusal to redress

grievances combined to make intervention by the United States, either alone or in combination with other powers, the only solution that appeared at all feasible. In a Fish's mannote of November 5, 1875, Secretary Fish expressed agement of himself in this sense to the Spanish government. the Cuban question

Copies of the note were transmitted to our representatives at London, Paris, Berlin, Vienna, Rome, and St. Petersburg with instructions to sound the governments to which they were accredited with a view to securing their approval or coöperation. 

Fish's proposal failed, the European cabinets refusing to lend any countenance to the American proposal for intervention. Reports of the negotiations got into the public press, and Fish was severely criticized for violating the Monroe Doctrine by consulting the powers of Europe on what had been uniformly considered since the days of John Quincy Adams and Henry Clay a question which concerned only Spain and the United States. Congress called for a report of the negotiations, but Fish returned an evasive answer, and it was twenty years before the full correspondence was made public.

The war dragged out its weary course for three more years. 

Finally in 1878 it was brought to a close through the exhaustion of both parties and the promise of definite reforms by Spain. The reforms were, however, not carried out in good faith, and the old policy of exploiting the resources of the island for the benefit of Spaniards was continued. 

The last Cuban insurrection began in 1895, and soon resembled closely the "Ten Years' War." The policy of 

Máximo Gómez, the insurrectionary chief, was The Cuban to fight no pitched battles, but to keep up in- insurrection cessant skirmishes, to destroy sugar plantations of 1895 and every other source of revenue, with the end in view of either exhausting Spain or forcing the intervention of the United States. With the opening of the second year of the

struggle General Weyler arrived in Havana as governor and captain-general and immediately inaugurated his famous "reconcentration" policy. The inhabitants of the island were directed by proclamation to "reconcentrate themselves" within a week in the towns occupied by Spanish troops, under penalty, if they refused, of being treated as rebels. The majority of those who obeyed the proclamation were women 

MORRO CASTLE AND LIGHTHOUSE AT THE ENTRANCE TO THE HARBOR OF HAVANA 

and children, who, as a result of being cooped up in crowded villages under miserable sanitary conditions and without adequate food, died by thousands. 

This ruthless treatment of the Cuban population aroused the sympathies of the American people and strengthened the demand for intervention. Numbers of persons claiming 

American citizenship were thrown into prison by Weyler's orders. Some of them were native Americans, but the majority were Cubans who had sought naturalization in the United States in order to return to Cuba and claim American protection.

The Cleveland administration found it difficult to prevent the insurgents from drawing arms and supplies from the United States. Early in the struggle the presi- Cleveland's dent issued a proclamation calling attention to the policy insurrection and warning all persons within American jurisdiction against committing acts unfriendly to Spain. He consistently refused to extend belligerent rights to the insurgents, who occupied no definite territory or seacoast and had no stable government. 

Congress was more eager for intervention than the president, and in February, 1896, passed a resolution recognizing a state of war in Cuba and offering Spain the good offices of the United States for the establishment of Cuban independence. The president was not bound by this resolution and, although it passed both houses by overwhelming majorities, he ignored it. In his last annual message to 

Congress, however, President Cleveland reviewed the Cuban question at length and declared that, if the struggle continued much longer, "a situation will be presented in which our obligations to the sovereignty of Spain will be superseded by higher obligations, which we can hardly hesitate to recognize and discharge."

FOREIGN affairs occupied most of President McKinley's attention, after the passage of the Dingley Tariff. As a result of this pressure the Spanish ministry resigned, and on October 14 the liberal ministry of Sagasta assumed office. Weyler was recalled and General Blanco appointed governor and captain-general of Cuba. The new ministry promised to grant autonomy to Cuba, and President, McKinley declared in his message of December 6, 1897, his intention of allowing time for the new policy to be tested. 

The revolution had gone too far for autonomy to pacify the tration 

WILLIAM MCKINLEY 

Cubans; they would no longer be satisfied with anything short of independence. On January 13, 1898, there was serious 639

World Politics rioting in Havana as a demonstration against the autonomy scheme, and Consul-General Fitzhugh Lee told his government that it might be necessary to send warships to protect Americans, as he doubted whether Blanco could control the situation. 

The blowing up of the Maine

Lee's hint was followed by the sending of the United States battleship Maine to Havana toward the last of the month. 

While she was lying quietly at anchor, a dramatic incident at Washington caused the retirement of the Spanish minister, Dupuy de Lôme. On February 9 the New York Journal published in facsimile a letter from the minister to a friend in Cuba which severely criticized President McKinley and contained reflections on his character. The letter was genuine, though surreptitiously acquired, and there was no satisfactory explanation which Dupuy de Lôme could offer. On being notified that the immediate recall of the minister was expected, the Spanish government replied that his resignation had been tendered and accepted by cable.

The excitement over this episode was only a preparation for the furore that spread through the country when the battleship Maine was suddenly blown up at her anchorage in Havana harbor on the night of February 15. In the explosion, which totally destroyed the Maine, two of her officers and 258 of her crew were killed. An American naval court of inquiry reported after a careful examination of witnesses and of the wreck that the destruction of the ship was due to a submarine mine. A Spanish board of inquiry claimed in a brief report made a few days later that the explosion had occurred in the forward magazine of the ship. It is generally admitted that the American report was correct, but the responsibility for the mine has never been disclosed. 

Although the sensational element in the press howled for war, the American people displayed great self-control until the report of the court of inquiry was made public. Then the

country witnessed an outburst of warlike fervor such as had not been seen since 1861. "Remember the Maine" became a watchword and the demand for war was over- End of whelming. President McKinley decided, how- diplomatic negotiations ever, before resorting to war to make one more effort at a diplomatic settlement. He proposed an armistice between Spain and the insurgents pending negotiations for a permanent adjustment through the good offices of the

United States. The Spanish government refused to grant an immediate armistice, but made vague suggestions about leaving the pacification of the island to a Cuban parliament. 

Because of this hedging attitude on the part of Spain, President McKinley closed negotiations, and announced that he had decided to refer the whole question to Congress. 

His message was delayed a few days at the urgent request of Consul-General Lee in order to give time for Americans to get out of Cuba. In an eleventh-hour attempt to put off a conflict, the Spanish minister informed the president on April

In his message of April 11 the president reviewed the Cuban question at length and concluded that forcible intervention was the only solution, and was justified not only on grounds of humanity, but as a measure for the protection of the lives and property of American citizens, and for the purpose of putting a stop to a conflict which was a constant menace to our peace. He referred to the Maine only incidentally as a patent and impressive proof of a state of things in Cuba that is intolerable." Congress demands the withdrawal of Spain 

The president and Congress both knew that referring the question to the latter meant war. On April 19, the anniversary of the battle of Lexington and of the first bloodshed of the Civil War on the streets of Baltimore, the fateful resolutions were adopted, declaring that the people of Cuba ought to be free and independent, demanding the immediate withdrawal of Spain from the island, and authorizing the president to use the land and naval forces of the United States and the militia of the several states for the purpose of carrying these resolutions into effect. from Cuba

These resolutions were practically a declaration of war. 

At the same time in another resolution Congress denied any intention to exercise sovereignty or control over Cuba except for its pacification, and asserted that the United States would then leave the government and control of the island to its people. As soon as the resolutions were approved by the president the Spanish minister asked for his passports.

REAR-ADMIRAL SAMPSON 

About this time the unexpected news of a great naval victory in Manila Bay sent a thrill through the country.

When war was declared, Commodore George Battle of Dewey was at Hongkong with the half dozen not Manila Bay very formidable cruisers and gunboats of the Asiatic station. 

Acting under instructions which were cabled to him from Washington, he set sail for Manila Bay with the purpose of capturing or destroying the Spanish fleet there. During the night of April 30 he entered the south channel leading into the bay and by daybreak was off Manila, near enough to see the shipping. South of his position, lying eastward from 

Cavite, the Spanish fleet was at anchor. With his flagship, the Olympia, in the lead Dewey closed in on the enemy and for more than two hours kept up a continuous fire on the

World Politics 

Spanish ships and shore batteries, inflicting great damage. 

At 7:35 A.M. the American fleet stood out into the bay and the men were ordered to go to breakfast. Shortly after eleven the squadron returned to complete its work and in less than an hour and a half the continuous fire of the American sailors had put most of the Spanish vessels in flames. Because of the poor aim of the Spaniards the American cruisers escaped all but slight injury and only seven men were slightly wounded. On receiving the news of this victory 

President McKinley appointed Dewey rear-admiral and recommended that he be promoted to the grade of admiral and receive the thanks of Congress. Dewey's position after the battle was peculiar and even embarrassing. He Dewey's critical posi- could have taken tion at the city of Manila, Manila but he did not

ADMIRAL DEWEY 

nave the men to hold it, and it was two months before reënforcements reached him. The most serious cause of embarrassment was the presence in the bay of five German war vessels superior in strength to Dewey's. At that time Germany was eager for colonial expansion and jealous of that of other nations. The German commander, Admiral Diederichs, displayed open sympathy with the Spaniards, disregarded Dewey's blockade of Manila, and committed breaches of naval etiquette. Dewey finally sent his flag-lieutenant to tell him that "if he wants a fight he can have it right now." The friendly attitude of the 

British commander at this crisis stood Dewey in good stead,

and Admiral Diederichs promptly disavowed the acts complained of. No satisfactory explanation of the German admiral's conduct has ever been given.

Dewey's victory hastened the annexation of the Hawaiian Islands. In June, 1897, President McKinley had submitted to the Senate a treaty providing for the annexation of the group, but it was found impossible to secure the consent of two thirds of the Senators. The advocates of annexation then determined to gain their end by a joint resolution, which requires only a majority vote, and this resolution was still under consideration when the war with Spain began. With the lesson taught by Dewey's position, the importance of a naval station in the mid-Pacific won over many to annexation, and the joint resolution passed the House June 15 and the 

Senate July 6.

Much uneasiness was felt in the United States as to the destination of Cervera's fleet. Sampson, in command of the 

Cuban blockade, grew restless and moved eastward Movements to Porto Rico with a part of it, intending to intercept of the Cervera in case he made a dash for the coast of Atlantic squadron the United States or to blockade him in case he put in at San Juan. While Sampson was off Porto Rico, Cervera slipped unobserved into Santiago, Cuba. 

When the reports came of the arrival of the Spanish fleet in the West Indies, the Navy Department dispatched Schley with the "flying squadron" from Hampton Roads to Key

West, and Sampson was hastily recalled from Porto Rico. 

When the latter reached Key West May 18, he ordered Schley to proceed around the west end of Cuba to Cienfuegos and in case he did not find Cervera there to go on to Santiago. 

Schley arrived before Santiago a week after Cervera's fleet, but as the cruisers on scouting duty before that port were ignorant of Cervera's arrival, Schley began the much discussed retrograde movement to Key West. Two days later, after receiving dispatches from the Navy Department indicat-

World Politics ing that Cervera was at Santiago, he returned and established a blockade. Sampson arrived June 1 and assumed command.

While the location of Cervera's fleet was unknown, much uneasiness was felt for the safety of the Oregon, which left the State of Washington before the war was declared and was making the long journey around the Horn. She had been last heard from at Bahia, Brazil, May 9, and it was feared that she might encounter the whole Spanish fleet, but she turned 

THE BATTLESHIP 

"OREGON " up safely off the Florida coast on the 24th ready for service after a memorable voyage of fourteen thousand miles. This long voyage was a dramatic proof of the pressing need of a canal through the isthmus. 

It was now decided to conduct a military campaign also in Cuba. The two hundred thousand volunteers who had responded to the call of the president in May had been kept in camps in different parts of the country. The regular infantry and cavalry, together with several volunteer regiments, had been assem- The Santiago campaign

bled at Tampa and organized as the Fifth Army Corps. The equipment and provisioning of these large bodies of men were wholly inadequate. The sanitation of the camps was bad, and dysentery, malaria, and typhoid fever soon made their appearance. The inefficiency of the War Department under 

Secretary Alger became painfully evident when the Fifth Army Corps was sent to Santiago. 

The expedition was placed under the command of Major- General William R. Shafter, who was physically unfit for military service and unable to leave his tent during the most critical period of the campaign. The force, which sailed from Tampa June 14, consisted of 815 officers and 16,072 enlisted men, regulars with the exception of the Seventyfirst New York, the Second Massachusetts, and the First 

Volunteer Cavalry of "Rough Riders," organized by Leonard

Wood and Theodore Roosevelt. With great difficulty, owing to the failure to provide wharves and launches, the army landed at Daiquirí, a few miles east of the entrance to Santiago Bay. The next day General Lawton advanced and seized Siboney, and on June 24 General Wheeler with Young's brigade defeated a Spanish force at Las Guásimas. During the next week the troops suffered badly from the heavy rains, poor rations, and lack of camp supplies.

attack was given, and the infantry division charged up the hill in the face of a hot fire and captured the blockhouse, while the cavalry division drove the Spaniards from the trenches on the right. For two days more the Spaniards kept up a constant fire from the trenches nearer Santiago.

During the entire fighting the 

American losses were 145 killed, 914 wounded, and 72 missing.

The Spaniards thought the capture of Santiago merely a question of a few days, though the Americans were by no means confident of an early conclusion of the campaign. In fact, Shafter was thinking of withdrawing his army to a safer and more sanitary position. Cervera finally decided, however, to go out and face destruction rather than to remain in Santiago Bay and surrender the fleet with the fall of the city. 

On Sunday morning, July 3, while Admiral Sampson was temporarily absent from the squadron, engaged in a conference with General Shafter, the smokestacks of the enemy's ships were sighted slowly steaming toward the narrow mouth of the bay. As the American ships with one accord closed in on them, Cervera's flagship turned west, followed by the other members of the fleet. At this point, Commodore 

Schley's flagship, the Brooklyn, suddenly turned out to sea,

making a loop across the course of the Texas, causing the latter to reverse her engines in order to avoid a collision. His object seems to have been to leave the slower Spanish vessels to the fire of the battleships and with the fast cruiser Brooklyn to overtake those in the lead and prevent the escape of a single one. In this running fight the inferiority of the Spanish ships was at once apparent. They were soon pierced by 

American shells and set on fire. One after another ran ashore, the last one being forced by the Brooklyn and Oregon to beach and surrender forty-five miles west of where the fight began. In this remarkable battle there were only two casualties on the American side, one man killed and one wounded, both on the Brooklyn.

Santiago surrendered two weeks after the naval fight. 

General Miles then embarked for Porto Rico with a force of 16,000 men and in a two weeks' campaign overran most of that island with the loss of three killed and forty wounded. A large number of troops had also been sent to the Philippines. Although capture of the war had been undertaken for the liberation of Cuba, the United States did not feel under any obligation to confine its military operations to that island. Having met all the demands of honor, Spain asked the French government, July 18, to authorize the French ambassador at Washington to arrange with President McKinley the preliminary terms of peace.

Accordingly, an agreement was reached with Spain August 12, which put an end to further hostilities. In it Spain agreed to the following demands: first, the immediate evacuation of 

Cuba and the relinquishment of Spanish sovereignty; second, the cession of Porto Rico and one of the Ladrones by way of indemnity; and third, the occupation by the United States of "the city, bay, and harbor of Manila pending the conclusion of a treaty of peace which shall determine the control, disposition, and government of the Philippines." Before

World Politics the news of this protocol reached the Philippines, American troops under General Merritt captured the city of Manila after a formal resistance, the governor-general agreeing not to use his heavy batteries provided Dewey would refrain from shelling the city.

Controver- Two controversies growing out of the war with Spain assumed such importance that they cannot be passed by. 

The first, relating to the conduct of the War Desies growing partment, was the charge made by Major-General Miles, commanding the army, that much of the refrigerated beef furnished the troops was "embalmed beef," preserved by secret chemicals of injurious out of the war

Harris & Ewing character. The commission appointed to investigate the matter made a report which did not fully sustain the charge, but the report was not convincing. In the course of the investigation 

Commissary-General Eagan made such an abusive attack on General Miles that he was sentenced by a court-martial to dismissal for conduct unbecoming an officer and a gentleman. Some months later the president called for 

Secretary Alger's resignation and Elihu Root of New York was appointed secretary of war.

The other dispute, which lasted for months, was as to whether Sampson or Schley was in command at the battle of Santiago. Finally, at the request of Schley, a naval court of inquiry was appointed in 1901 to investigate charges of ineffi-

ciency and cowardice. The court expressed the opinion that his conduct prior to the battle of Santiago had been characterized by "vacillation, dilatoriness, and lack of enterprise." 

Admiral Dewey, a member of the court, differed from his colleagues, however, and declared that at the battle of Santiago Schley "was in absolute command and is entitled to the credit due to such commanding officer for the glorious victory which resulted in the total destruction of the Spanish ships." 

This made matters worse than ever. President Roosevelt, when appealed to, declared that Sampson was technically in command, but that after the battle began not a ship took orders from either Sampson or Schley. "It was a captains' fight." 

The peace commissioners met at Paris October 1. An entire month was taken up with the Cuban question, the Spanish commissioners striving in vain to saddle The treaty the Cuban debt either on the United States or on of peace the people of Cuba. The discussion over the Philippines occupied most of the next month. When President McKinley appointed the American commissioners he had not fully made up his mind on this important question. His first intention seems to have been to retain the bay and city of Manila as a naval base, and probably the whole of Luzon. Public sentiment in the United States in favor of acquiring the whole group made rapid headway, and after an extended trip through the South and West, during which he sounded opinion on this question, the president instructed the commissioners to demand the entire group. The commissioners were later authorized to offer $20,000,000 for the cession, and the offer was accepted. On other points the United States secured what had been demanded in the protocol, and the treaty was signed December 10, 1898.

For the first time the United States was seeking control of a well-populated distant territory without regard to the wishes of the inhabitants. The treaty caused an earnest debate in

World Politics the Senate. Senator Hoar declared that the proposal to acquire and govern the Philippine Islands was in violation of the Declaration of Independence, the Constitution, and the whole spirit of American institutions. The treaty could not be ratified without the aid of Democrats and the result was in doubt until Bryan went to Washington and advised his friends to vote for ratification, saying that the status of the Philippines could be determined in the next presidential campaign. The outbreak of hostilities between the Filipinos and the American troops occupying Manila put an end to the debate, and on February 6, 1899, the treaty was ratified. 

The United States government now had to face an additional burden, that of governing 7,500,000 Orientals of alien The Philippine insurrection speech and race, 600,000 of whom were Mohammedan Moros or members of wild pagan tribes. 

The civilized part of the population were members of the Roman Catholic Church, but for years there had been widespread opposition to the domination of the friars, who controlled most of the land, and there had recently been an insurrection which threatened the authority of the Spanish government which upheld the friars. 

This revolt had been led by a young Filipino named Aguinaldo, who had left the islands a few months before the beginning of the Spanish war. Shortly after the battle of 

Manila Bay, Dewey sent one of his ships to Hongkong to bring Aguinaldo and his staff over to assist in operations against Manila. When the city surrendered, Aguinaldo and his forces were not allowed to enter, and were forced to remain outside the American lines. This situation caused strained relations, and when it became evident that the United States had no intention of recognizing a Filipino republic, hostilities began. 

On the night of February 4, 1899, some of Aguinaldo's men approached the American lines without making known their intentions and were fired upon. The conflict soon be-

came general and an insurrection against American control rapidly spread through the islands. As the Americans extended their lines out from Manila the main body of insurgents retired northward to the great plain of central Luzon. As the time of the volunteers who had enlisted for the Spanish war was up, operations were delayed until new troops could arrive. By autumn General Otis had over 30,000 men under his command and in October the forward movement began. The Filipinos were able to check only temporarily the advancing columns of Generals Mac- Arthur, Lawton, and Wheaton, and by the middle of November they were driven from the plain of central Luzon and scattered among the mountains. 

The troops also brought to an end open resistance in the other main islands, but the Filipinos resorted to guerrilla warfare. For the next two years the struggle was 

Two years waged by the Filipinos with great cruelty, and our of guerrilla troops soon learned to retaliate in kind. warfare The American commanders were very anxious to capture Aguinaldo. Finally, in February, 1901, his hiding place was revealed through letters intercepted by Lieutenant J. D. 

Taylor, and General Funston with a party of Macabebe scouts disguised as insurgents succeeded in capturing him. 

Yet surprisingly enough, the capture of Aguinaldo had very little effect on the insurrection, which dragged on for another year and was finally suppressed only after the Americans adopted a rigid concentration policy, confining the friendly inhabitants in the insurrectionary districts to the towns occupied by the troops and treating all others as enemies. lishment of

Another commission headed by Judge William H. Taft of

Ohio was sent out the following year for the purpose of helping to organize civil government. On July 4, 1901, the civil powers hitherto exercised by the military governor were by the direction of the president vested in the head of the commission, and Judge Taft was inaugurated as the first civil governor. A little later three native Filipinos were added to the commission. 

Congress provided a permanent government for the islands by act of July 1, 1902. The action of the president in appointing the commission and in creating the office of civil governor was approved and made permanent. The inhabitants of the islands were declared to be "citizens of the Philippine Islands, and as such entitled to the protection of the United States," and certain provisions of the Constitution of the United States guaranteeing life, liberty, and property were extended to the Filipinos. The act further provided for the ultimate creation of a legislative assembly, with the Philippine Commission as the upper house. Such an assembly was organized in 1907. On March 24, 1934, President 

Roosevelt signed the bill for Philippine Independence, to be completely effective in ten years. Shortly after, the Filipino voters approved a constitution and elected officers, thus making the Commonwealth of the Philippine Islands a reality. 

The status of depend- encies Questions new to the Constitution and to American experience were raised by the annexation of Porto Rico, Hawaii, and the Philippines. President McKinley took the view that the Constitution and laws of the United States did not apply to newly acquired territory until extended by Congress, and Congress later assumed that in legislating for the new possessions it was not bound by all of the provisions of the Constitution. After two years of popular discussion as to whether "the Constitution followed the flag" the Supreme Court sustained the positions taken by

the president and by Congress. In the famous "Insular 

Cases" five of the nine justices held that the new dependencies were not a part of the United States within the meaning of that clause of the Constitution which requires that all duties shall be uniform throughout the United States. 

In 1900, the Hawaiian Islands were fully incorporated in the United States and given a form of territorial government like that of Arizona and New Mexico. By the Porto Rican act passed about the same time tariff duties were imposed on commerce between that island and the United States for a period of two years. The form of government prescribed for 

Porto Rico was of the same general kind as that provided for the Philippines. Most of the real power was placed in the hand of a governor and executive council appointed by the president with the consent of the Senate. 

During the war with Spain China seemed on the point of being partitioned out among the powers of Europe. In 

November, 1897, Germany established herself

The threat- tion of China at Kiaochow; in March, 1898, Russia procured ened partifrom China a lease of Port Arthur; and a little later England secured Weihaiwei. In addition to cessions of territory these powers acquired extensive concessions for the construction of railways and exclusive mining privileges in their respective "spheres of influence," in utter disregard of 

China's treaty obligations to other nations.

The partition of China was well under way when the Philippine Islands came within the grasp of the United States, and the possibility of their affording a naval base for the protection of American rights in China undoubtedly influenced President 

McKinley in coming to the decision to retain them.

Since China traded more with the United States than with any other country except Great Britain, our government did not relish the idea of being excluded from the The open- Chinese market. John Hay, the secretary of state, door policy with the backing of England and Japan made a clever diplo-

World Politics matic move to check the aggressions of Russia and Germany. 

In a note of September 6, 1899, addressed to the principal European powers and Japan on the subject of the "open door" in China, he requested each power to make a formal declaration to the effect, (1) that it would not interfere with the vested interests of other powers in its sphere of influence, (2) that the existing Chinese tariff should continue in force and be collected by Chinese officials, and (3) that foreigners should not be discriminated against in the matter of port dues and railroad rates.

As it was expected, England and Japan agreed to this policy, but the other powers, though professing in a general way their adherence to the principle, avoided making a formal declaration in the sense requested by Secretary Hay. The move was not wholly successful, but it came at an opportune time and had a good effect. Later, however, Hay had to ask permission of Russia to send American consuls into Manchuria, which we regarded as Chinese territory. 

A strong antiforeign sentiment grew up in China with the attempt to exploit the country, and an organization formed 

The Boxer movement in China ostensibly for the practice of athletics and known as the Society of Boxers began an indiscriminate attack on foreigners. The movement was secretly encouraged by the empress dowager and in many cases imperial troops united with the Boxers. Numbers of foreigners were murdered, and by May, 1900, the foreign legations were endangered. About June 1 three hundred and fifty guards from foreign vessels succeeded in getting through to Peking (now Peiping), but the larger detachments which followed a few days later were defeated and driven back. 

While on his way to the foreign office on June 20 the Baron von Ketteler, the German minister, was murdered, and from that date until August 14 the legations were closely besieged by a half-disciplined army of Boxers and imperial troops. The foreign powers decided to send an army to Peking to release

their ministers, if alive, or avenge them, if dead. This expedition, in which 2500 American infantry and a troop of cavalry participated, had to fight its way slowly to the Chinese capital, which it reached August 14, rescuing the diplomats and missionaries, who had with difficulty held back their assailants by fortifying themselves in the British legation.

The powers involved compelled the Chinese government to put to death guilty officials and to pay an indemnity of over $300,000,000. The portion assigned to the United States, $24,000,000, was found to be greatly in excess of the claims for injuries sustained, and over half of it was returned by the United States to China. The Chinese government showed its gratitude by setting this sum aside as a fund for the education of Chinese students in America. 

The United States has always been a world power in the sense that it has been the great exponent of civil liberty and a stanch upholder of legality in international A new era in relations, but the events of 1898 brought the American American government into direct contact with diplomacy some of the complicated problems of world politics. The acquisition of the Philippines, the dispatch of troops to China, and the appointment of delegates to the Hague Conference of 1899 caused serious misgivings in the minds of those wedded to the old order.

However, when the American delegates signed the treaty establishing the Hague court of arbitration, they included a formal reservation to the effect that it would not require the United States to depart from its traditional policy in regard to questions that were European on the one hand or purely American on the other. An active participation in international affairs did not lead to any weakening of the Monroe Doctrine. In fact, that principle of our foreign policy has been more frequently and broadly asserted since the Spanish 

War than ever before.

World Politics of 1900 When the campaign of 1900 opened, it was generally believed that the main issue would be the so-called Republican The election imperialism, which had aroused strong opposition. 

The Republican convention met in Philadelphia, nominated McKinley and Roosevelt, and indorsed all that the Republican administration had done. The Democratic convention, which met at Kansas City, declared imperialism to be the paramount issue, but it nominated Bryan for the presidency and reaffirmed the faith of the party in the free coinage of silver at the ratio of 16 to 1. Bryan was also nominated by the fusion wing of the Populist party and by the Silver Republicans.

McKinley's second campaign was again cleverly conducted by Mark Hanna, who took the "full dinner-pail" as an emblem of "McKinley prosperity." The president remained at home and took little part in the canvass, while Bryan pursued his familiar method of traveling over the country and personally addressing hundreds of thousands of voters.

But his record as a speech-maker was rivaled in this campaign by Theodore Roosevelt, who was determined not to be submerged by the vice-presidential nomination which had been forced upon him against his will. He made a tour through the northern and western states, attracting large crowds and creating enthusiasm by his aggressive manner of handling political issues. The campaign was, however, less exciting than that of 1896. Many Republicans were opposed to imperialism and lukewarm in their support of McKinley, while many Democrats refrained from voting for Bryan on account of their opposition to the free coinage of silver.

McKinley carried all of the northern and most of the western states and had a majority of 137 votes in the electoral college. 

Death of McKinley and succes- sion of

Roosevelt On September 6, 1901, while attending the 

Pan-American Exposition at Buffalo, President

McKinley was shot by an anarchist, and died on the 14th of

the same month, the third president of the United States to fall by the hand of an assassin. He had enjoyed great popularity as president and his death was universally regretted.

Of all the presidents, Theodore Roosevelt, who was thus unexpectedly called to the presidency, was the most energetic and aggressive. In spite of his declaration on taking the oath of office that he would "continue absolutely unbroken the policy of President McKinley," his attitude from the first was that of aggressive leadership, and during the next three years he broke many of the precedents of our political history. 

Probably no other man in American public life has ever succeeded in keeping himself so constantly before the people, either in cartoon and caricature or in photographs and sketches in the papers and magazines. His popularity soon became the despair and confusion of the Republican machine and of the Democrats alike. He had the enthusiasm and idealism of the reformer combined with unusual political astuteness, and whatever people might think of his policies, his handling of public questions never failed to provoke discussion, which is the life of democracy. CHAPTER XXXIII RELATIONS WITH LATIN AMERICA SINCE THE SPANISH 

WAR American occupation of Cuba

WHEN Congress demanded the withdrawal of Spain from Cuba in 1898, it was with the declaration that "The United States hereby disclaims any disposition or intention to exercise sovereignty, jurisdiction or control over said island except for the pacification thereof, and asserts its determination, when that is accomplished, to leave the government and control of the island with its people." Never has a pledge made by a nation under such circumstances been more faithfully carried out. 

The American military occupation of Cuba was a model of its kind. General Leonard Wood, the military governor, and his associates found things in utter confusion in most parts of the island. They established order, relieved distress, organized hospitals and charitable institutions, undertook extensive public works, reorganized the public school system, and put Havana, Santiago, and other cities in firstclass sanitary condition. The discovery, by Major Walter 

Reed, a surgeon in the United States army, and his coworkers, of the fact that yellow fever is transmitted by the bite of a mosquito is regarded as one of the great achievements of modern medical science. This discovery was tested in 

Havana, with the result that the city was rendered free from yellow fever for the first time in one hundred and forty years.

Meanwhile a constitutional convention, summoned by General Wood, adopted a constitution modeled after that of the 

United States. 660

The future relations of Cuba with the United States were not defined in the new constitution. Nevertheless, the 

United States had no intention of withdrawing from the island until a definite understanding on this vital point was reached.

In order to clear up the uncertainty and to make known its wishes, Congress inserted in the army appropriation bill of March 2, 1901, a provision, known as the Platt The Platt 

Amendment, directing the president to leave Amendment the control of the island to its people as soon as a government should be established under a constitution which guaranteed (1) that the government of Cuba would never make any treaty impairing the independence of the island, (2) that it would never contract any debt which could not be met by the ordinary revenues, (3) that the United States should have the right to intervene for the protection of Cuban independence and the maintenance of a stable government, (4) that the acts of the military government during the period of American occupation should be ratified, (5) that the government of Cuba would continue to carry out the measures adopted for the sanitation of the cities, and (6) that the United States should be granted naval stations in Cuba. 

The Cuban authorities finally agreed to these provisions and they were added as an appendix to the Cuban constitution and later were also embodied in a treaty with the United States. The Platt Amendment was drafted by Secretary 

Root shortly before the close of McKinley's administration and carefully considered by the cabinet before being imposed upon Cuba. Cuba thus became an American protectorate. 

On May 20, 1902, Tomás Estrada Palma was inaugurated as first president of Cuba and General Wood handed over the government of the island to him. No under- The Cuban standing was reached before the withdrawal of republic American troops on the subject of commercial relations be-

World Politics tween Cuba and the United States. It was of vital importance to the Cubans to have their sugar, the principal product of the island, admitted to the American market on special terms. Otherwise it could not compete with the bounty-fed beet sugar of Europe, or with the sugar of Porto

Rico and Hawaii, now admitted free. 

A CUBAN SUGAR MILL 

For two years Congress was urged by Roosevelt to make a reciprocity agreement admitting Cuban sugar at a reduced rate, but his efforts to do justice to Cuba were thwarted for two years by the beet-sugar interests of the Northwest and the cane-sugar growers of Louisiana. The cause of 

Cuban reciprocity was delayed rather than helped by the active support of the American Sugar Refining Company,

known as the "Sugar Trust," which wanted raw sugar as cheap as possible and therefore favored the president's policy. 

In December, 1903, a reciprocity treaty was put into effect, and trade with the United States rapidly increased. 

But the Cubans had not learned the primary lesson of democracy submission to the will of the majority. After the reëlection of President Palma in 1906, a serious insurrection began with the object of overthrowing the government. 

The United States finally had to send troops to Cuba and proclaim a provisional government. The second period of 

American occupation lasted a little over two years; then the control of the government was again restored to the people of the island with the warning from President Roosevelt that it was "absolutely out of the question that the island should continue independent" if the "insurrectionary habit" should become "confirmed." 

The Monroe test The Monroe Doctrine was again applied in the Venezuela episode of December, 1902. Germany, England, and

Italy had joined in blockading the coast of Venezuela for the purpose of forcing the govern- Doctrine ment of President Castro to pay interest on put to the bonds and other debts due to their subjects.

Through the mediation of the American minister, Herbert W. Bowen, Venezuela agreed to submit the claims to arbitration, and this proposal was accepted by England and Italy. 

Germany, however, refused to arbitrate until President 

Roosevelt threatened to send the entire Atlantic fleet, which had been collected at Porto Rico under Admiral Dewey, to Venezuela to prevent any further action by the German navy. As soon as Germany was convinced that the United

States would fight to maintain the Monroe Doctrine, she agreed to arbitrate, being influenced, no doubt, by the fact that England was satisfied with the recognition of her claims and showed no desire to push matters further.

World Politics 

President Roosevelt's experience in the Venezuelan affair led him to the conclusion that, if the United States wished 

The bigto prevent European intervention in Latin-Amerstick policy ican states, it must make those states behave themselves. Roosevelt announced his new policy in his message of December 6, 1904, in these words: "Any country whose people conduct themselves well can count upon our hearty friendship. If a nation shows that it knows how to act with reasonable efficiency and decency in social and political matters, if it keeps order and pays its obligations, it need fear no interference from the United States. 

Chronic wrongdoing, or an impotence which results in a general loosening of the ties of civilized society, may in America, as elsewhere, ultimately require intervention by some civilized nation, and, in the western hemisphere, the adherence of the United States to the Monroe Doctrine may force the United States, however reluctantly, in flagrant cases of such wrongdoing or impotence to the exercise of an international police power." This announcement of what became popularly known as the "big-stick" policy raised a storm of criticism and ridicule both at home and abroad, but the president was about to give the world an example of its practical application.

JOHN HAY 

The Panama Canal was beyond all other issues the storm center of Roosevelt's first administration. The voyage of the 

Oregon during the war with Spain impressed upon The Haythe American people, as nothing else could, the Pauncefote importance of an isthmian canal from a naval treaty, 1901 point of view. When President McKinley applied himself to the question, at the close of the war, his first task was to secure a modification of the Clayton-Bulwer treaty. Lord 

Pauncefote, the British ambassador, met Secretary Hay halfway in his negotiations, and a first treaty signed February 5, 1900, authorized the United States to construct and assume the management of the canal, either directly or through a company. The canal was to be neutralized and rules were adopted which were substantially the same

World Politics as those of the Constantinople Convention governing the Suez Canal. This treaty was so amended by the United States 

Senate as to render it unacceptable to the British government. 

The next year President Roosevelt submitted to the Senate a second treaty, which was ratified December 16, 1901. The new Hay-Pauncefote treaty abrogated in express terms the Clayton-Bulwer convention and provided that the United States might construct a canal under its direct auspices to be under its exclusive management. The canal was to remain neutral, but under the sole guarantee of the United States with power to police it, and the clause of the first draft forbidding fortifications was omitted. 

The choice of a canal route

With the right to build the canal established, the next question was the choice of a route. American engineers had almost all favored the Nicaragua route, and a commission headed by Admiral John G. Walker, after a series of investigations covering two years and costing over $1,000,000, reported November 16, 1901, in favor of that route. On January 9, 1902, the Hepburn Bill providing for the construction of a canal through Nicaragua passed the House by the almost unanimous vote of 308 to 2. 

The proposal of the Nicaragua route had created a crisis in the affairs of the New Panama Canal Company of France, whose property and interests on the isthmus, which it estimated at $109,000,000, would be worthless unless it could sell out to the United States. Early in January the French company made an offer by cable to sell at $40,000,000, whereupon the Walker commission revised its report and recommended to the president the Panama route instead of that through Nicaragua.

Instead of passing the Hepburn Bill, therefore, the Senate adopted the Spooner amendment, which directed the president to acquire the rights and property of the Panama Canal Company at a cost not exceeding $40,000,000, to acquire from the Republic of Colombia the right of way through

Panama; and to construct a canal as soon as these rights were acquired. However, should the president be unable to secure a satisfactory title to the property of the French company and the necessary right of way from Colombia "within a reasonable time and upon reasonable terms," then he was instructed to secure a right of way through Nicaragua and to proceed to build a canal at that point.

The Spooner amendment was adopted by the House, Attorney-General Knox reported that the French company could give a clear title, and on January 22, 1903, The Panama 

Secretary Hay signed with Herran, the Co- revolution lombian representative in Washington, a treaty by which the United States agreed to pay Colombia $10,000,000 cash and an annuity of $250,000 for the lease of a strip of land six miles wide across the isthmus. This treaty was ratified by the United States Senate, but rejected by the Colombian 

Senate, by unanimous vote. This rejection tended to force

Several years later Roosevelt, in a public speech, said: "If I had followed traditional conservative methods I should have submitted a dignified state paper of probably two hundred pages to the Congress and the debate would be going on yet, but I took the Canal zone and let Congress debate, and while the debate goes on the canal does also." The 

Panama episode created strained relations with Colombia and made a bad impression throughout Latin America. 

The United States has since been eyed with suspicion by its weaker southern neighbors. The construction of the canal

World Politics was finally placed in the hands of General Goethals and a corps of army engineers, and it was opened to commerce August 15, 1914, though it was not entirely completed at that time and traffic was afterward interrupted by landslides.

Colombia naturally felt much aggrieved at the loss of Panama and the Canal Zone, which she considered her greatest asset. In order to appease her, Secretary Root proposed an indirect payment of $2,500,000, on condition that she recognize the Republic of Panama. This paltry sum was indignantly declined. The Taft administration made a more liberal offer, but this also was rejected, and Colombia demanded that her claims be submitted to arbitration. The 

Wilson administration signed a treaty agreeing to pay Colombia $25,000,000, but ex-President Roosevelt denounced it as blackmail and the Senate delayed action. Finally, shortly after the beginning of Harding's administration, the treaty was ratified with minor changes. 

Porfirio Díaz, who had been president of Mexico since 1884, was forced to retire in May, 1911, and Francisco Ma- Mexican dero, the leader of the revolt, was elected presiquestion dent. His efforts to improve the condition of the native race aroused factional opposition, and on February 18, 1913, he was seized and imprisoned as the result of a conspiracy formed by one of his generals, Victoriano Huerta, who forthwith proclaimed himself dictator. Four days later

Madero was murdered while in the custody of Huerta's troops. 

Henry Lane Wilson, the American ambassador, promptly urged his government to recognize Huerta, but President Taft, whose term was rapidly drawing to a close, took no action and left the question to his successor. 

The murder of Madero, who was rather popular, caused numerous insurrections, which Huerta was unable to suppress. President Wilson refused to recognize him, and demanded his elimination from the presidential contest. This

action made Huerta deaf to advice from Washington and utterly indifferent to the destruction of American life and property. cruz Many Mexican revolutions were financed by American capitalists who had large investments in mines, rubber plantations, oil wells, and other enterprises. The The occupa- 

American ambassador was a partisan of Huerta, tion of Veraso that the Department of State could not rely upon information derived from him and had to recall him at a critical moment. Meanwhile the financial interests which had backed the Huerta revolution were clamoring for his recognition, but President Wilson paid no heed to their demands or criticisms and continued to pursue his "policy of watchful waiting." 

On April 20, 1914, the president asked Congress for authority to employ the armed forces of the United States in demanding redress for the arbitrary arrest of American marines at Tampico. The next day Admiral Fletcher was ordered to seize the customhouse at Veracruz. This he did after a sharp fight with Huerta's troops in which 19 

Americans were killed and 70 wounded. The American chargé d'affaires, Nelson O'Shaughnessy, was at once handed his passports, and all diplomatic relations between the 

United States and Mexico were severed.

Argentina, Brazil, and Chile tendered their good offices within a few days for a peaceful settlement of the conflict, and President Wilson promptly accepted their Recognition mediation. The resulting conference, which con- of Carranza vened at Niagara, May 20, was not successful in its immediate object, but it resulted in the elimination of Huerta, who resigned July 15, 1914. On August 20 General Venustiano

Carranza, head of one of the revolutionary factions, assumed control of affairs at the capital, but his authority was disputed by General Francisco Villa, another insurrectionary chief. On Carranza's promise to respect the lives and prop-

World Politics erty of American citizens the United States forces were withdrawn from Veracruz in November, 1914.

OBREGÓN AND VILLA 

Wilson recognized the government of Carranza, who now controlled three fourths of the territory of Mexico, as the de facto government of the republic. As a result of this action Villa began a series of attacks on American citizens and raids across the border, which in March, 1916, compelled the president to send a punitive expedition into Mexico in search of Villa, and later to dispatch most of the regular army and large bodies of militia to the border. The fact should not be overlooked that the rapid advance of the United States in the Caribbean Sea during the past two decades had created violent opposition and alarm in certain parts of Latin America. As a result of the Spanish War the United States acquired Porto Rico and a protectorate over Cuba; a little later President Roosevelt seized the Canal Zone from Colombia and established financial supervision over Santo Domingo; and at the time of the Mexican crisis 

American marines occupied Haiti and Nicaragua. It was widely believed in Latin America that the United States had converted the Monroe Doctrine from a protective policy into an excuse to cloak imperialistic aggression. Another step in

Caribbean expansion was taken in 1917, when the Danish 

West Indies were purchased.

This steady expansion caused every move in the Mexican situation to be viewed with suspicion. The understanding which had existed for some years between the three leading Latin-American states, Argentina, Brazil, and Chile, generally referred to as the A B C powers, was believed to have been formed for the purpose of checking the encroachments of the United States.

In accepting the mediation of the A B C powers in Mexico and later asking their advice, President Wilson took a long step toward overcoming the resentment and alarm created by Roosevelt's aggressive action in seizing Panama and waving the big stick over our southern neighbors. As a result of President Wilson's policy, our relations with Latin America became much better than they had been for a generation,

 put President Wilson's Pan-American policy to a severe test. In announcing that relations with 

Germany were broken, he expressed the hope Latin Amerthat other neutral governments would follow the ica and the same course, probably having in mind our Latin- World War American neighbors. His expectations were not fully realized. Thirteen Latin-American states severed relations with 

Germany, and of these only eight eventually declared war. 

Seven remained neutral, including the important states of 

Argentina, Chile, Colombia, and Mexico. Brazil was the only one of the larger states that entered the war. German influence was strong in some of these countries, especially in Mexico, which, though proclaiming its neutrality, became a hot-bed of German intrigue.

Of the thirteen that severed relations with Germany, eleven sent representatives to the peace conference and signed the Treaty of Versailles. All of these except Ecuador ratified the treaty and thus became members of the League

World Politics of Nations. Most of the remaining states joined the League at the first opportunity. Eighteen Latin-American countries in all became members of the League, and their delegates have taken an active part in its work. 

For several years Brazil was a member of the 

Latin America and the 

League of

Nations Council and she has contributed two judges to the World Court. A Chilean was elected president of the third Assembly and a Cuban president of the fourth. Cuba has also contributed a distinguished judge to the World Court.

The refusal of the United States Senate to ratify the Covenant of the League, and the emphasis placed on the Monroe Doctrine as the main reason for not doing so, The Monroe

Doctrine and caused much uneasiness in Latin America and the League tended to confirm the fear that the United States was reserving the Monroe Doctrine as an instrument of American imperialism. Under the Monroe Doctrine the 

United States might object to the League's undertaking to settle a dispute between two of its Latin-American members. In fact, when Panama and Costa Rica were on the point of going to war over a boundary dispute in 1921 and the secretary of the League sent them a cable reminding them of their obligation to submit the dispute to mediation, Secretary Hughes promptly intervened and insisted that the dispute be referred to the United States. A little later the famous Tacna-Arica dispute between Chile and Peru, which might very well have gone to the League or the World Court, was referred to the president of the United States. General Pershing was sent down to

Tacna and Arica to hold a plebiscite, but his efforts were unsuccessful. Though the League has so far shown no desire to assume jurisdiction over American questions, there may arise at any time a case which will require League action, and there seems no valid reason why such a case should not be referred to the League or the World Court.

 brought about a great change in our relations with the rest of the world, as well as with Latin America. 

Before the war the United States was a debtor Foreign nation. We had borrowed money in Europe, loans and where interest rates were low, to develop our vast resources, to build railroads, and to establish huge industries. To-day the situation is just the reverse. The 

United States has become the world's greatest creditor nation. Our government loaned ten billions of dollars to the governments of Europe for war and postwar purposes, and since the war Americans have been making private loans and investments abroad at the rate of over a billion dollars a year. 

This tremendous stake in foreign countries is certain to have far-reaching effects on our foreign policy. America The

Latin America is one of our most important fields of foreign investment. At the beginning of the present century the total American investment in this area was less Investments than three hundred millions, and this was mainly in Latin in Cuba and Mexico. By 1928 it amounted to the enormous sum of five and a quarter billions, and more than three billions of this was in the Caribbean area. overflow of American capital into this region is undoubtedly destined to continue. The flow of European capital to South 

America was interrupted by the World War, but it is beginning to recover lost ground in the larger states, especially 

Argentina, Brazil, and Chile. The Caribbean area has, however, been marked off for American development or exploitation, as the case may be. On the one hand, we have one of the most highly industrialized nations in the world, with surplus manufactures to sell and surplus capital to invest abroad; on the other hand, we have the agricultural and unstable countries of Mexico, Central America, and the Caribbean, which need American capital and American enterprise to develop their vast natural resources. Investors in backward countries usually look to their own governments

World Politics for protection. American investors in the Caribbean area have repeatedly called upon the government of the United States to protect their investments and the government has usually responded, sometimes too quickly.

The oil dispute with Mexico

When Mexico adopted a new constitution in 1917 affecting adversely the holdings of American oil companies, the United States promptly protested. A long controversy followed, and upon several occasions the two countries were on the verge of war. 

Mexico offered to submit the dispute to arbitration, but President Coolidge declared that the American people did not believe in the confiscation of private property and that consequently there was nothing to arbitrate. Relations became strained almost to the breaking point, but fortunately the Senate took a different view of the situation. 

On January 25, 1927, a resolution urging the president to submit the dispute to arbitration was unanimously adopted. 

As the result of this action on the part of the Senate and a widespread popular opposition to the president's Mexican policy, he accepted the resignation of Ambassador Sheffield and sent Dwight Morrow to Mexico to take his place. The conciliatory policy of the new ambassador soon bore fruit and the Mexican crisis was tided over. As soon as the threat of coercion was withdrawn, the Supreme Court of Mexico rendered a decision favorable in part to the oil companies. United States marines in Nicaragua

In 1911 President Taft had sent a body of marines to Nicaragua for the purpose of protecting the lives and property of Americans against disorders resulting from revolution. From that date to 1925 a small force of one hundred marines was maintained at the capital of Nicaragua, and a warship was stationed at Corinto, to afford them aid, if necessary. In 1925 the marines were withdrawn, but another revolution broke out the next year, and seven thousand marines and a number of warships were sent to Nicaragua.

The United States actively espoused the cause of the Conservative Díaz, who favored the United States, against the Liberal Dr. Sacasa, who claimed to be the consti- The Stimson tutional president, and we undertook at first to re- agreement strain and later to suppress the armed forces of the Liberals. 

In the spring of 1927 President Coolidge sent Henry L. Stimson, a former secretary of war, to Nicaragua for the purpose of reconciling the contending factions. the commander of the Liberals, finally agreed to disband his forces and surrender their arms on the promise that the 

United States would supervise the next presidential election and insure a fair vote. 

General Sandino, one of the

Liberal commanders, refused to accept these terms and took to the jungle with his followers. For a year he kept up an amazing fight against overwhelming odds. Num-

In the election, which was held under the supervision of the marines November 4, 1928, the Liberals won by a substantial majority and General Moncada was elected president. 

Criticism of the presi- Nicaraguan policy dent's 

President Coolidge's Nicaraguan policy was the subject of vehement criticism both in Congress and throughout the country. It was also violently denounced in the press of Latin America. Senator

World Politics 

Borah and other members of the president's party, as well as many Democrats, declared that the use of the marines had gone far beyond the protection of American life and property, and that the president was in fact waging war, contrary to the Constitution, without the consent of Congress. 

In Latin America it was charged that the president had deliberately intervened in the internal affairs of an independent nation for the purpose of furthering the imperialistic designs of the United States. 

At the sixth Pan-American 

Conference, held at Havana in January, 1928, the subject of intervention led to earnest and prolonged discussion. 

Charles E. Hughes, head of the delegation of the 

United States, made a clever defense of American policy. 

He undertook to draw a distinction between intervention and interposition, claiming that the action of the 

United States in Nicaragua 

CHARLES EVANS HUGHES 

was mere interposition for the protection of life and property and not intervention in the domestic affairs of the country. 

The dread

The rapid advance of the United States in the Caribbean area during the past quarter of a century has naturally aroused the fears of our southern neighbors. of American It is not likely that the United States will forimperialism mally annex any more territory in that region, but what these states fear is economic imperialism and the control of their governments in the interest of American capitalists. Foreign investors sometimes exercise undue influence over the policies of their governments. The de-

velopment of Latin America by American capital and enterprise can be carried on to the advantage of both parties, provided the government pursues a wise policy and does not permit exploitation to degenerate into what amounts to conquest. The adoption of a sound Latin-American policy is probably the most important and urgent question in the whole range of our foreign relations. Herbert Hoover seemed to recognize this fact when, immediately after his election to the presidency, he made an extended good-will tour through South America. However, it was not until toward the end of his term that the American marines were finally withdrawn from Nicaragua on January 3, 1933.
