CHAPTER XXXIV PROGRESSIVE POLITICS 

EVER since the war with Spain, foreign affairs have occupied more and more of the attention of our government. Nevertheless, during Roosevelt's first administration, first ad- there was a notable revival of interest in the ministration problems of labor and capital which the war with Roosevelt's

Spain had temporarily overshadowed. 

Roosevelt was an independent progressive in politics, and was always doing the unexpected. He astonished the country by intervening in a great coal strike; he alarmed the capitalistic classes by beginning an attack on trusts; he frightened the politicians by pushing the investigation of public land and postal frauds, which resulted in the criminal conviction of two United States senators; he offended the 

South by inviting Booker Washington, the Negro head of Tuskegee Institute, to his table at the White House and by appointing a Negro postmistress in Mississippi and a Negro collector at Charleston; these and many other acts were bitterly assailed, but public sentiment in the main sustained the president. Roosevelt introduced a new epoch in American politics. His appeal was always to the moral sense of the average American, and he showed little regard for special interests, classes, or sections. 

In foreign affairs, in spite of his occasional belligerent attitude, Roosevelt was a stanch advocate of international The Hague arbitration. The United States had taken a prominent part in establishing the Permanent Court of Arbitration at The Hague, but the court had not been called upon to adjudicate any question until the United Court 680

Progressive Politics 681 States, on Roosevelt's initiative, brought the first case before it in 1902. The case was against Mexico and involved the ownership of a trust fund raised by the Jesuits in the seventeenth century for the conversion of the California Indians. 

After the purchase of Upper California by the United States in 1848, the Mexican government as administrator of the fund refused to pay any part of it to the Catholic bishops of that state. The Hague Court decided that they were entitled to their share. To President Roosevelt was also due the submission of the second case to the Hague Court, for he suggested that tribunal as the proper body to decide an important question arising out of the intervention of Germany, England, and Italy in Venezuela in 1902. 

It was not compulsory for members to submit their disputes to the Hague Court, but in 1903 and 1904 a number of European powers concluded treaties binding each other to arbitrate disputes which involved points of law or the interpretation of treaties. Secretary Hay made such treaties with France, England, Germany, and other powers, but the Senate amended them so as to prevent the president from submitting any dispute to the court without its consent. 

President Roosevelt regarded this action as nullifying the compulsory feature of the treaties and did not refer them back to the other powers. The second Hague peace conference of 1907, which codified important sections of international law, was proposed by President Roosevelt, though the call was actually issued by the Czar of Russia, who had also called the first conference.

Another dispute with Canada came up in 1897 over the Alaskan boundary, when the discovery of gold in the Klondike made that region important. The shortest and The Alaskan quickest route to the gold-bearing region was by boundary trails leading up from Dyea and Skagway on the dispute headwaters of Lynn Canal. These insignificant points soon became important places and were claimed by the Cana-

World Politics dians. The claim was a new one, for the official maps issued by the Canadian government over a long period of years showed the places in dispute to be on the American side of the boundary. 

Despite his liking for arbitration, President Roosevelt was not willing to take that means of determining rights which seemed so clear. He agreed, however, to submit the question to a commission composed of three Americans, two Canadians, and Lord Alverstone, chief justice of England. If 

Lord Alverstone decided with the American members of the commission, the United States would win; if he decided with the Canadians, there would be no decision. He did decide with the Americans and the two Canadians dissented. 

The deep-water outlets were all awarded to the United States, though the boundary line was drawn nearer to the coast than the Americans had claimed. The Canadians were much disappointed and it was charged that Lord Alverstone had sacrificed their interests in order to advance the British policy of friendly relations with the United States. of 1904 The Republican leaders never liked President Roosevelt, but they did not dare to nominate any one else, as he was The election immensely popular with the rank and file of the party. After the death of Senator Hanna in

February, 1904, all opposition stopped, and the Republican national convention, which met at Chicago in June, unanimously nominated Roosevelt. The party platform again contained nothing new, but demanded a vote of confidence upon Roosevelt's record.

David B. Hill and the advocates of a return to "safe and sane democracy" dominated the Democratic convention which met at St. Louis in July. The nomination was tendered to Judge Alton B. Parker, of New York. World Politics as a result of charges made during the campaign. This committee, of which Charles E. Many municipal governments were overturned by the force of the reform movement. Exposure became the order of the day, and the public eagerly read the daily papers, weeklies, and monthlies, which devoted their columns to laying bare corruption and fraud in state and national government or in business enterprises which affected the public. While many of the newspapers and magazines were perfectly sincere in their efforts to bring about reform, others were less scrupulous, and their attacks were prompted purely by sensationalism or by hope of blackmail. President Roosevelt tried to check the more radical agitators by comparing them to Bunyan's man with the muck-rake, and the term "muckrakers" soon came into general use.

The indiscriminate attack on big business and "predatory wealth" undoubtedly caused the banks to tighten credit and led to financial disturbances in the fall of 1907, The crisis of 1907 which threatened to become very serious. A number of banks failed and the financial leaders became alarmed. They claimed that the president's attack on trusts, the passage of restrictive laws, and the enforcement of the pure food regulations had brought about the panic. 

Their attack on the Roosevelt policies merely convinced the people that the president was right and that it was time for big business to be brought under public control. 

The settlement of the Russo-Japanese War was the biggest

Progressive Politics 685 War diplomatic achievement of Roosevelt's second administration. As has been stated, Secretary Hay's efforts to maintain the open door in Manchuria were not en- The Russotirely successful. Russia continued her encroach- Japanese ments there, and in 1904 Japan finally delivered an ultimatum which resulted in war. Throughout the remarkable contest that followed the sympathies of the American people were mainly with Japan. Japan won a series of brilliant naval and military victories, but her resources were finally at the point of exhaustion, and at the suggestion of the Japanese emperor, as we now know, President Roosevelt intervened and urged the two powers to bring the war to a close. 

Each side accepted the president's mediation and the peace commissioners of Russia and Japan met at Portsmouth, New Hampshire, in the summer of 1905. The 

Japanese commissioners had been instructed to demand a large war indemnity. This Russia refused to grant, and, following President Roosevelt's advice, the Japanese negotiators gave up the demand. When the terms of the treaty of Portsmouth reached Tokyo, there were rioting in the streets and great indignation against the government for making what were considered unfavorable terms. The commissioners put all the blame on President Roosevelt, so that public opinion in Japan was thoroughly aroused against the United States.

The anti-Japanese agitation in California, which about this time, as described before, led to an attempt in San Francisco to establish separate schools for Japanese children, added fuel to the flames. Japanese resentment of the school incident was so great that the press of both the Orient and America was filled with predictions of war, and there were frequent reports that Japan was preparing to seize the 

Philippines. President Roosevelt was so greatly annoyed at the attitude of Japan that, in the autumn of 1907, he decided

World Politics to send a great American fleet on a voyage around the world and to have it visit Japanese waters. The fleet left Hampton Roads in 1907, made the long voyage around the Horn and across the Pacific, was received with marked courtesy by the Japanese government, and returned to America without any untoward incident.

President Taft had to fill more vacancies on the Supreme Bench in one term than any other president. He appointed

Though his appointees were all men of high character and professional standing, it was felt in some quarters that they would tend to take a conservative view of the great social and economic questions that were agitating the country. 

The prosecution of the trusts under the Sherman law, which had been renewed under Roosevelt, was continued under Taft. In the Trans-Missouri Case in 1897 the Supreme 

Court had decided in effect that all combinations in restraint of trade, whether reasonable or unreasonable, were contrary to the Sherman Antitrust Act. In 1911, in cases against the Standard Oil Company and the American Tobacco Company, the court ordered the dissolution of these combinations, but Chief Justice White in delivering the opinion of the court said that by restraint the statute meant “undue” restraint of trade, thus introducing the element of "reasonableness." These companies were dissolved, but big business was reassured by the new doctrine laid down by the court.

Soon after he took office, President Wilson called Congress to meet in extra session in April, 1913, and appeared before the two houses to urge in person the re- Constructive vision of the tariff, one of the planks of the party legislation platform. Anti- Japanese legislation in California

Difficult problems in foreign affairs faced President Wilson from the very first. His administration had scarcely begun when the anti-Japanese agitation again broke out in California. This time the state legislature wanted to deny to aliens who were ineligible to American citizenship the right to acquire agricultural land. The president sent Secretary of

State Bryan to California to urge moderation upon the legislators, but his mission was not wholly successful. The act as finally passed safeguarded the treaty rights of aliens, but as the Japanese treaty did not specifically cover the point in question, the Japanese were left without redress. 

The Panama tolls question

The dispute with England over the Panama Tolls Act was another question which the president had to handle with care. The British government claimed that the exemption of American vessels engaged in the coastwise trade from the payment of tolls was a violation of the Hay-Pauncefote treaty. The president believed that the British interpretation of the treaty was correct, and he had the difficult task of persuading Congress to repeal the exemption clause of the Tolls Act. This was done June 15, 1914, on the eve of the World War. (For Topical References, see page 773.)

CHAPTER XXXV THE WORLD WAR 

war WHEN the World War broke out in August, 1914, President Wilson issued the usual proclamation of neutrality. No one foresaw how the vital interests of the United The States would soon be involved. The first task was European to bring home the thousands of American tourists who were stranded in all parts of Europe by the sudden mobilization of armies. The unexpected stop in international trade, particularly the export of cotton, caused a general business depression, and the country was saved from a serious financial panic only by the measures of the Treasury Department under the new Federal Reserve Act. 

Before long business not only revived but boomed, when American firms began taking orders from England, France, and Russia for large supplies of arms and munitions of war. 

The sale of contraband was perfectly permissible under international law, but as the British navy controlled the seas, the Germans and Austrians were unable to get munitions from America, and denounced the trade in war supplies as one-sided and unneutral. Meanwhile the German invasion of Belgium had shocked the moral sense of the world and enlisted the sympathies of the great majority of Americans on the side of Germany's enemies. 

Direct trade in contraband extended during the World War a term which was widely with the Central Powers

Interfer- was easily stopped by the British navy. But the trade continued through the ports of Italy, Hol- ence with land, and the Scandinavian countries. In order neutral to stop this indirect trade in contraband the British government inaugurated, in the early stages of the trade 697

World Politics war, a policy of search and detention which imposed great hardships on neutral commerce. On the plea that large freight ships could not be properly searched at sea, they were taken into port, sometimes far out of their course, and detained for indefinite periods.

Another new assumption made by Great Britain was that contraband articles shipped to neutral countries adjacent to Germany and Austria were intended for the latter, unless proof to the contrary was shown. The United States protested vigorously against this policy, but the force of its protest was weakened by the fact that during the Civil War it had itself pursued much the same policy toward goods shipped by neutrals to Nassau, Havana, Matamoros, and other ports adjacent to the Confederacy. 

Although no German battle fleet was on the high seas, her mine-layers soon began scattering floating mines in the path Submarine of British commerce. On November 3, 1914, the warfare

British government, as an act of retaliation, declared the North Sea a "war area" and warned neutral vessels not to enter without receiving sailing directions from the British squadron. Under pressure of what amounted to a blockade, the German naval authorities decided to use their large submarine flotilla, which had not been able to inflict any serious damage on the British navy, in an attack on British commerce. On February 4, 1915, Germany proclaimed a war zone around the British Isles, including the whole of the Channel, declared that all enemy merchant vessels encountered in these waters after the 18th would be destroyed, even though it might not be possible to save the passengers and crews, and added the warning that neutral vessels could not always be prevented from suffering from the attacks intended for enemy ships. The United States at once protested against this decree and warned the German government that it would be held to a "strict accountability" for the destruction of American ships or the loss of American lives. The

submarine policy was nevertheless inaugurated on the date set, and within a few weeks two Standard Oil tankers bearing the American flag had been torpedoed and several American citizens had lost their lives. Before the American government had decided what action to take, the whole world was startled by the deliberate torpedoing, without warning, off the southern point of Ireland, of the great English liner

The United States accepted this assurance as an abandonment of the submarine policy announced on February 4, 1915, and for some months there was a marked cessation of submarine activity. German States

In vain the German and Austrian governments tried to persuade the American government that the trade in munitions of war was unneutral. After the German propagandists had failed to get Congress to forbid activities in the export of munitions, they formed a conspiracy the United to break up the trade by criminal methods. 

Numerous explosions occurred in munitions plants, destroying many lives and millions of dollars' worth of property, and bombs were placed in a number of ships that carried supplies to the Allies. The Austrian ambassador, Dr. Dumba, lent active support to a plan to cripple the munitions plants by

World Politics widespread strikes among employees. As a result, his recall was demanded by Secretary Lansing in September, 1915. 

These conspiracies were not confined to Germans, for many naturalized Americans of German origin were involved in plots against the government of the United States. The term "hyphenated" American was applied to them and soon came into general use. In his annual message of December, 1915, President Wilson publicly denounced those men who had "poured the poison of disloyalty into the very arteries of our national life," and urged Congress to enact laws which would enable him to handle the situation. The German propagandists resolved to defeat Wilson for reëlection at all hazards and thus made the "hyphen" a distinct issue in 

American politics. The National

Defense Act 

The Congress which met in December, 1915, passed a number of measures of far-reaching importance. The National Defense Act provided for a regular army of 186,000 officers and men, a federalized National Guard of over 400,000 men, a system of civilian training camps for reserve officers, and the establishment of plants for the production of munitions. The naval program, enacted in August, 1916, went far beyond the original proposals of the secretary of the navy. It provided for an expenditure of over $500,000,000 for new construction within the next three years.

To meet these increased expenditures Congress passed in September a new revenue act which doubled the normal income tax and raised the surtax on large incomes to a maxi- Other im- mum of 13% on incomes of $2,000,000 or over; portant acts the taxes on inheritances, on munitions, and on corporations were also increased. 

Congress also passed other important measures during the same session: the act establishing a Shipping Board, the act extending more autonomy to the Filipinos and promising them ultimate independence, the act excluding from interstate

commerce products made by child labor, and the usual river and harbor bill involving millions of needless expenditure. Renomina- Wilson

Governor Hiram John- California son, who had been the Progressive candidate for vice president four years before, was elected to the United States Senate on the Republican ticket by nearly 300,000 votes over his Democratic opponent, while Wilson carried the state by a majority of 3800 over Hughes. The latter lost the state by identifying himself during his visit to California with the leaders of the reactionary faction of the Republican party, thus alienating the former Progressives. President

During the summer and fall of 1916 the European armies were at a deadlock on the western front, but in the East the Germans made a successful drive Wilson's into Roumania and captured the capital city, peace move

Bucharest. On December 12 Germany, acting for herself and

World Politics her allies, announced to the Entente Powers her willingness "to enter forthwith upon negotiations for peace." No terms were proposed and she let it be known that none would be announced until the offer to negotiate was accepted. President 

Wilson transmitted the German note to England and France without comment. On the 18th, however, he addressed an identical note to the governments of all the nations at war requesting them to state definitely the terms on which they would deem it possible to make peace. 

England and France at first regarded this note as meddling and as indorsing, in a way, the German proposal, but when the replies of the warring nations were made public, the first impressions of the president's move were modified. The 

Central Powers merely replied that they were ready to enter into negotiations and tried to fasten on their enemies the responsibility for continuing the war. The Entente Powers, on the other hand, stated fairly definitely the measure of reparation and restitution and the guarantees which they considered indispensable conditions of a permanent peace. 

The announcement of unrestricted submarine warfare after Febru- 

All the while Germany was constructing ocean-going submarines of a new and larger type and it was rumored that she intended to resume unrestricted submarine warfare on a still larger scale. On January 22, 1917, President Wilson delivered a notable address to the Senate, in which he outlined the principles on which the United States would be willing to enter into a league for peace, hoping that thus the war might be brought to a close. Instead of heeding these proposals, the German government nine days later handed Secretary Lansing a formal note announcing a new zone around Great Britain and France and warning him that all ships, those of neutrals included, found within the zone after February 1 would be sunk. ary 1, 1917 The war passions of the country were inflamed to a degree which had not been felt since the sinking of the Lusitania.

All eyes turned to the president, who, on February 3, appeared before Congress and in calm and measured tones announced that the Count von Bernstorff had that day been given his passports and that all diplomatic intercourse with Germany was at an end. This announcement was enthusiastically received by the great majority of the American people, who were soon in a state of hourly expectation of the "overt act" which the president said he would await before recommending further action.

Ship- 

The debate on the promerchant ships During the next three weeks two American ships were sunk by German submarines, but without loss of life. owners were, however, unwilling to send their vessels to sea, and American commerce was tied up in American ports under a practical embargo posal to arm laid by decree of the German government. Under these circumstances President Wilson again appeared before Congress, February 26, and asked for authority to arm American merchantmen, in order that they might protect themselves in passing through the danger zone. 

The House voted overwhelmingly for the resolution giving the president the necessary authority, but under the rules of the Senate permitting unlimited debate, a small group of eleven senators, who were opposed to war, led by La Follette of Wisconsin and Vardaman of Mississippi, prevented voting, and Congress adjourned March 4 without action by the Senate.

A storm of popular condemnation was hurled upon these senators, which was inflamed by the disclosure on March 1 of the famous “Zimmermann note," in which the The German foreign secretary invited Mexico to unite Zimmerwith Germany and Japan in a war against the mann note United States. The dispatch was addressed to the German minister in Mexico and was transmitted through the Count von Bernstorff at Washington, but was intercepted and came into the possession of the Department of State. Both

Mexico and Japan indignantly denied any knowledge of the note or any possibility of their being led into such a scheme.

its rules, placing reasonable limits on debate and making it impossible for a small group to delay action indefinitely. 

Before the session convened, however, the president had been forced to the conclusion that the arming of merchantmen would not deal effectively with the submarine terror. On April 2 he appeared before a joint session of the two houses and urged "that the 

Congress declare the recent course of the German government to be in fact nothing less than war against the government and people of the United States; that it formally 

The president's war address

accept the status of belligerent which has thus been thrust upon it; and that it take immediate steps not only to put the country in a more thorough state of defense, but also to exert all its power and employ all its resources to bring the government of the German Empire to terms and end the war." declared

After a four days' discussion over the form the resolution should take, Congress finally declared on April 6 that a state of war existed between Germany and the United War with States. A few days later the vast sum of seven Germany billion dollars was appropriated for carrying on the war. This was the largest single appropriation made by any legislative body in the history of the world. Nearly half of it was to be used in loans to foreign governments. The foreign loan was to be raised by bond issues, but the president urged that our own expenditures for the war be raised as far as possible by increased taxation. 

By the sale of bonds and War Savings Stamps and by increased taxation the vast sums needed for carrying on the war and for loans to the Allies were raised. Five The Liberty loans were floated during the war. The first Loans four were known as the Liberty Loans and the last as the Victory Loan. All of them were largely oversubscribed, the number of subscribers increasing from 4,000,000 in the case of the first loan to nearly 22,000,000 in the fourth. The total amount raised by these loans was $18,500,000,000. 

The successive Liberty Loan "drives" were organized very skillfully under the general direction of Secretary McAdoo and were accompanied by great patriotic demonstrations. 

Although the bonds were regarded as a safe investment, they bore a low rate of interest and soon fell below par, but the people continued to subscribe as cheerfully as ever, their prime object being to win the war. 

The new war taxation was put into law by the War Revenue Act of October 3, 1917. It increased greatly the tax on in-

World Politics comes, levied an excess profits tax on corporations and partnerships, increased the internal revenue taxes and import duties, and raised the postal rates. Few wars have been financed so largely by taxation. The draft

The problem of raising a huge army now confronted the government. An act of June 3, 1916, had authorized an army of 175,000 men and made important changes selective in the organization of the army and the War Department. As soon as war was declared, Congress began the consideration of a bill to organize an army on the old principle of voluntary enlistment. The president considered this measure inadequate, and urged a selective draft. Though this interference with pending legislation was resented in the House, the military committee finally adopted the president's plan. After passing the House the bill was amended in the Senate to authorize the president to raise four divisions by voluntary enlistment. It was finally signed by the president May 18, 1917, but he let it be known that he did not intend to avail himself of the amendment.

This act authorized the president to increase the regular army to 287,000 by voluntary enlistment, to take into the service of the United States all members of the National Guard (state militia), and to raise immediately by selective draft a force of 500,000 and later, if necessary, successive drafts of 500,000. To this end he was authorized to enroll all men between the ages of 21 and 31. By June 5 over 

9,500,000 men were enrolled. As the men registered in their several districts, each was given a serial number by the local board.

A country-wide draft was soon put into operation, starting in Washington July 20. When a certain number was drawn the men having that number in the nearly 5000 districts throughout the country were called to the service, unless coming within one of the exempt classes. The law provided

for the exemption of state and federal officials, ministers of religion, members of churches forbidding resort to arms, munition workers and others engaged in industries essential to the war, persons mentally and physically unfit, and men on whom others were dependent for support. There were special exemption boards to administer this part of the act. Contrary to the predictions of its opponents, the selective draft

Never in all history was carried out with amazing success. had so many men been called into military service with so little friction or complaint.

The War Department was faced with a serious problem in training enough new officers for the vast army that was to be sent to France. To meet this need, training Training camps for officers were opened in June at Fort camps for

Myer, Plattsburg, and other points, where candidates for commissions went through three months of intensive training and were then sent to the great cantonments to train the men who were called to the colors. officers Sixteen

World Politics cantonments, each a city in itself, with water-supply and sewer systems, barracks, hospitals, laundries, storehouses, and post offices, were constructed during the summer in different parts of the country. Munitions and supplies

To equip such a huge army was a herculean task. The whole character of warfare had changed so completely in the three years' fighting on the western front that we were novices at the game. Trench warfare had developed every diabolical device that the ingenuity of man could devise, and science had devoted its great resources, to an extent never before imagined, to the destruction of human life. The airplane, gas, the machine gun, and the tank were the most novel factors in the struggle, and the new army had to be trained to meet the conditions of modern warfare.

The Naval Appropriation Act of 1916 had provided for a number of new destroyers, and as the likelihood of war increased, work on these vessels had been pushed to the utmost. As it was generally supposed at first that our part would be mainly that of combating the German submarines, the navy rushed the construction of destroyers and a new type of motorboat known as the submarine chaser. Hundreds of private yachts and other vessels were purchased by the government to be used as submarine chasers, transports, and hospital ships, and for various other purposes. The 

German ships interned in our ports, over 100 in number, were seized by the government, overhauled and repaired, and put into service.

A number of regular destroyers were sent to European waters on the declaration of war to coöperate with the British 

Extent of and French navies. They were placed under operations command of Rear-Admiral W. S. Sims. In 

December, 1917, a division of six battleships under Rear- 

Admiral Hugh Rodman joined the British Grand Fleet in the

North Sea and served with it until the surrender of the

German High Seas Fleet at Scapa Flow, Orkney Islands, November 21, 1918.

Our naval operations outside the North Sea covered the Atlantic, the Mediterranean, and the Pacific. Our task was to patrol the high seas, to hunt and destroy German submarines, and to convoy troop and cargo ships to Europe. 

American destroyers became very expert in the use of the depth bomb, the most important means of combating the submarine 

ANTISUBMARINE GUN AND DEPTH BOMBS ON THE U. S. S. "RAMBLER' 

developed during the war. The plan of establishing a mine barrage across the North Sea, from the Orkney Islands to the coast of Norway, was suggested and in large part carried out by our navy. The magnificent record of the navy is further attested by the fact that not a single American troop ship was lost on its way to Europe. 

In August, 1916, Congress had provided for the creation of a Council of National Defense, composed of the secretaries of war, navy, interior, agriculture, commerce, and labor. In accordance with the provisions of the act, an advisory commission was later organized with Daniel Willard, president

World Politics of the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad, as chairman. The work of this body became of very great importance in developing and mobilizing the resources of the nation for war. Through various subordinate committees it brought into the service of the gov- Mobili- zation of national resources ernment many of the leading financiers, business men, and technical experts of the country. It also suggested to the states the organization of state councils, which rendered invaluable service in directing the war activities of every description. Through these organizations thousands of citizens gave their services to the government without cost. 

Herbert C. Hoover was made chairman of a committee on food supply created by the Council of National Defense in The food adminis- tration order to conserve and increase the food supply for our home needs, our armies abroad, and our allies. 

He was later made Food Administrator and given very extensive powers under an act of Congress. A general campaign to increase production of all food products and to economize in the use of food was carried on under the slogan "Food will win the war."

The fuel tion 

Harry A. Garfield, president of Williams College, was appointed Fuel Administrator in August, 1917, and given extensive powers to regulate the price and disadministra- tribution of coal. The large consumption of coal in the various war industries and the increased demands of shipping, together with the wage demands of the miners and the difficulties of transportation, rendered prices uncertain and interrupted the normal distribution to private homes until by December there was a serious coal shortage, and in January the situation grew desperate. Factories had to be closed for a time in order that private homes might be supplied and the bunkers of ships, loaded with supplies for our troops abroad, be filled.

The railroads were so inefficient in handling coal and carrying troops and supplies to the ports that in December

the president, who had been authorized by Congress, took control of them. William G. McAdoo, secretary of the treasury, was appointed Director-General of Railroads Government with full power to operate them. Government operation of management proved expensive, but the object railroads was to move coal, military supplies, and troops, and not to make money for the roads. The government had to make good the losses, but the centralized railroad administration was necessary to win the war.

Germany, and on March 3, 1918, the treaty of Brest Litovsk was concluded. Russia had deserted her allies, and MB Germany was free to concentrate all her efforts on the western front. Even before the peace with Russia the Germans had shifted many divisions from the eastern to the western front. On

The artillery fire north of Reims did the French no harm, as they had learned of the attack beforehand from a prisoner and had withdrawn from the first-line trenches. Between 

Reims and Château-Thierry the Germans met with greater success and succeeded in crossing the Marne at several points. 

On the right of our Third Division the French gave way and advised our commander to do the same, but General Dickman refused to accept this advice and announced that he was

World Politics going to counterattack. "On this occasion," General 

Pershing says, "a single regiment of the Third Division wrote one of the most brilliant pages in our military annals. It prevented the crossing at certain points on its front, while on either flank the Germans who had gained a footing pressed forward. Our men, firing in three directions, met the German attacks with counter-attacks at critical points and succeeded in throwing two German divisions into complete confusion, capturing 600 prisoners." 

Foch takes the offen- sive On the third day the German offensive had exhausted itself, its farthest advance being only four miles. Meanwhile Foch had been preparing a counterstroke, and on July 18 he drove a wedge into the west side of the Marne salient south of Soissons. In this attack the place of honor was assigned to the First and Second American Divisions and the First French Moroccan Division. 

Without any preliminary bombardment these three divisions broke through the enemy's lines and advanced to the heights south of Soissons, cutting important communications leading into the salient. 

The second battle of the Marne was over, and the Germans, quickly realizing their precarious situation, began a general retreat. The turning point in the world war had been reached. From July 18 to November 11 the Germans were steadily driven eastward, and Foch delivered blow after blow with quickness and precision. On the west side of the Marne salient, south of the Second Division, the Fourth, Twenty- 

Sixth, and Forty-Second (Rainbow Division) were engaged under Major-General Hunter Liggett, while east of Château- Thierry the Third, Thirty-Second, and parts of the Twenty- 

Eighth did valiant service under Major-General Robert Lee 

Bullard. By August 6 the French and American divisions had reached the Vesle, and the Marne salient was completely wiped out. On that day Foch was given a marshal's baton, the highest military distinction a French soldier can attain.

About 500,000 men, including some French, comprised the First American Army, which now assembled under the personal command of Pershing. On the salient east of Saint- 

Mihiel was deployed the Fourth Corps, commanded by 

Major-General Joseph T. Dickman; on their right stretched the First Corps, commanded by Major-General Liggett; and on the west face of the salient the Fifth Corps was stationed under Major-General George H. Cameron. Three small French divisions were opposite the tip of the salient, and were to occupy Saint-Mihiel when the Germans retired. 

The attack was planned for September 12 along the entire south face of the salient. After a heavy bombardment the 

Americans went over the top and dashed forward. Foreseeing what was in store for them, the Germans had already begun to retire from the tip of the salient. In their rapid advance, the Americans captured 16,000 German prisoners, 443 guns, and large stores of supplies. American casualties totaled less than 7000. By the end of the second day all objectives had been reached, and during the next two days the line was advanced still farther. The Saint-Mihiel action showed the superiority of American troops over their adversaries in open warfare, and did more than any form of propaganda to break down the German morale.

In comparing the Meuse-Argonne campaign with the battle of the Wilderness, fought May 5-12, 1864, in the Civil War, Colonel Ayres makes the following interesting remarks:

The United States Turns the Tide 735 "Both were fought over a terrain covered with tangled woods and underbrush. The Wilderness was regarded as a long battle, marked by slow progress, against obstinate resistance, with very heavy casualties. Here the similarity énds. The Meuse-Argonne lasted six times as long as the 

Battle of the Wilderness. Twelve times as many American troops were engaged as were on the Union side. They used in the action ten times as many guns and fired about one hundred times as many rounds of artillery ammunition. 

The actual weight of the ammunition fired was greater than that used by the Union forces during the entire Civil War. 

Casualties were perhaps four times as heavy as among the Northern troops in the Battle of the Wilderness. The Battle of the Meuse-Argonne was beyond compare the greatest ever fought by American troops, and there have been few, if any, greater battles in the history of the world." 

The Meuse-Argonne fight lasted 47 days, and 1,200,000 American troops were engaged. The losses were very heavy, but without them the war would have lasted American another year, entailing untold suffering throughout losses the belligerent countries and probably costing the lives of fully as many soldiers in the end.

The moral leadership of the United

In replying to the speeches of Lloyd George and President Wilson, both the German chancellor and the Austro-Hungarian minister of foreign affairs professed their willingness to accede to certain points, but others they utterly rejected. From now on President Wilson became more and more the spokesman of the States Allies. In fact, the moral leadership of the United 

States played as great a part in winning the war as the initiative and dash of our soldiers. In a speech at Baltimore on April 6, the anniversary of our entrance into the war, and in another at Mount Vernon on July 4, the president further defined "the ends for which the associated peoples of the world are fighting," and finally, on September 27 in New York, he declared: "We are all agreed that there can be no peace obtained by any kind of bargain or compromise with the governments of the Central Empires. . . . They have convinced us that they are without honor and do not intend justice. They observe no covenants, accept no principle but force and their own interest. We cannot come to terms with them. They have made it impossible. The German people must by this time be fully aware that we cannot accept the word of those who forced this war upon us. We do not think the same thoughts or speak the same language of agreement." 

This and other utterances of the president made it plain that sweeping constitutional changes in Germany, if not the complete overthrow of the Kaiser, must precede further negotiations for peace.

World Politics 

On October 4 the German ministry resigned and Prince

Maximilian of Baden became chancellor. He immediately dispatched a note to Washington requesting Presi- Germany dent Wilson to take steps for the calling of a peace conference, and stating that the German government "accepts as a basis for peace negotiations the program laid down by the President of the United States in his message to Congress of January 8, 1918, and in his later pronouncements, especially in his address of September 27." 

After Prince Maximilian gave assurances to President Wilson that he was speaking for the German people and that the ministry was now dependent upon the Reichstag instead of upon the emperor, the president finally expressed his willingness to take up with the associated governments the question of an armistice. Meanwhile, Germany's allies were rapidly deserting her. On September 30 Bulgaria surrendered. A month later, October 31, Turkey signed an armistice, and finally, on November 4, the rapidly disintegrating Austro-Hungarian monarchy did the same. 

Flight of the Kaiser and accept- ance of the armistice

The Inter-allied Council drew up the terms of the armistice at Versailles on November 5, and the document was delivered to the Germans on the 7th. They were given 

72 hours to accept or reject it. The terms were very severe. Germany was required immediately to evacuate Belgium, France, Alsace-Lorraine, and Luxemburg; to withdraw her armies from the entire territory on the left bank of the Rhine and from Russia, Austria-Hungary, Roumania, and Turkey; she was to surrender enormous quantities of heavy artillery and airplanes, all her submarines, and most of her battleships, cruisers, and destroyers.

These terms indicated the utter collapse of the mighty German war machine, and the decision was awaited with intense interest. On the 9th the Kaiser abdicated, and on the following day he ignominiously fled across the border into Holland.

The president's illness Opposition to the treaty was not confined to the Senate. 

In the country at large some favored the League of Nations but objected to the terms imposed on Germany; others did not object to a severe peace, but thought that membership in the League of Nations would mean the sacrifice of our freedom of action. The main object of attack was Article 10, which guaranteed the territorial integrity of the members of the League. It was declared that this provision would embroil the United States in the internal affairs of Europe, and that it deprived Congress of its constitutional right to declare war. 

In an attempt to overcome this widespread opposition and explain the treaty, the president went on an extended tour of the country. He visited the Pacific coast states and addressed large audiences, who received him with enthusiasm.

CHAPTER XXXVII POSTWAR REACTIONS 

THE Republican victory in 1920 was complete. Harding's plurality was about seven millions. There was a Republican majority of 150 in the House and 22 in Lack of a the Senate, but neither the president nor the constructive leaders in Congress had a constructive program. program 

The campaign had been based almost exclusively on criticism of Wilson and his policies, and all the dissatisfied elements in the country had voted the Republican ticket.

The president was bewildered by the magnitude of his success, and did not know how to turn his victory to account. 

Large legislative majorities are not easily managed, and in this case the majorities were large enough to be unwieldy. Few congresses in the history of the country have accomplished less in the way of constructive legislation than the sixty-seventh. 

As the president was convinced that the American

Wide World Photos WARREN G. HARDING 

people had repudiated Wilson's foreign policies, he withdrew from all active part in European affairs. During Return to the campaign Harding's position on the League of isolation Nations had been so indefinite that the public did not know 747

World Politics what to expect. Hughes and Hoover, the two most prominent of his cabinet appointees, were known to be in favor of entering the League. The president, however, ignored the 

League entirely, and for some months took no notice of the establishment of the Permanent Court of International Justice provided for in Article 14 of the Covenant, although Elihu Root, a leading Republican, had taken a prominent part in drafting the statute of the court, and John Bassett Moore, the best-known American authority on international law and diplomacy, had been elected a judge. 

Treaty of peace with Germany

As the Senate's refusal to ratify the Treaty of Versailles had left the United States in a technical state of war with Germany, Congress declared the war at an end by a joint resolution, signed by the president July 2, 1921. This resolution undertook to reserve to the United States "all rights, privileges, indemnities, reparations or advantages" to which it was entitled under the terms of the armistice, or by reason of its participation in the war, or which had been stipulated for its benefit in the Treaty of Versailles, or to which it was entitled as one of the Principal Allied and Associated Powers, or to which it was entitled by virtue of any act or acts of Congress. 

On August 25 the commissioner of the United States to Germany signed at Berlin a separate treaty of peace with Germany, reserving in detail the rights referred to in the resolution of Congress. A similar treaty was signed with 

Austria, and the two treaties were ratified by the Senate of the United States, October 18. These treaties produced no immediate results of importance. American troops continued on the Rhine, and there was no apparent increase in trade, which had been carried on before the signing of the treaty with Germany under a system of special licenses. 

Many thought that a tremendous expansion of business would follow the war, and that the United States would need a great merchant marine to carry its products and manufac-

Postwar Reactions 

749 pression tures to all parts of the world. This expectation was not immediately to be realized. The war was followed not only by a slump in idealism, but by a slump in in- Agricultural dustry, in commerce, and in agriculture, with a and indusresulting unemployment that created grave unrest trial deamong the laboring classes. By August, 1921, the Department of Labor reported over 5,000,000 unemployed. The agricultural depression extended to both the wheat and the cotton sections. The crops of 1920, which had been planted at the highest wages known in the history of agriculture, had to be sold at prices lower than any known since the beginning of the World War. The farmers were soon clamoring for special legislation, asserting that existing laws had been framed in the interest of the industrial, financial, and commercial classes. As a result there appeared in Congress for the first time an agricultural bloc, led by Senators Capper of Kansas, Kenyon of Iowa, and La 

Follette of Wisconsin.

The Budget and Accounting Act of 1921 revolutionized the methods of carrying on the business of the government. 

Under the former system of appropriations no at- A national tempt was made either by the president or by Con- budget gress to consider at one time the whole problem of financing the government, or to balance the two sides of the account and see whether a surplus or a deficit would result from the operations of the year. Proposed expenditures bore very little relation to prospective revenues. The estimates submitted by the departments were referred to several different committees, and the reports were embodied in a number of separate appropriation bills. No business corporation would have thought of carrying on its operations in such a haphazard way.

The act of 1921 changed all this. The president is now recognized as the general manager of the government as a business organization. He acts through a special agency

World Politics created by the act known as the Bureau of the Budget. The first director of the bureau was General Charles G. Dawes, an experienced financier and man of action, who successfully put the new system into operation. He resigned July 1, 1922, and was succeeded by General H. M. Lord. 

It does not require a deep study of the events leading up to the World War to explode the fallacy that the way to preserve peace is to prepare for war. Competition in armament inevitably leads to war, and it can lead to nothing else. Yet, after the terrible lessons of the World War, the race for armaments continued

with increased momentum. 

The victorious powers of continental Europe maintained huge armies, while the United

United States. The Anglo- 

Japanese alliance was the main reason for the naval 

Harris & Ewing program of the United States. 

So long as there were only three great navies in the world and two of them united in a defensive alliance, it was considered of vital importance for the United States to safeguard its position as a sea power. The Anglo-Japanese alliance, it is true, was not popular in Canada, Australia, or New Zealand, and at the British Imperial Conference held in London in the summer of 1921, opposition to its renewal was freely expressed. It appeared probable, therefore, that

The committee of the League of Nations on limitation of armament could do nothing, as the United States refused to have anything to do with the League. Presi- The dent Harding showed no intention of making Washington limitation of armament an administration policy.

November 11. As it was useless to propose the limitation of armaments without at the same time removing some of the disputes and rivalries that make armaments necessary, the invitation included in the objects of the conference the discussion of Pacific and Far Eastern questions. In this latter discussion Belgium, the Netherlands, Portugal, and China were invited to participate.

At the Washington Conference, which convened November 12, 1921, the popular demand for open diplomacy was met in a highly dramatic way by Secretary Hughes. The naval 

In his opening speech he presented the American treaty plan for naval reduction to the assembled representatives of the powers, the newspaper correspondents, and the public who filled the galleries. The real work of the conference was, however, carried on by committees, and from the meetings of these committees the press representatives and the public were as a matter of course excluded. The Hughes

World Politics proposals were in brief (1) that all programs for the construction of capital ships be abandoned, (2) that a large number of battleships of older classes be scrapped, and (3) that the allowance of auxiliary craft, such as cruisers, destroyers, submarines, and airplane carriers, be in proportion to the tonnage of capital ships. On the basis of existing strength he proposed that the United States should be allowed 500,000 

THE HEADS OF THE DELEGATIONS TO THE WASHINGTON CONFERENCE 

tons of capital ships, Great Britain 500,000 tons, and Japan 300,000 tons. Japan objected to this 5-5-3 ratio, and it was several weeks before she could be persuaded to accept it. 

When the tonnage allowance for France and Italy was discussed, France came near upsetting the whole program by putting forth a demand for 350,000 tons of capital ships, when 175,000 tons was what the other powers thought she was entitled to. The French delegates were offended at what they considered the dictation of the other powers, and they also wanted more submarines than the ratio proposed by Hughes would have allowed them. The final result was that France accepted the 1.75 ratio, but she refused to agree to any reasonable limits upon submarines, airships,

753 and subsidiary naval craft. Thus an important part of the 

Hughes program failed, and the treaty as finally adopted left the contracting parties free to direct their energies to the comparatively new fields of submarine and aërial warfare.

By the terms of the so-called Four-Power Treaty, the United States, Great Britain, France, and Japan agreed "to respect their rights in relation to their insular possessions and insular dominions in the region of the Pacific Ocean," and in case the said rights should be "threatened by the aggressive action of any other power, the high contracting parties shall communicate with one another fully and frankly in order to

World Politics arrive at an understanding as to the most efficient measures to be taken, jointly or separately, to meet the exigencies of the particular situation." This treaty superseded the Anglo- 

Japanese alliance, which, it was stated, should terminate on the exchange of ratifications. The new treaty was to remain in force for ten years, after which it might be terminated by any of the contracting parties on twelve months' notice. She wished, however, to keep the matter in suspense till the last. Other Chinese matters were disposed of in two treaties, one dealing with the tariff and the other with the open door. In the latter treaty all the powers represented in the conference pledged themselves to respect the sovereignty and independence of China and the principle of the open door.

The coal strike of 1922 In the spring of 1922, the miners in both the anthracite and the bituminous coal fields went on a strike to maintain their wage scale, which the operators proposed to reduce to what they considered a more normal wage. The strike involved over 500,000 union miners, and they were joined by 90,000 men in the nonunion fields of West Virginia and Pennsylvania. In August, an agreement was reached by which the old rate of wages was to continue pending the investigations and report of a commission to be appointed by the president. 

A strike of railroad shopmen July 1 aggravated the coal strike and interfered with the shipment of coal from the non-

Postwar Reactions 755 union fields of the South. The strike of the railroad shopmen was the result of a twelve per cent reduction in wages effective July 1. President Harding called the managers and union heads to a conference at the White House, but without results. Meanwhile, the railroads, which had a considerable surplus of rolling stock, were not so badly crippled as the strikers had expected. On September 23, the men accepted a compromise and returned to work. As compared with earlier strikes, those of 1922 were remarkably free from serious disorders. In September, 1925, another strike occurred in the anthracite mines, but President Coolidge refused to interfere and the public showed little concern, resorting where necessary to the use of soft coal and oil-burners. 

After five months of idleness the men returned to work. 

The Fordney-McCumber Tariff Act, signed by the president September 21, 1922, put into effect the highest duties the country had ever known. No attention was Tariff act paid to the warning of the bankers that the countries of Europe could not pay their debts if the United States put up the rates so high as to exclude European goods. of 1922

Congres- sional elec- tions of 1922

The mid-term elections showed a drift away from the Republicans, when the Republican majority in the House was cut down from 150 to 15, and in the Senate from 22 to 10. In fact, as was shown later, the administration was no longer in control of the Senate, for the farm bloc, headed by Senator La Follette, was greatly strengthened by the accession of several new senators from the states of the Northwest, and now held the balance of power.

The United States had spent during the World War over three billions of dollars in building merchant vessels, at war costs, when waste and extravagance were in- Ship evitable. It was expected that there would be subsidy a great expansion of foreign trade after the proposal war, and that these ships would be in demand for carrying

World Politics our manufactures and farm products abroad. It turned out that after the war there were twice as many ships as were needed, and their operation was seriously handicapped by acts of Congress, designed to protect seamen, which greatly increased costs. There was no sale for the ships that the 

Shipping Board was operating at a loss of $50,000,000 annually.

President Harding favored a large merchant marine, and he believed that the only way of realizing it was through governmental subsidies. On November 21, 1922, he delivered a message to Congress outlining his ship subsidy program. He pointed out that the government aided industry through tariffs, and railroads by land grants. Why not aid shipping? A bill embodying the president's views passed the House, but failed to pass the Senate, much to the president's chagrin. 

The Agricultural 

Credits Act and farm relief The Senate next turned to the consideration of the question of agricultural credits. The farmers were clamoring for relief and complained that the financial institutions of the country were designed to provide credit for industry and commerce, but not for agriculture. The Federal Farm Loan Bank, established by act of Congress in 1916, loaned money on mortgages for long terms, but did not help in the moving and marketing of crops. For short-term credit the farmer was dependent to a large extent on local stores and on dealers in farm products. To provide the relief demanded, Congress passed the Agricultural Credits Act in March, 1923, just before adjournment. This act established twelve banks in the cities already having land banks, to be managed by the officers and directors of the land banks. 

These credit banks are empowered to make loans to livestock companies and various farmers' coöperative associations, for the purpose of enabling them to hold their products until they can be properly marketed.

Postwar Reactions 

757 This measure of relief did not satisfy the farmers, however, and in 1927 Congress passed the McNary-Haugen Bill, which undertook to provide government aid and elaborate machinery for marketing the surplus that has to be exported and sold abroad. President Coolidge vetoed this bill, and farm relief became one of the main issues in the campaign of 1928. Harding bonus bill

Shortly before the end of the session in March, 1923, Congress passed a bonus bill in response to a wide-spread demand from the men who had served overseas during the war and who felt that, in view of the high wages vetoes and war profits made by those who stayed at home, the soldiers were entitled to extra compensation. As both the president and Secretary Mellon were committed to a reduction in taxation, they opposed the bonus bill, which carried such huge appropriations that it would have interfered with their plans for tax reduction. The president accordingly vetoed the bill.

Another bonus bill was introduced in the new Congress in December, 1923, and finally passed in May, 1924. President Coolidge vetoed this bill likewise, but it was immediately enacted into law over his veto.

The problems of enforcing prohibition continued to receive a large amount of attention in government circles and in the press. Bootlegging and smuggling Prohibition continued on a large scale, and in order to put a stop to the activities of the so-called rum fleet engaged in smuggling liquor from foreign countries, there arose a demand that the jurisdiction of the United States be extended beyond the three-mile limit for the purpose of searching and seizing foreign vessels engaged in the traffic. On April 30, 1923, the Supreme Court of the United States delivered a decision by a vote of 7 to 2, declaring that under the Eighteenth Amendment and the Volstead Act American ships could carry liquor outside the three-mile limit, but that no

World Politics ships, American or foreign, could bring liquor within the territorial waters of the United States. The prohibition agents proceeded in accordance with this decision to seize sealed liquors on board foreign vessels in American ports, and the British and other governments protested. 

In an attempt to solve the question, Secretary Hughes proposed to the British government that if it would consent to the search of British ships beyond the three-mile limit, the United States would agree not to disturb liquors brought into American ports under seal for use aboard the ships at sea. The British government at first rejected the offer, but the matter was discussed at the Imperial Conference held at London during the summer of 1923, and views favorable to the American proposition were freely expressed by the overseas dominions. As a result the British government signed a treaty October 31 permitting the United States to seize rum ships within a zone of approximately twelve miles, dependent upon the speed of the vessels concerned. This treaty was duly ratified by the Senate. 

President Harding declared that he would have nothing to do with the League of Nations and that it was a dead issue, but he soon found that absolute isolation from European affairs was impossible. Two months after his inauguration, Secretary Hughes instructed Colonel George Harvey, the new am Inter- national isolation and the system of unofficial observers bassador to Great Britain, to take part as the representative of the president of the United States in the deliberations of the Supreme Council. At the same time the American ambassador to France was instructed to resume his place as "unofficial observer" in the Conference of Ambassadors at Paris, and Roland W. Boyden was instructed to sit again "in an unofficial capacity" on the Reparation Commission. The system of "observers" thus inaugurated was objected to by some as an "involvement" in European affairs, and ridiculed by others as a wholly

Postwar Reactions 759 inadequate means of rendering assistance to Europe or of properly safeguarding the interests of the United States. 

In accord with the observer system, Secretary Hughes refused to send an official representative to the conference at Genoa in April, 1922, but directed Richard Washburn Child, ambassador to Italy, to attend it as a silent observer. At the Lausanne Conference, which met in 

November, 1922, to negotiate a treaty of peace with Turkey, the United States was represented by three observers. American oil interests were concerned in the 

Turkish negotiations, and this time the American observers were not silent. As the United 

States had not been at war with Turkey, but had merely severed diplomatic relations, it did not become a party to the general treaty of

President Coolidge's first annual message, delivered in person at a joint session of the Senate and House of Representatives December 6, 1923, was short and to Coolidge's the point. He still opposed America's joining the first annual 

League of Nations, but favored the World Court. message 

He stated his reasons for refusing to recognize Soviet Russia. He did not favor cancellation of inter-Allied debts, but saw no objection to adjusting them according to the principles adopted in the funding of the British debt. He

World Politics approved Secretary Mellon's plan of tax reduction, and opposed the bonus. He declared it his duty to enforce prohibition. He favored restriction of immigration. He recommended the passage of a law authorizing him to appoint a permanent coal commission. He favored indirect relief for the farmer, but warned against resort to the public treasury. 

The oil scandal The country was favorably impressed by this message and the general opinion prevailed that Coolidge would receive the nomination of his party for president without opposition and that he would be elected. 

Though the Republican party had not accomplished much in the way of constructive legislation, it was felt that Coolidge could not be held responsible for this, and that he should be given a chance. A shocking scandal, however, was brought to light about the middle of January, 1924, when vague rumors, which had been floating around Washington, of fraud and corruption in connection with leases of naval oil reserves, were shown by an investigating committee of the Senate, of which Senator Walsh of Montana was chairman, to be founded upon fact, and to involve members of 

President Harding's cabinet. reserves Although the story of the leases of the naval oil reserves is obscure and complicated in many of the details, it may Naval oil be told in brief as follows. In 1909 President 

Taft withdrew from entry three large areas of oil lands, two in California and one in Wyoming, in order that the navy, which was turning more and more to the use of oil as fuel for battleships, might have a supply at home which it could fall back upon in case of emergency. In 1912 the two California areas were definitely set aside as Naval Oil Reserves Numbers 1 and 2. In 1915 President Wilson set aside for the use of the navy the Wyoming area described officially as Naval Oil Reserve Number 3, but popularly known as the Teapot Dome.

Postwar Reactions 765 President Harding less than three months after his inauguration issued an executive order transferring the control of the oil reserves from the Navy Depart- The leases ment to the Department of the Interior. to Sinclair 

The order was drafted by Albert B. Fall, secreand Doheny tary of the interior, and approved by Edwin Denby, secretary of the navy. Soon after the transfer was made, Secretary Fall proceeded to dispose of the oil. The Teapot

Dome reserve was leased to Harry F. Sinclair, and Naval 

Reserve Number 1 to a company controlled by Edward L. Doheny. The leases were made secretly and without calling for bids, and according to the statement of Secretary Hughes they "were never brought before the Cabinet for its decision."

Doheny stated that he expected to clear $100,000,000 from his lease, and Sinclair's profits were expected to be equally large. Thus were the navy's oil reserves, which had been set aside for an indefinite period to meet some great emergency, shamefully handed over to the exploitation of private corporations.

In addition to these transactions, others were exposed which suggested criminal fraud on the part of Secretary Fall and stupidity on the part of Secretary Denby. Fraud and 

It was discovered that some one had loaned stupidity Secretary Fall $100,000 about the time the leases were signed. He claimed that the loan was made by a personal friend, Edward B. McLean. The latter at first confirmed this statement, but later became alarmed and denied it. 

On January 24 Doheny testified before the Senate committee that he had made a personal loan of $100,000 to Fall and had had the money carried to him in a satchel. About the same time Archie Roosevelt, who had just resigned the vice-presidency of one of Sinclair's companies, testified that Sinclair's confidential secretary had told him that he had paid $68,000 to the foreman of Fall's New Mexico ranch,

World Politics and Sinclair's attorney testified that the latter had loaned 

Fall $25,000 after he resigned from the cabinet. 

Steps taken to cancel the leases and prosecute the guilty

As a result of the investigation Congress passed a joint resolution declaring that the leases "were executed under conditions indicating fraud and corruption," and that the naval reserves should be recovered and "held for the purpose to which they were dedicated." As Attorney-General Daugherty had been intimate with Fall, McLean, Doheny, and Sinclair, and had taken no steps to protect the public interests, the president appointed special counsel to represent the government in the legal proceedings instituted to annul the leases. Fall had resigned from the cabinet in March, 1923. In February, 1924, the Senate passed a resolution calling for Secretary Denby's resignation. The president resented this interference with the executive, but a week later he accepted Denby's resignation. On March 2 the 

Senate voted to investigate the Department of Justice, and before the end of the month the president asked for Daugherty's resignation.

The annulment proceedings encountered the usual delays in the lower courts, but the oil reserves were finally restored to the government in 1927 by decision of the Supreme Court, which declared that the leases were "tainted by fraud." 

Death of Woodrow Wilson

Public attention was temporarily diverted from the oil scandal by the death of ex-President Wilson at his home in 

Washington on Sunday, February 3, 1924. Rarely has the death of a public man excited such emotion and sympathy as were shown when the announcement was flashed throughout the country. Wilson's active public career, covering six brief years from his inauguration in 1913 to his illness in 1919, was short compared with that of most men who have achieved greatness, but it was crowded with momentous events. He was great as president in time of peace, great as the leader of a mighty nation in war,

Postwar Reactions 767 and greater still as the leader of the liberal forces of humanity the world over during the critical years of the war, but history will probably hold him greatest as founder of the 

League of Nations. of 1924

As the campaign of 1924 drew near, the political situation was marked by uncertainty and confusion. Although 

Coolidge's nomination was generally conceded, National he was utterly unable to assert his leadership nominating over his party in Congress. Within a few weeks conventions of the time for the Republican national convention to meet, the Republican Congress and the president were in opposition on almost every important question of public policy. Congress passed a bill increasing Civil War pensions, which the president vetoed; a bonus bill, which he also vetoed, but which was immediately enacted into law over his veto; an immigration bill, to some provisions of which he was strongly opposed, but which he signed; and a revenue bill which was known to be in direct conflict with the views of the president and Secretary Mellon. Meanwhile the

Senate refused to ratify the protocol establishing the World 

Court as advocated by the president and Secretary Hughes.

The Republican national convention met in Cleveland, Ohio. When the first ballot was taken two days later, Calvin Coolidge was nominated with almost no opposition, & few votes being cast for Hiram Johnson and La Follette. 

The nomination for the vice-presidency was offered to 

Charles G. Dawes of Illinois.

The Democratic convention, which met in Madison Square Garden, New York, was marked by a bitter contest between the faction supporting William G. McAdoo of California and the followers of Governor Alfred E. Smith of 

New York. The attempt to deal with the Ku-Klux issue came near disrupting the convention, and the party found it almost equally difficult to agree on a statement of its attitude toward the League of Nations. Finally, after all the

World Politics delegates were utterly exhausted by the wrangling and uproar of the long sessions, John W. Davis, of West Virginia, was nominated on the 103d ballot. To offset the nomination for president of an Eastern conservative, who was described by those opposed to him as a "Wall Street lawyer," the convention then proceeded to nominate for vice-president 

Governor Bryan, of Nebraska, a brother of William Jennings Bryan.

Coolidge was helped by the generally prosperous condition of the country, while Davis was handicapped by the The Repub-factional fight in his party and by a weak and lican victory inconsistent platform. Coolidge was elected by a large majority. His popular vote was 15,718,000, while

Northwest he drew heavily from the Republicans. In the 

Electoral College the vote stood: Coolidge, 382; Davis, 136;

La Follette, 13. The Progressive movement threatened both of the major parties, but the death of La Follette, June 

18, 1925, and that of Senator Ladd four days later deprived the Progressives of two of their ablest leaders.

President Coolidge continued to devote attention to the problems of readjustment to conditions arising out of the war. He continued to follow the "return to nor- Coolidge's second ad- malcy" policy of his predecessor and added to ministration it a policy of preaching economy, which, while not actually reducing public expenditures, undoubtedly held Congress in check and prevented wasteful appropriations. The income tax was further reduced, and progress was made in arranging with European powers the terms on which their debts to the United States were to be adjusted.

The naval program proposed in December, 1927, program of raised an even greater storm of opposition. Early in 1927 the French foreign secretary Briand proposed that France and the United States should sign a treaty renouncing war "as an instrument of policy." Secretary

World Politics 

The "out- lawry of war 

Kellogg saw objections to a treaty of such a character limited to two powers and made the counter proposal that the principal powers of the world be invited to sign the proposed treaty. After a further exchange of notes the text of the Briand-Kellogg treaty was agreed upon and submitted to the other great powers. 

On August 27, 1928, the treaty was signed at Paris by Kellogg, Briand, and the representatives of Great Britain, Germany, Belgium, Italy, Japan, Poland, Czechoslovakia, and all the British overseas dominions. A general invitation was extended to other powers to adhere to the treaty. The belief is widely held that, if it is generally ratified by the powers which have signed it, it will be a great step toward the establishment of world peace. The Senate ratified the treaty in January, 1929, after Senator Borah, chairman of the Committee on Foreign Relations, had explained that it did not affect our right to engage in a defensive war. Coolidge chooses not to run in 1928 In spite of the criticism of President Coolidge's Latin- American and naval policies and in spite of his inability to control Congress, his popularity was immense. 

The legend of the "strong, silent man" had taken hold of the popular imagination. On the other hand many considered that another term for him would be equivalent to a third term, and would upset an unbroken precedent. There seems little doubt, however, that if he had sought a renomination in 1928, he could have had it. There were many surmises as to what his course would be until in the summer of 1927 he made the laconic announcement: "I do not choose to run for president in 

1928." Various interpretations were given to this utterance at the time, but it soon became evident that he would not seek a renomination.
